In terms of Section 70(1) of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act, No. 16 of 2023, the Central Bank 
is required to prepare and publish the Financial Stability Review (FSR) on or before the thirty-first 
day in the month of October of each year.  Fulfilling this obligation, FSR of 2026 encapsulates the 
developments in the financial system, the risks and vulnerabilities identified thereof, and the policy 
measures taken by the Central Bank and other regulatory institutions in addressing such risks during 
the review period, which primarily covers data up to end June 2026. However, more updated selected 
developments are also reported in the publication. Data may include calculations made specially for 
this publication based on information obtained from various sources.
For inquiries, comments and feedback please contact:

XIV
Amidst multiple shocks, Sri Lanka’s financial system remained stable during the first half of 2026, supported 
by the continued economic recovery, sustained adequacy of capital and liquidity buffers across banks and 
Finance Companies (FCs), and improved fiscal performance. While domestic macrofinancial conditions 
remained stable, intensifying uncertainties in the global environment increased the risk of adverse spillovers 
to the domestic economy. Stability during the review period was supported by the continued recovery in 
economic activity, improved fiscal conditions and stronger financial sector performance. These developments 
provided an important cushion against heightened external uncertainties and supported the overall stability of 
the financial system. Nevertheless, the external environment remained challenging. Heightened geopolitical 
tensions, resurgent global inflationary pressures, elevated energy and commodity prices, tighter global financial 
conditions, growing trade fragmentation and increasing climate related risks continued to pose potential spillovers 
to the domestic economy. Sri Lanka remained particularly exposed to adverse external developments, given 
its significant exposure through trade, tourism receipts, workers’ remittances, capital flows, external financing 
conditions and exchange rate dynamics. On the domestic front, credit growth, particularly in household lending 
including vehicle financing and gold backed lending, continued to widen the private sector Credit Gap, signaling 
a potential build-up of systemic vulnerabilities. Moreover, although financial sector exposure to the public 
sector reduced, it remained significant, underscoring the considerable sovereign-financial sector nexus. Rising 
household indebtedness, volatility in collateral values with increased exposure to collateral backed lending, the 
continued rise in real estate prices and inflationary pressures further highlighted emerging risks. In response to 
these developments, the Central Bank increased the overnight policy interest rate in May 2026 and introduced 
macroprudential measures, including Loan-to-Value (LTV) limits on vehicle and gold backed lending, aimed at 
containing the build-up of vulnerabilities within the economy.
Domestic financial markets remained largely stable during the period, with the Financial Stress Index remaining 
at relatively low levels. Financial market conditions were shaped by heightened global uncertainty, domestic 
inflation concerns, and tighter monetary conditions. Equity market performance moderated amid subdued 
investor sentiment, while market liquidity weakened and volatility increased. Yields of Government securities 
increased across maturities during the review period with evolving market expectations and subsequently due 
to monetary policy tightening. Secondary market liquidity remained relatively subdued pointing to limited depth 
and trading activity in the domestic debt market. Meanwhile, foreign investor participation continued to be low 
despite a modest recovery towards the latter part of the reference period. The domestic foreign exchange 
market experienced periods of heightened pressure particularly with the escalation of tensions in the Middle 
East, reflecting increased demand for foreign currency arising from higher import expenditure, rising energy 
prices, and shifts in investor sentiment. These developments contributed to the depreciation of the Sri Lanka 
rupee against the US dollar. Market conditions subsequently improved, supported by policy measures and 
continued inflows from workers’ remittances, tourism, exports and intermittent fall in oil prices. Money market 
activity strengthened during the period, while overall liquidity remained in surplus and interest rates remained 
broadly aligned with the monetary policy stance. Payment and settlement systems continued to demonstrate 
operational resilience, supported by further digitalisation and improvements in settlement infrastructure. The 
continued expansion of digital financial services enhanced efficiency and financial inclusion, albeit increasing 
the financial system’s exposure to cyber, operational, and third party risks. As digital connectivity deepens and 
technology evolves rapidly, ensuring adequate cyber resilience and operational preparedness remains critical 
to safeguarding financial stability.
Executive Summary

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
XV
Financial institutions continued to demonstrate overall resilience during the period under review, supported by 
the recovery in economic activity, stronger profitability and adequate capital and liquidity buffers. The banking 
sector credit expanded significantly amid robust private sector demand, with notable growth in consumption, 
trade, financial services, construction, and offshore-related lending. The decline in the Stage 3 loans ratio along 
with the improvement in the Stage 3 impairment coverage ratio depicted improved resilience of the banking 
sector. However, Stage 2 loans increased during Q2 of 2026, indicating a potential build-up of credit risk among 
borrowers amid elevated credit expansion. While liquidity ratios in the banking sector moderated during the 
review period, they remained well above regulatory thresholds. This decline primarily reflected a shift in asset 
allocation from high quality liquid assets, particularly Government securities, to private sector lending. Meanwhile, 
short term maturity mismatches widened, increasing potential refinancing and liquidity risks within the sector 
under unexpected stress conditions. Further, banking sector profitability continued to improve, although the 
pace of growth moderated somewhat from the levels recorded during the first half of 2025. Despite continued 
buildup of capital, driven by stronger profitability, the banking sector’s capital adequacy ratios declined as the 
growth of risk weighted assets exceeded the pace of capital accumulation. Notwithstanding this moderation, 
capital buffers remained well above regulatory thresholds, providing adequate capacity to absorb potential 
shocks.
FCs sector witnessed a significant credit expansion driven by heightened demand for vehicle financing and 
gold backed lending. Despite the improvement in the Stage 3 loans ratio, the sharp increase in Stage 2 loans 
indicated rising credit risks within the FCs sector. This was partly attributable to the adverse effects of Cyclone 
Ditwah and the Middle East conflict on affected borrowers and underscored the need for continuous monitoring 
of asset quality developments and the potential buildup of sectoral vulnerabilities. Moreover, the impairment 
coverage ratio declined, indicating a deterioration in loss absorption capacity within the sector. While liquidity 
buffers in the FCs sector remained adequate and well above regulatory thresholds, liquidity ratios declined amid 
strong credit expansion. Meanwhile, faster growth in borrowings compared to deposits highlighted the increasing 
interconnectedness between FCs and banks. Profits in the FCs sector continued to increase, supported by 
net interest income, although the rate of profit growth moderated during the first quarter of the financial year 
2026/27. Capital buffers of the sector declined alongside the increase in risk weighted assets driven by the 
expansion in credit. The insurance sector remained adequately capitalised, although profitability moderated. 
Significant claims arising from Cyclone Ditwah increased reinsurance receivables and heightened underwriting, 
liquidity, and counterparty risks.
Lending to both the Household and Institutional sectors1 increased during the first half of 2026. Although 
household credit growth remained elevated, a marginal moderation was observed towards the latter part of 
the period. The share of credit extended by Non-Bank Financial Institutions to the Household sector increased 
further during the first half of 2026, although the banking sector remained the primary source of formal financing 
for households. Moreover, risk profiles of Household borrowers, as reflected by overall credit scores, remained 
broadly stable during the first half of 2026. Credit to the Institutional sector also expanded at a rapid pace, with 
the banking sector accounting for the vast majority of lending to the sector. Meanwhile, the listed Non-Financial 
Corporate (NFC) sector2 recorded stronger revenue growth during the first half of 2026, although aggregate 
profitability weakened. The decline in aggregate profits was largely attributable to higher costs of sales and 
operating expenses. Against this backdrop, creditworthiness of the listed NFC sector showed some signs of 
moderation, reflecting a slowdown in aggregate profitability and debt servicing capacity.

FINANCIAL STABILITY REVIEW 2026
XVI
In response to developments and emerging risks within the financial sector, a range of policy measures were 
implemented during the review period. Against the backdrop of rapid credit expansion in vehicle financing 
and gold backed lending, borrower based macroprudential measures were tightened to contain excessive 
leverage and mitigate emerging risks. These measures included simplification and tightening of maximum 
LTV limits on motor vehicle financing and the introduction of maximum LTV limits on gold backed lending, 
aimed at promoting prudent lending practices and containing the buildup of systemic vulnerabilities. In 
addition to the LTV limits on gold backed lending, applicable risk weights were also tightened during the 
review period. In response to the adverse effects of Cyclone Ditwah, the Central Bank issued circulars to 
both banks and FCs, requiring relief measures to be provided to affected individuals and businesses. 
The Directions on recovery planning for both banks and FCs were issued, alongside consolidation initiatives 
aimed at strengthening the resilience of the banking and FCs sectors. Amid the increasing prevalence of 
financial frauds and scams involving digital payment channels, the Central Bank introduced policy initiatives 
aimed at strengthening the security of digital payment methods and improving public awareness of related 
risks. Measures were also taken to strengthen the resolution framework, financial consumer protection, 
and Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing 
(AML/CFT/CPF) framework, alongside preparations for Sri Lanka's third Mutual Evaluation of its AML/CFT/CPF 
framework by the Asia Pasific Group on Money Laundering (APG), as well as initiatives aimed at improving 
financial inclusion.
Outlook
The outlook for financial stability remains broadly positive, provided that the ongoing economic recovery remains 
sustained, fiscal consolidation progresses, and prudent policy implementation continues. However, the outlook 
is contingent on external developments, including geopolitical and financial market uncertainties, as well as 
domestic vulnerabilities arising from any excessive expansion and sectoral concentration of credit, along with 
evolving cyber risks. Continued monitoring and timely policy intervention will therefore remain important in 
preserving financial stability. Prolonged geopolitical tensions and energy price shocks could weaken external 
balances and increase inflationary pressures, thereby impacting the repayment capacity of borrowers. These 
effects could amplify existing domestic vulnerabilities, including higher growth in collateral backed lending to 
households, rising Stage 2 exposures and declining liquidity and capital buffers. Financial market resilience 
will increasingly be shaped by the ability to strengthen investor confidence, improve market liquidity, deepen 
domestic capital markets, and attract a broader and more stable foreign investor base, thereby enhancing 
the market’s capacity to absorb shocks and support efficient price discovery. Overall, maintaining financial 
stability will require a well calibrated combination of prudent monetary, macroprudential and regulatory policies, 
supported by sustained progress in structural reforms. Priorities of the financial sector should therefore focus 
on preserving strong capital and liquidity buffers across financial institutions, strengthening the management 
of climate related and cyber risks, enhancing resolution and crisis-preparedness frameworks, and ensuring 
that credit expansion remains commensurate with underlying economic activity and risk conditions. These 
efforts will be essential in mitigating the buildup of systemic vulnerabilities, strengthening the financial system’s 
shock absorbing capacity, and safeguarding financial stability over the medium term.

FINANCIAL STABILITY REVIEW 2026
XX

Sri Lanka's macrofinancial environment remained stable, supporting financial stability during H1 of 2026 while external 
headwinds intensified.  Global macrofinancial conditions became more challenging, exerting negative spillovers on 
the domestic economy. Heightened geopolitical tensions, including the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, 
elevated global uncertainty, renewed inflationary pressures, tightened global financial conditions, increasing trade 
fragmentation, policy uncertainty, climate related risks such as the El Niño phenomenon and elevated volatility in 
financial markets created a challenging external environment, with potential implications for domestic macroeconomic 
and financial stability. Rising energy and commodity prices, disruptions to key trade routes, and heightened uncertainty 
contributed to a resurgence of inflationary pressures and increased downside risks to the global outlook. These 
developments heightened the exposure of emerging markets and developing economies including Sri Lanka to 
adverse spillovers through trade, capital flow, financing, and exchange rate channels, as well as climate related 
shocks.
Against this backdrop, domestic macrofinancial conditions remained broadly conducive to financial stability, underpinned 
by continued economic growth, improved fiscal performance and conducive financial sector developments. However, 
the rapid expansion of credit and emerging pressure from global macrofinancial conditions warranted close monitoring 
of the financial system. Credit to the private sector expanded significantly amid the recovery in economic activity and 
relatively accommodative monetary conditions that prevailed during much of the review period, with particularly strong 
expansions observed in household lending, vehicle financing, and gold backed lending. Consequently, financial 
intermediation strengthened, as credit growth continued to outpace deposit growth. Moreover, the private sector credit 
cycle remained in an expansionary phase, with the widening private sector credit gap indicating the potential buildup 
of systemic vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, renewed inflationary pressures, stemming mainly from higher global energy 
and commodity prices and strengthening domestic demand, along with significant growth in credit to the private 
sector prompted a tightening of domestic monetary policy in May 2026. Consequently, this contributed towards further 
upward adjustments in market interest rates and Government securities yields. In addition, macroprudential measures 
in the form of Loan to Value (LTV)  limits on vehicle and gold backed lending, were introduced amid significant credit 
growth to mitigate the buildup of systemic risks within the financial sector.
Fiscal performance strengthened further, reducing reliance on domestic financing and supporting the reallocation of 
financial sector resources towards private sector activities. Nevertheless, the external sector remained vulnerable to 
adverse global developments, particularly through commodity prices, with potential spillovers through trade, tourism, 
workers’ remittances, and exchange rate channels. At the same time, growing interconnectedness among financial 
institutions, increasing digitalisation of financial services and rapid developments in financial technologies, together 
with rising cyber security threats, have emerged as important considerations for financial sector resilience. Further, 
the increasing frequency and severity of climate related events added to the macrofinancial risk landscape, posing 
challenges to stability. 
Looking ahead, Sri Lanka's macrofinancial outlook remains broadly stable despite potential headwinds on several 
fronts. Continued economic growth, stronger fiscal performance, and improved financial sector resilience would 
provide important safeguards against potential shocks. Nevertheless, heightened geopolitical tensions, renewed 
inflationary pressures, tighter global financial conditions, climate related risks, and rapid credit expansion could pose 
challenges to financial stability going forward. Accordingly, preserving macroeconomic stability, maintaining adequate 
capital and liquidity buffers, strengthening risk management practices and ensuring that credit expansion remains 
consistent with underlying economic fundamentals will be important for safeguarding the stability of the financial 
system. Thus, the Central Bank will continue to closely monitor and assess emerging risks and vulnerabilities to the 
financial system and take proactive and timely macroprudential measures, where necessary.

Global Inflation and Commodity Prices
Global inflationary pressures intensified during 
2026 with elevated and volatile commodity prices. 
According to the IMF WEO Update of July 2026, 
global headline inflation is projected to increase to 
4.7% in 2026 from 4.1% in 2025, before moderating 
to 3.9% in 2027. Concerns over energy supply 
disruptions, transportation bottlenecks and risks to 
critical shipping routes in the Middle East contributed 
to heightened volatility in crude oil prices, while higher 
energy costs generated broader inflationary pressures 
through increased fuel, electricity, manufacturing, 
transportation and logistics costs. Food prices also 
remained vulnerable to higher energy and fertiliser 
costs, climate related shocks and disruptions 
to agricultural supply chains, disproportionately 
affecting EMDEs where food and energy account for 
a relatively larger share of household expenditure. 
For Sri Lanka, as a net energy importing economy, 
sustained increases in global energy and food prices 
raises the merchandise import bill, exerting pressure 
on the external current account and domestic 
inflation while reducing household purchasing power 
and increasing operating costs for businesses, 
with consequent effects on debt servicing capacity, 
asset quality and overall financial system stability. 
Meanwhile, global gold prices reached their historical 
high in January 2026 amid heightened geopolitical 
uncertainty and increased safe haven demand, and 
subsequently prices recorded downward adjustment 
by nearly 25%. These significant fluctuations in gold 
prices also warrant attention in jurisdictions such as 
Sri Lanka where financial institutions have material 
exposures to gold backed lending.

amid heightened geopolitical tensions, renewed 
inflationary pressures and increased uncertainty 
surrounding the global monetary policy outlook. 
The escalation of the Middle East conflict prompted 
broad repricing across global financial markets as 
investors reassessed the outlook for inflation, interest 
rates and economic growth. Sovereign bond yields 
increased, equity markets experienced temporary 
corrections and financing conditions tightened 
across several market segments. Nevertheless, 
the tightening remained less pronounced than 
during previous major episodes of global market 
stress, while overall financial conditions remained 
broadly accommodative by historical standards. 
Financial markets continued to function in a broadly 
orderly manner, supported by resilient economic 
activity, relatively favourable liquidity conditions and 
expectations of eventual monetary policy easing 
in several major economies. Financing conditions 
remained uneven across economies. Advanced 
economies generally continued to benefit from 
deeper and more liquid financial markets, while 
several EMDEs faced more challenging financing 
environments due to elevated external vulnerabilities, 
weaker fiscal positions and relatively high borrowing 
costs. Moreover, a stronger US dollar, the potential 
unwinding of carry trades and the growing participation 
of relatively risk sensitive non-bank financial investors 
could increase the likelihood of capital outflows and 
exchange rate pressures. 
These developments could tighten financial 
conditions particularly for vulnerable economies. 
Increasing refinancing costs amid tightening financial 
conditions could adversely impact economies with 
substantial foreign currency liabilities or significant 
external financing requirements. Meanwhile, a 
prolonged geopolitical conflict, persistent energy 
driven inflation or an abrupt reassessment of the 
global monetary policy outlook could lead to further 
tightening in financial conditions. These developments 
would lead to an increase in external financing costs

Global Financial Markets
Financial market volatility increased during the 
review period as the escalation of the Middle East 
tensions heightened geopolitical uncertainty 
and weakened investor confidence. Concerns 
over energy security, renewed inflationary pressures 
and disruptions to global trade prompted investors 
to reassess financial market risks, resulting in 
heightened price fluctuations across equity, sovereign 
bond, foreign exchange and commodity markets. 
Reflecting these developments, key measures of 
implied volatility recorded notable increases during 
early 20261. The simultaneous increase in volatility 
across different asset classes highlighted the

increased the rollover and market liquidity risks in 
major sovereign markets. Persistent geopolitical risks, 
stretched asset valuations, elevated sovereign debt 
and uncertainty surrounding the outlook for inflation 
and monetary policy continued to create conditions 
for abrupt changes in global risk sentiment. A 
prolonged deterioration in global risk sentiment could 
therefore generate mutually reinforcing pressures 
through sovereign bond markets, capital flows, 
exchange rates and funding conditions, with potential 
adverse implications for financial institutions' balance 
sheets and global financial stability. Hence, such 
episodes could increase exchange rate and capital 
flow volatility, affect foreign investor participation and 
contribute to tighter domestic financial conditions

Implications for Domestic Financial Stability
Global macrofinancial developments are expected 
to increase external risks to the domestic financial 
sector. Emerging and developing economies remain 
vulnerable to adverse external spillovers, particularly 
through trade, capital flow, exchange rate and 
commodity price transmission channels. Higher 
energy and commodity prices, together with potential 
disruptions to global trade and supply chains, could 
adversely affect domestic inflation dynamics, external 
balances, and economic activity going forward as 
well. Further, it could reduce the profitability and 
debt servicing capacity of exporters, tourism related 
businesses, and importers. These developments may 
also weaken the repayment capacity of households 
if higher food, fuel and utility costs reduce their 
disposable income. In addition, these could result 
in increasing non-performing loans and impairment 
charges of financial institutions, particularly if global 
uncertainty persists. Nevertheless, the tightening 
of monetary policy in May 2026, together with the 
introduction of LTV2 related measures is expected 
to contribute to a gradual moderation in credit 
expansion and help contain the buildup of financial 
vulnerabilities. At the same time, the persistence 
of relatively restrictive monetary policy in major 
advanced economies and shifting global investor 
sentiments may contribute to continued exchange 
rate pressures, tighter external financing conditions,

Developments in Credit
Total domestic credit3 expanded at a rapid 
pace during the review period, supported by 
the continued recovery in economic activity 
and the relatively accommodative monetary 
conditions that prevailed during much of the 
period. However, the operating environment became 
increasingly challenging following the escalation 
of the conflict in the Middle East, which contributed 
to heightened global uncertainty and renewed 
inflationary pressures through higher energy and 
commodity prices, with consequential spillovers to 
the domestic economy. The subsequent tightening 
of domestic monetary conditions in May 2026 along 
with macroprudential measures in relation to LTV 
ratios, is expected to moderate credit growth going 
forward. Credit extended by regulated Deposit Taking 
Financial Institutions (DTFIs), comprising banks and 
Finance Companies (FCs), recorded strong growth, 
with y-o-y growth in total credit accelerating from 
14.0% in June 2025 to a peak of 27.9% in March 
2026, before moderating marginally to 26.4% by June 
2026 reflecting the gradual tightening of domestic 
monetary conditions. Moreover, this credit expansion 
was particularly observed in gold backed lending and 
vehicle related financing. Although the banking sector 
continued to account for the largest share of lending, 
the FCs sector recorded a substantially higher growth 
rate, contributing to the expansion in credit across the 
financial system.

Financial Intermediation and Credit Cycle

the review period with the continued expansion 
in credit. The banking sector Credit-to-Deposit

increase in the CDR occurred alongside broadly stable

intermediation and credit demand outpaced changes 
in overall economic activity. This increase reflected 
the widening differential between credit and deposit 
growth, as credit growth accelerated markedly amid 
the continued recovery in economic activity and the 
accommodative monetary conditions that prevailed 
during much of the period, while deposit growth 
remained comparatively moderate. Nevertheless, 
the CDR remained below the levels observed prior 
to the recent economic crisis, indicating that the

Moreover, results of the Credit Supply Survey 
indicated that loan demand continued to strengthen 
in Q2 of 2026, with increases observed across the 
retail, corporate, SME and SOE sectors, although at 
a more moderate pace compared to Q1 of 2026. The 
expansion in credit demand was largely supported 
by higher working capital requirements, demand for 
short term loans, and revival of investment activity. 
However, banks expected both lending activity and 
credit demand to remain positive in Q3 of 2026, 
although banks’ willingness to lend is expected to 
increase at a slower pace, reflecting a more cautious 
outlook amid anticipated inflationary pressures, 
rising operating costs, exchange rate volatility and 
geopolitical uncertainties. While the recovery in 
financial intermediation supports the financing needs 
of the economy, a sustained widening of the gap 
between credit and deposit growth could increase 
funding pressures and contribute to a gradual erosion 
of liquidity buffers if credit expansion continues to 
significantly outpace growth in stable deposit funding.
The private sector credit cycle continued to 
progress within the expansionary phase with 
widening gap highlighting the potential buildup 
up of systemic risk. The private sector credit-
to-GDP ratio continued to increase throughout 
the period, supported by the strong expansion in 
credit mainly driven by personal loans receivables, 
including vehicle financing and gold-backed lending, 
alongside higher lending to the services sector and 
selected industrial subsectors. At the same time, the 
Credit Gap remained in positive territory and widened 
further, indicating that private sector credit growth 
continued to outpace its long term trend. While the 
emergence of a positive credit gap is consistent 
with the recovery of credit expansion following the 
prolonged contraction observed during 2022–2024, 
its continued widening particularly alongside rapid 
private sector credit growth, warrants close monitoring 
from a financial stability perspective. A sustained 
expansion in credit significantly above its long-
term trend could contribute to a buildup of borrower 
leverage, increased risk taking and sectoral credit 
concentrations if not accompanied by commensurate 
growth in borrowers’ income and repayment capacity. 
Nevertheless, the tightening of monetary policy in 
May 2026, together with the introduction of LTV 
related measures, is expected to contribute to a 
gradual moderation in credit expansion and contain 
the further buildup of credit related vulnerabilities. 
As the effects of these measures are expected to 
transmit with a lag, their impact on the pace and 
composition of credit growth would warrant continued 
monitoring. Accordingly, close monitoring of credit 
dynamics remains important to assess whether the 
ongoing expansion in the credit cycle is giving rise to 
emerging systemic vulnerabilities.

Market Interest Rates and Yield Rates 
Following the broad-based easing observed 
during 
2025, 
market 
interest 
rates 
and 
Government securities yields adjusted upwards 
during the first half of 2026. Market interest rates 
remained under upward pressure mainly driven by 
heightened uncertainty emanating from geopolitical 
tensions, market expectations on inflation and 
tightening of policy interest rates. Short term money 
market rates increased in response to the monetary 
policy tightening, while lending rates also further 
adjusted upwards as the change in the policy stance 
was transmitted through the financial system. Despite 
these upward adjustments, market interest rates 
remained well below the elevated levels observed 
during the post-crisis period, suggesting that financing 
conditions remained comparatively supportive of 
financial intermediation during the period under review. 
Meanwhile, Government securities yields increased 
across maturities, contributing to an upward shift in 
the yield curve amid evolving market expectations 
and investor sentiments along with heightened 
uncertainty. Further real interest rates moderated 
during the period as inflation gradually increased. 
Against this backdrop, private sector credit growth, 
which had strengthened markedly during 2025 and 
early 2026, showed some moderation towards the 
latter part of the period amid the tightening of financing 
conditions and evolving macrofinancial landscape. 
Overall, financial markets and institutions continued 
to adjust to the changing interest rate environment in 
an orderly manner without signs of significant stress.

Volatility in gold market, alongside geopolitical

financial stability. Gold prices4 increased steadily 
during the second half of 2025 and early 2026, 
reaching a peak of around USD 1,393 per sovereign 
at end January 2026 amid heightened market activity. 
Subsequently, following significant fluctuations, gold 
prices corrected and remained volatile, falling to 
around USD 1,141 per sovereign by end August 2026, 
underscoring the potential risks to institutions with 
sizeable gold backed lending exposures from further 
price adjustments. Further corrections in gold prices 
could weaken collateral values and increase asset 
quality risks, particularly given the strong growth in 
gold backed lending. In addition, ongoing geopolitical 
tensions may lead to higher energy prices and supply 
chain disruptions, placing pressure on household and 
business incomes, thereby affecting debt servicing 
capacity. In recognition of these risks, the Central 
Bank has implemented targeted macroprudential 
measures, including LTV restrictions on gold backed 
lending, aimed at containing excessive risk taking 
and mitigating vulnerabilities arising from asset price 
volatility.

How a climate event is transmitted to a financial

Climate related risks can be transmitted to the financial 
system through several interconnected channels covering 
multiple sectors of an economy.
In the Sri Lankan context, climate shocks can reduce 
the income and repayment capacity of climate sensitive

may lead to higher arrears, restructuring and defaults,

potential credit losses. For example, repeated flooding or 
coastal hazards may reduce the marketability and value of 
properties located in such areas. Consequently, even where 
a borrower initially remains current on a loan, a deterioration 
in collateral quality could exacerbate the bank's potential 
loss in the event of a default.

repeating such events in the future. While any climate 
catastrophe could disrupt production and impact the general

output.

Early diagnosis of stability implications
Climate shocks are likely to first appear through migration 
of loan arrears of banks and Finance Companies (FCs) 
from Stage 1 to Stage 2 exposures. As borrower repayment 
capacity deteriorates, expected credit loss provisions rise. 
If conditions persist, a portion of these exposures may 
migrate to Stage 3. Institutions with concentrations in 
agriculture, rural lending, leasing and SMEs are expected 
to experience greater sensitivity. The share of SME sector 
loans of the banking sector amounts to about 11% of the 
total loan portfolio. Climate shocks could therefore generate 
system-wide consequences even if individual institutions 
remain resilient.
By the end of first half of 2026, bank lending to Agriculture 
sector was 8.7% of the total loan portfolio with a gross 
Stage 3 loans ratio of 9.2%. Similarly, Consumption loans 
accounted for 19.5% of total bank lending, with a gross 
Stage 3 loans ratio of 3.3%. As forecasted by the 
Department of Meteorology, if an El Niño event with 
90% probability occurs, it could be among other sectors, 
transmitted into agriculture and consumption sectors with a 
higher magnitude through the aforementioned transmission 
channels.

of climate related shocks suggest that climate risk warrants 
greater attention within the macroprudential surveillance 
framework. In this regard, the following measures could 
strengthen the resilience of Sri Lanka's financial system.
•	 Strengthening climate risk surveillance by monitoring 
sectoral and geographical exposures to climate sensitive 
hazards and identifying concentrations in vulnerable 
sectors and locations.

constraint internationally is the non-availability of sufficiently

Stress in domestic financial markets, as measured by the Financial Stress Index (FSI)1, remained subdued during the 
first eight months of 2026, despite a temporary increase in March 2026 amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty. The 
FSI remained contained at low level, as relatively stable conditions in the Government securities market and money 
market offset intermittent increases in stock and domestic foreign exchange market stress.
Stock market performance moderated during the first eight months of 2026, amid heightened geopolitical tensions, 
global financial market uncertainty, rising energy prices, the domestic inflation outlook and tighter monetary conditions. 
Stock price indices remained subdued, while market liquidity moderated and volatility increased. Market valuation 
indicators increased modestly but remained broadly in line with their long term averages and below those of most 
regional peers. Persistent net foreign outflows underscored the importance of attracting stable, long term capital 
inflows to strengthen market liquidity and resilience.
Conditions in the Government securities market tightened, with yields increasing across maturities. Evolving market 
expectations, geopolitical uncertainty and tighter monetary conditions were reflected in the upward adjustment in 
yields. Despite strong fiscal performance and robust demand for Government securities, secondary market liquidity 
remained constrained, with trading concentrated within a limited range of maturities. Foreign investment recorded a 
modest recovery towards the latter part of the review period as yields adjusted upwards and exchange rate conditions 
improved, although overall foreign participation remained low.
The domestic foreign exchange market experienced some pressure, with conditions improving in the latter part of 
review period. Heightened geopolitical tensions, rising energy prices, increased import demand and changing investor 
sentiment caused to the depreciation of the Sri Lanka rupee against the US dollar and several other major currencies. 
Nevertheless, conditions subsequently improved, supported by policy measures and continued foreign exchange 
inflows from workers’ remittances, export proceeds and tourism earnings, while exchange rate volatility moderated 
and interbank transaction volumes exhibited a gradual recovery.
Domestic money market activity strengthened further, with increased repo and call money market transactions. State-
owned banks remained key net lenders, while domestic private banks continued to be net borrowers, reflecting the 
asymmetric distribution of liquidity. The Average Weighted Call Money Rate (AWCMR) and Average Weighted Repo 
Rate (AWRR) exhibited some intermittent upward pressure during the review period and subsequently returned to 
broad alignment with the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR), while overall money market liquidity remained in surplus. 
Payment and settlement infrastructure remained operationally resilient during the review period, while continued 
growth in digital payments and measures to strengthen settlement risk management, interoperability and accessibility 
supported payment system resilience. Nevertheless, the increasing reliance on digital channels continued to warrant 
close monitoring of cyber, operational and third-party risks.
Overall, domestic financial markets and payment infrastructures remained resilient during the review period despite 
heightened global uncertainty, tighter domestic monetary conditions and moderate pressure on foreign exchange 
and stock markets. Maintaining macroeconomic stability, strengthening investor confidence, broadening foreign 
investment base and deepening domestic financial markets and payment infrastructures would enhance resilience 
against external and domestic shocks.

including the decline in yields during 2023 and 2024 
and the subsequent upward movement in 2026, have 
not materially altered investor trading preferences or 
the overall liquidity profile of the market. Persistently 
limited liquidity has constrained effective yield curve 
formation and price discovery, as the actively traded 
maturity spectrum remained narrow. Further, reliance 
on quoted prices for less actively traded maturities 
could underestimate market volatility. While the 
overall turnover ratio of both Treasury bills and bonds 
increased to 45.6% in July 2026 before moderating 
to 37.3% in August 2026, the continued variability 
in trading activity and its concentration across a 
limited range of maturities suggest that the recent 
increase in turnover does not yet indicate a sustained 
improvement in secondary market liquidity.

2.3	 Domestic Foreign Exchange Market 
The Sri Lanka rupee depreciated by 5.5% against 
the USD during the first eight months of 2026 
extending the depreciation recorded in 2025, 
after two consecutive years of appreciation in 
2023 and 2024. Following marginal appreciation 
during the first two months of 2026, the rupee 
came under renewed pressures from late February 
amidst a sharp increase in global energy prices 
and heightened uncertainty in international financial 
markets mainly due to escalating geopolitical 
tensions in the Middle East. These developments, 
combined with increased import-related demand 
for foreign exchange particularly on fuel and other 
speculative market activity together with stock market 
outflows, intermittent Government securities market 
outflows and subdued conversion of export proceeds 
in several months have exerted pressure on the 
domestic foreign exchange market. Depreciation and 
volatility intensified during the second quarter of 2026 
as elevated energy import costs, growing demand 
for foreign exchange associated with expanding 
economic activity and imports, and adverse market 
sentiment weighed on the exchange rate. However, 
market conditions started to improve from the latter 
part of May 2026 following the policy measures and 
interventions by the Central Bank to ease pressures 
in the domestic foreign exchange market and contain 
excessive volatility and recorded an appreciation of 
2.4% during August 2026. Meanwhile, the surcharge 
imposed by the Government on motor vehicle imports, 
together with the  tightening of Loan to Value (LTV)6 
restrictions by the Central Bank on vehicle related 
lending, is expected to moderate demand for vehicle 
imports and thereby help contain associated foreign 
exchange demand and pressures in the domestic 
foreign exchange market. The domestic foreign 
exchange market continued to benefit from resilient 
inflows from worker remittances, export proceeds and 
tourism earnings, which helped cushion the impact 
of heightened foreign exchange demand to a certain 
level. Further, exchange rate volatility7 eased towards 
August 2026 compared to the sharp increases 
observed during the peak of market pressures at 
the beginning of the second quarter, indicating a 
gradual improvement in market conditions. During 
the first eight months of the year 2026, the Central 
Bank intervened in the domestic foreign exchange 
market, where necessary, to rebuild foreign reserves 
in line with the IMF-supported EFF programme, to 
strengthen external buffers, to mitigate excessive 
exchange rate volatility, and to facilitate the financing 
of essential energy related imports. Nevertheless, 
the exchange rate remained exposed to external 
developments, particularly geopolitical uncertainties, 
fluctuations in global energy prices, disruptions in 
maritime transport, changes in investor sentiment and 
capital flows. Continued growth in foreign exchange

accounted for the largest share of total transaction 
volume during the review period, contributing 38% of 
overall transactions, followed by cash transactions 
and spot transactions, which accounted for 30% and 
21% respectively. In the forward market, the majority 
of the transactions entered into were more than one 
week up to a one-month period indicating a strong 
preference for short term hedging. Although forward 
contract activity helps businesses and financial 
institutions manage their risk, the concentration of 
forward contract at short term maturities may create 
liquidity pressure if market conditions further tighten.
The one-month forward premium exhibited 
a temporary surge during the review period 
amid increased uncertainties related to global 
tensions and domestic market conditions. The 
sharp rise in the forward premium indicated market 
expectations of near term depreciation pressures 
on the rupee and a greater preference among 
market participants to hedge against exchange rate 
risk. These developments were likely influenced 
by heightened geopolitical tensions, volatility in 
global energy prices, and the resulting uncertainty 
in domestic foreign exchange market conditions. 
However, the subsequent moderation of the one-
month forward premium suggests an improvement 
in market sentiment and foreign exchange liquidity 
conditions, supported by the easing of uncertainties 
and measures taken by the Central Bank.
The Central Bank remained a net purchaser during 
the review period. However, amid heightened 
pressures in the domestic foreign exchange market, 
the Central Bank supplied foreign exchange to the 
market from March 2026 onwards to curb excessive 
exchange rate volatility and facilitate essential energy 
related imports, thereby becoming a net seller during 
the months of April and May 2026, on value date basis. 
As market conditions improved from the latter part of 
May 2026, the Central Bank recorded net purchases 
of foreign exchange. Over the first eight months of 
2026, the Central Bank recorded net purchases of

2.4	 Domestic Money Market
Domestic money market activity remained robust 
during the first eight months of 2026. Total monthly 
transaction volume reached an all-time high level in 
May 2026, driven by increased activities in both the 
repo and the call money markets. The repo market 
continued to account for the larger share of money 
market activity, with average monthly transaction 
volumes increased to Rs. 1,468.5 bn during the 
period from January to August 2026, from monthly 
average of Rs. 923.4 bn in 2025. Similarly, average 
monthly call money market turnover during the 
first eight months of 2026 notably increased to Rs. 
805.2 bn from monthly average of Rs. 480.2 bn 
recorded in 2025. Monthly repo market volumes 
remained consistently higher than the monthly 
call money market volumes, reflecting more active 
involvement by market participants in securitised 
lending compared to clean lending. Participant level 
activity indicates differences in liquidity positions 
across financial institutions. On a net basis, domestic 
private banks and standalone primary dealers were 
net borrowers in the repo market during the first eight 
months of 2026, while state-owned banks continued 
to be net lenders. In the call money market, state-
owned banks and foreign banks continued to be the 
net lenders during the same period, while domestic 
private banks remained net borrowers. The role of 
state-owned banks as suppliers of liquidity helped for 
improved money market activities during the review 
period. However, the concentration of system liquidity 
intermediation among state-owned banks could give 
rise to vulnerabilities, given the linkages between 
their liquidity positions and Government financing 
operations. Accordingly, unexpected increases in the 
Government’s financing requirements could affect the 
liquidity positions of state-owned banks and, in turn, 
influence overall money market liquidity conditions.

2.5	 Payment and Settlement 
Infrastructure 
Payment and settlement systems continued to 
remain operationally resilient during the first 
half of 2026.  Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) 
system, which facilitates the smooth, secure and 
timely settlement of large value and time critical 
transactions among participating institutions, settled 
318,231 transactions with a total value of Rs. 263 tn, 
reflecting 10.4% and 31.5% increases in the volume 
and value of transactions, respectively, during the first 
half of 2026 compared to the corresponding period 
of 2025. Retail payment systems also demonstrated 
sustained growth throughout the first half of 2026. In 
particular, the fast payment system of the country, 
the Common Electronic Fund Transfer Switch 
(CEFTS), continued to facilitate instant interbank 
fund transfers and remained a key channel for digital 
payments. The value of transactions processed 
through CEFTS increased by 31.9% during the first 
half of 2026 compared to the corresponding period 
of 2025, reflecting the growing preference for instant 
account to account transfers. From a financial system 
stability perspective, the increasing reliance on digital 
payment channels and the growing volume and 
value of transactions processed through systemically 
important payment infrastructure heighten the 
potential impact of operational disruptions, cyber 
incidents and technology failures, underscoring 
the importance of maintaining robust operational 
resilience, cybersecurity safeguards and contingency 
arrangements.

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka has been conducting the 
Systemic Risk Survey (SRS) on a semi-annual basis since 
2017, to assess the risks to the Sri Lankan financial system 
based on the perceptions of executives responsible for risk 
management in financial institutions.1 SRS is a forward 
looking survey, and this special note summarises the key 
findings2 for year 2026 with a particular focus on the results 
of the latest survey3 conducted for the second half (H2) of 
the year.
Confidence in the Financial System
Respondents’ overall confidence4 in the financial system, 
as measured by the net percentage balance, declined in H1 
of 2026 before recording a slight improvement in H2 2026. 
Overall, short term confidence remained lower in 2026 
compared to 2025, although it remained in positive territory. 
Medium term confidence exhibited a broadly similar pattern 
across the two survey rounds. A substantial proportion 
of respondents expressed a ‘Fairly Confident’ outlook, 
indicating that confidence in financial system stability 
remained moderate.
Perceived Probability of a High Impact Negative 
Event 
The survey requested respondents to assess the likelihood 
of a high impact negative event occurring within the financial 
system over the short to medium term. The perceived 
probability of such an event materialising in the short term 
increased, as reflected by the net percentage balance,5 
reversing the declining trend observed in previous years. In 
contrast, the perceived probability of a high impact negative 
event occurring in the medium term moderated slightly in 
H2 of 2026, following a marginal increase in H1 of 2026, 
indicating a slightly more favourable assessment of medium 
term risks.
Sources of Risks to the Financial System 
According to the survey responses, ‘Global Macroeconomic 
Risks’ emerged as the most critical risk category in H2 of 
2026 in terms of its potential impact on the financial system, 
largely reflecting uncertainties related to geopolitical tensions 
and associated spillovers.  This was followed by ‘General 
Domestic Macroeconomic Risks’.  Meanwhile, the perceived 
impact of ‘Risks Related to Financial Infrastructure’ increased 
slightly in H2 of 2026 compared to H1 of 2026 indicating a 
rising trend in recent surveys, while the perceived impact of 
other risk categories declined. 
Respondents identified ‘Geopolitical Tensions and Risk 
Spillovers from Other Countries’ as the most critical sub 
risk6, with the potential to exert the greatest impact to the 
financial system in H2 of 2026. This was followed by ‘Cyber-
attacks and Phishing’ and ‘Inflation’. The prominence 
of geopolitical and inflation related risks likely reflected 
heightened geopolitical tensions, particularly developments 
in the Middle East, and concerns over their potential 
spillovers to the domestic economy during the survey

attacks and phishing’, also continued to feature prominently 
among respondents’ concerns. Furthermore, institutions 
across the financial sector identified ‘geopolitical tensions 
and external risk spillovers’ as the most challenging risks 
to manage at the firm level. These findings underscore 
the importance of continued vigilance, strengthening risk 
management frameworks, enhancing cyber resilience, and 
closely monitoring global developments to safeguard the 
stability of the financial system.

Financial institutions remained resilient during the twelve month period that ended in June 2026, supported by 
continued recovery in economic activity, increased earnings, and adequate capital buffers, despite the adverse 
impacts from natural disasters and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Financial intermediation improved across the 
banking and finance companies (FCs) sectors, supporting the overall economic recovery during the period. Credit 
demand was particularly high for certain sectors, including vehicle and gold backed facilities. However, elevated credit 
expansion contributed to some moderation in liquidity and capital positions, although the sectors continued to maintain 
adequate buffers above the respective regulatory minimum requirements. Nevertheless, rapid and concentrated 
credit growth, increases in Stage 2 loans, cross-border lending, and interconnectedness between banks and FCs 
arising from excessive lending to FCs warrant close monitoring. Considering the potential build-up of systemic risks 
from excessive credit growth, the Central Bank introduced several macroprudential policy measures, including 
tightened loan-to-value (LTV) limits for vehicle loans and introduced LTV limits and higher risk weights for gold backed 
facilities.1 These measures, together with the policy rate adjustment in May 2026 and the extension of the temporary 
surcharge on motor vehicle imports, are expected to moderate credit growth over the coming quarters.
The Banking Soundness Index, an indicator to assess the overall soundness of the banking sector, declined marginally 
during the first half of 2026. The banking sector credit expanded significantly amid robust private sector demand, with 
notable growth in consumption, trade, financial services, construction, and offshore lending. Asset quality indicators 
continued to improve, supported by the expansion of the credit base and a reduction in outstanding Stage 3 loans, 
while the improvement in the Stage 3 impairment coverage ratio provided an additional cushion against unexpected 
credit losses. However, increasing Stage 2 loans during Q2 of 2026 highlights the potential risk of future downward 
migration of loans. The sector’s exposure to the Government and state owned enterprises declined amid strong 
private sector credit demand during the period, although it remained sizeable. Liquidity coverage ratios and net stable 
funding ratio remained well above the regulatory minimums, though moderated slightly as banks reallocated liquid 
assets towards lending. Capital ratios also declined, as risk weighted assets expanded faster than capital due to 
strong credit expansion, narrowing the sector’s capacity to absorb unexpected losses.
The FCs sector also demonstrated robust growth during the period, with lending accelerating sharply amid increased 
demand for motor vehicle financing, following the relaxation of vehicle import restrictions, and the continued expansion 
of gold backed lending, supported by the elevated gold prices. The concentration of credit in vehicle and gold backed 
lending increased the sector’s vulnerability to adverse movements in the underlying collateral values. To contain 
these risks, the Central Bank proactively introduced several macroprudential policy measures. Asset quality indicators 
improved, supported by the significant expansion of the credit portfolio and a reduction in outstanding Stage 3 loans. 
However, increase in Stage 2 exposures and the moderation in impairment coverage warranted continued vigilance on 
asset quality. The sector’s liquidity buffers declined amid the rapid balance sheet expansion. Meanwhile, borrowings 
remained elevated at end June 2026, underpinned by the sector’s growing reliance on funding from banks. The 
aggregate capital ratio of the sector remained well above the regulatory requirements, despite a decline in capital 
buffers resulting from the growth in lending.
The insurance sector continued to expand with an improvement in insurance penetration during the period, supported 
by strong growth in gross written premiums and assets. Profitability in both the long term and general insurance 
subsectors moderated, although their capital adequacy ratios remained well above the respective regulatory minimum 
requirements. Cyclone Ditwah generated substantial insurance claims, and the settlement of these claims could exert 
certain pressure on the underwriting performance, liquidity, and capital positions of general insurers.

The overall soundness of the banking sector, as 
measured by the BSI, declined marginally at end 
of Q2 of 2026 compared with the corresponding 
period in 2025, primarily reflecting the effects 
of strong credit growth on liquidity and capital 
adequacy. Accordingly, the liquidity sub index 
weakened as rapid credit expansion outpaced 
funding growth, while high quality liquid assets
declined, partly due to the reallocation of funds from 
government securities to lending activities. The capital 
adequacy sub index also deteriorated, reflecting 
declined capital adequacy ratios amid an increase in 
risk weighted assets associated with credit expansion. 
Meanwhile, the profitability sub index moderated, 
contributed by the declines recorded in return on 
equity, return on assets, and the net interest margin. 
However, the asset quality sub index recorded a 
notable improvement, supported by a decline in the 
Stage 3 loans ratio, while the efficiency and resilience 
to market risk sub indices also improved during the 
period.

The banking sector credit significantly grew 
during the period under review, supported by 
conducive macroeconomic conditions, despite 
the recent unfavourable global uncertainties. 
The credit growth momentum observed since latter 
half of 2023 continued during the first half of 2026, 
recording a year-on-year (y-o-y) credit growth of 
23.6% at end Q2 of 2026 compared to 11.4% at 
end Q2 of 2025. The sector’s credit accelerated 
significantly amid the recovery in economic activity 
and relatively accommodative monetary conditions 
that prevailed during much of the review period, with 
particularly strong expansions observed in vehicle

acceleration in lending also indicates a notable

The credit expansion during the period under

domestic bank, completed in July 2026, is expected to 
moderate the reported credit position of foreign banks 
in Q3 of 2026, while correspondingly increasing that 
of domestic banks.

The Stage 3 impairment coverage ratio recorded 
an improvement at end Q2 of 2026 compared to 
end Q2 of 2025, driven by the decline in Stage 3 
loans with a growth in impairment. The Stage 3 
impairment coverage ratio of the sector notably 
improved to 61.3% at end Q2 of 2026 compared to 
54.8% recorded at end of the corresponding period of 
the previous year, mainly due to a growth of Stage 3 
impairment by 5.2% y-o-y, along with the contraction 
of Stage 3 loans by 5.8% at end Q2 of 2026. The 
increase in impairment offers an additional buffer 
for banks to absorb any future credit losses, thereby 
strengthening their resilience against potential asset 
quality deterioration. Moreover, a higher impairment 
coverage ratio reflects a prudent and proactive risk 
management approach by banks.
The net Stage 3 loans to common equity Tier 1 
(CET 1) capital ratio notably declined at end Q2 
of 2026 compared to a year ago, due to a growth 
in CET 1 capital, while net Stage 3 loans notably 
contracted. The net Stage 3 loans to CET 1 capital 
ratio, which measures the capacity of quality capital 
to absorb potential losses from defaults that have 
not been covered by impairment, notably declined to 
28.3% at end Q2 of 2026 compared to 40.2% at end 
Q2 of 2025. The growth of CET 1 capital by 14.5% 
y-o-y amidst the contraction of net Stage 3 loans 
by 19.3% at the end of the period contributed to the 
decline in the ratio, indicating enhanced resilience 
against potential credit losses not covered by 
impairment.

Liquidity Risk
Reflecting the rapid credit expansion, liquidity 
ratios of the banking sector continued to decline 
since the beginning of 2025 yet remained well 
above the minimum regulatory requirements. The 
rupee liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) decreased to 
272.5% by end Q2 of 2026 from 328.5% by end Q2 
of 2025. A similar trend was observed in all-currency 
LCR, which decreased to 229.7% by end Q2 of 2026 
from 283.7% by end Q2 of 2025. Nevertheless, both 
ratios remained well above the minimum regulatory 
requirement of 100%, indicating that banking sector 
maintained sufficient liquidity buffers to withstand 
short term liquidity stress scenarios. Further, the 
prevailing liquidity buffers provide a cushion for 
banks to continue the balance sheet expansion and 
financial intermediation. Moreover, the net stable 
funding ratio (NSFR) also declined to 148.1% at end 
Q2 of 2026 from 162.7% a year ago, yet remained 
above the minimum regulatory requirement of 100%, 
manifesting that banks maintained sufficient stable 
funding relative to their asset profile and remained 
better positioned to withstand longer term funding 
pressures.

by the contraction in high quality liquid assets 
(HQLA), as banks reallocated funds for the

y-o-y by end Q2 of 2026, compared to a growth of 
27.0% recorded at end Q2 of 2025. This contraction 
largely reflected a shift in banks’ asset allocation from

the longer term buckets also point to a more persistent 
structural mismatch between the maturity profiles of

and funding costs if maintained over time. In addition, 
HQLA in excess of the cumulative negative gap up to

Profitability
The banking sector’s profitability improved in the 
first half (H1) of 2026, though the pace of the growth 
moderated compared to the corresponding period 
of 2025. The sector reported a profit after tax (PAT) of 
Rs. 208.7 bn in H1 of 2026, recording a y-o-y growth 
of 12.9%. However, this was significantly lower than 
the growth of 67.2% recorded in H1 of 2025, which

expenses and impairment charges substantially

Market Risk
Near term repricing portfolio of the banking 
sector improved at end Q2 of 2026, as 
interest-bearing assets were higher than the 
interest-bearing liabilities up to one month bucket 
amid increasing market interest rate conditions. 
However, material negative gaps persisted beyond 
one month horizon. The cumulative position within 
1 month shifted from a negative Rs. 111.2 bn at end 
Q2 of 2025 to a positive Rs. 457.3 bn at end Q2 
of 2026, while the negative positions within 3 and 
6 months narrowed substantially to Rs. 277.7 bn 
and Rs. 709.0 bn, respectively. The cumulative 
negative position within the 12 month horizon also 
narrowed from Rs. 2.7 tn to Rs. 2.5 tn. This indicates 
that, beyond the 1 month horizon, a greater volume 
of interest-sensitive liabilities remained subject to 
repricing compared to assets. Following the 100 bps 
increase in the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) in May 
2026, the remaining negative repricing gaps could 
result in liabilities repricing faster than assets, leading 
to some moderation in NIM. However, given that NIM 
remains elevated, such moderation may not be an 
immediate concern for sector’s profitability.
The banking sector’s net FCY exposure increased 
at end Q2 of 2026, indicating increased sensitivity 
to exchange rate movements. The net FCY

regulatory capital ratio increased from 18.9% at end 
Q2 of 2025 to 21.3% at end Q2 of 2026. Although 
the on-balance sheet position shifted from a net 
asset position of Rs. 51.5 bn at end Q2 of 2025 to 
a net liability position of Rs. 106.8 bn at end Q2 of

Capital Adequacy
The banking sector maintained capital adequacy 
ratios (CARs) above the regulatory requirements, 
although the ratios declined due to the higher 
credit expansion witnessed during the period. 
The banking sector recorded a total CAR of 18.2% 
at end Q2 of 2026 compared to 19.4% at end Q2 
of 2025. This was mainly due to increase in risk 
weighted assets (RWA) by 23.8% y-o-y, largely 
reflecting the significant credit expansion during this 
period, against a relatively lower growth in regulatory 
capital by 15.9% y-o-y at end Q2 of 2026. Moreover, 
common equity Tier 1 (CET 1) CAR of the sector also 
deteriorated to 14.6% at end Q2 of 2026 compared 
to 15.7% a year ago, indicating a moderation in the 
sector’s high quality capital buffer relative to its RWA, 
increasing the sector’s vulnerability to unexpected 
losses.
The decline in CAR was broad based across 
all bank categories, reflecting a sector-wide 
increase of RWA compared to regulatory capital.

Capital Adequacy 
The capital position of the FCs sector remained 
resilient at end Q2 of 2026, in terms of both 
regulatory minimum capital adequacy requirement 
and minimum core capital requirement. Except 
for three companies which represented a market 
share of 3.0%, all other FCs remained compliant 
with the regulatory minimum total capital adequacy 
requirement as at end Q2 of 2026. Moreover, 
except for one FC, all other FCs were compliant 
with minimum core capital requirement of Rs. 2.5 bn 
during the same reference period.
The capital adequacy ratios (CARs) of the FCs 
sector declined at end Q2 of 2026 compared to 
the corresponding period of the previous year, 
mainly due to increase in risk weighted assets 
(RWA) driven by the significant credit expansion. 
Accordingly, total CAR and Tier 1 CAR of the sector 
declined to 19.3% and 17.3%, respectively, at end Q2 
of 2026 compared to 22.0% and 20.8%, respectively, 
reported at end Q2 of 2025. However, as a sector, 
these ratios remained above the regulatory minimum 
requirement during the period considered. The RWA 
grew substantially by 37.6% y-o-y at end Q2 of 2026 
against a relatively slower capital growth of 20.8%, 
exerting downward pressure on CAR.
Total capital of the sector further strengthened 
during the period, supported by increase in 
retained earnings and Tier 2 capital. Total capital 
recorded a y-o-y growth of 20.8% at end Q2 of 2026 
compared to 18.0% y-o-y growth recorded a year 
ago. The increase in the total capital of the sector was 
primarily driven by the increased retained earnings, 
with the inclusion of the audited profits for the financial 
year 2025/26, and infusion of Tier 2 capital through 
approved unsecured subordinate debt instruments.
Reflecting the robust expansion in the credit 
portfolio, the FCs sector's RWA under the credit 
risk category recorded a significant growth by 
end Q2 of 2026. Accordingly, RWA for credit risk, 
which accounted for 89.5% of the sector’s total 
RWA, increased by 39.7% y-o-y at end Q2 of 2026 
compared to 30.2% at end Q2 of 2025. The increase

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being adopted across the 
global financial services industry at a pace that has drawn 
sustained supervisory attention. AI is elevating cyber risk 
from an operational concern to a core financial stability 
issue, principally through the scale effects it unleashes 
across shared technologies.1 Against this background, 
the Central Bank surveyed all Licensed Banks (LBs) in 
Sri Lanka in November 2025 on AI adoption, governance, 
risk management, data readiness and strategic priorities.2 
However, as AI is rapidly evolving, current status could be 
slightly different. This Special Note summarizes the key 
findings3 and examines the emerging risks with potential 
systemic implications with particular emphasis on cyber 
security resilience of LBs.
Current State of AI Adoption in LBs
In total, 69% of LBs have commenced some form of AI 
activity, although the depth of adoption remains shallow. No 
AI usage and no immediate plans were reported by 31% of 
LBs, while 21% were at exploratory or feasibility stage and 
17% had pilot projects under development. Further, 31% 
have moved to live deployment, 10% in limited areas, 17% 
across multiple functions and 4% with extensive integration. 
No bank reported an AI-first operational model.
Prevailing use cases cluster around fraud and anti-money 
laundering monitoring, credit scoring, customer facing 
chatbots, document processing and internal productivity 
applications. 
Faster 
service 
delivery, 
round-the-clock 
availability and lower service costs were identified as the 
principal customer benefits, while clear disclosure of AI 
usage was the most cited trust building measure. Generative 
AI applications are emerging in customer service and internal 
knowledge management.
Governance and Risk Management Practices
AI governance structures are still in the early stages of 
forming. 23% of LBs manage AI through integration with 
existing risk committees and an equal share through cross 
functional working groups, while 8% have established a board 
level AI oversight committee and 15% a senior management 
AI steering committee. AI governance arrangements are yet 
to be formed in 17% of LBs.
Risk assessment practices display a comparable skew. 
Banks concentrate on technology, operational, compliance 
and model risk, while credit, market and liquidity risk receive 
less attention. AI is presently treated as a technological 
deployment matter rather than a driver of financial risk.
Third Party Dependence and Concentration
62% of LBs reported partnerships with a small group of 
international technology companies. Engagement with local 
technology firms (24%), regional fintech companies and 
open source solutions (21% each) and system integrators 
and AI consultancies (17% each) is substantially lower.
Due diligence on AI service providers and data security 
requirements in contracts stand at 17%, service level 
agreements at 16%, exit strategies and data portability 
clauses at 14%, board approval for AI outsourcing and 
vendor business continuity arrangements at 13%, and the 
right to audit vendor operations at only 10%. Narrow provider 
concentration combined with contractual controls that need 
strengthening is the most consequential finding of the survey.
Implications for Cyber Security Resilience and 
Financial Stability 
Cyber security and risk concerns ranked among the three 
most cited adoption challenges (15% of responses), alongside 
limited local AI talent (17%) and high implementation 
costs (15%). The concern is well founded.

The principal systemic risk arises not from novel attack 
techniques but from the speed, frequency and breadth with 
which AI allows vulnerabilities to be discovered and exploited 
across widely used technologies. Industry data indicate that 
activity by AI enabled adversaries rose by 89% between 
2024 and 2025, while the average time taken by attackers 
to move laterally within a compromised network fell by 65% 
to 29 minutes.4 The window for detection and containment is 
narrowing towards machine speed.
These dynamics bear directly on LBs. AI lowers the cost and 
raises the impact of attacks on banks and their customers. 
Generative models enable phishing and business email 
compromise in fluent Sinhala, Tamil and English at scale, 
while synthetic voice and video permit impersonation 
of customers and senior officers, threatening remote 
onboarding, video based customer identification and 
payment authorization controls. In this context, an emerging 
risk can be observed in relation to fraud typologies in 
domestic retail payment channels.
Adoption also expands the attack surface. Model endpoints, 
application 
programming 
interfaces, 
training 
data 
repositories and vector databases sit outside conventional 
perimeter controls, and attack vectors specific to AI systems, 
such as prompt injections, training data poisoning and model 
inversion are not addressed by existing control baselines. 
Unsanctioned staff use of public generative AI tools creates 
a further channel for confidential data to leave the bank's 
control boundary.
Most consequentially for financial stability, AI concentrates 
exposure. Where banks rely on the same limited set of 
cloud and model providers, a compromise or outage at a 
single provider ceases to be idiosyncratic and becomes a 
common mode failure across institutions. Emerging markets 
and developing economies are disproportionately exposed, 
sharing the same global digital infrastructure as advanced 
economies, but with fewer defensive resources, more 
limited supervisory capacity and greater reliance on smaller 
vendors whose patching cycles are longer, extending the 
window during which known vulnerabilities remain open. For 
Sri Lanka, this is the operative warning.
Offsetting these exposures, AI strengthens defensive 
capability through anomaly detection, behavioral analytics 
and automated triage. The supervisory expectation is 
therefore symmetrical that banks investing in AI for revenue 
generating functions are expected to invest commensurately 
in machine speed defense. Prevention alone is no longer 
sufficient. Segmentation, zero trust architecture, disciplined 
access control and secure by design practices that limit the 
blast radius of a breach and constrain lateral movement are 
now central to resilience.

Conclusion
AI adoption in the Sri Lankan banking sector is broad in intent, 
and more work is required on execution and governance 
and third party controls. The window in which supervisory 
expectations can be set ahead of scale therefore remains 
open. Cyber security resilience is the binding constraint that 
the same technology that improves detection also equips 
adversaries and concentrates dependence upon a small 
number of external providers. Strengthening board oversight, 
contractual control over AI service providers, investments in 
infrastructure, incident reporting discipline and resilience 
testing calibrated to AI specific threats will be essential to 
ensure that AI adoption enhances financial system stability.

3.4	 Cyber Risks and Operational 
Resilience of Financial Institutions
As digitalisation continues to accelerate across 
Sri Lanka’s financial system, strengthening 
operational and cybersecurity resilience remains 
important for safeguarding the overall financial 
system 
stability. 
Financial 
institutions 
have 
continued to expand digital financial services and 
payment channels, improving accessibility, efficiency 
and convenience of financial services. However, 
increased digitalisation, greater interconnectedness 
and growing reliance on technology and third party 
service providers may also broaden the financial 
system’s exposure to cyber and operational risks. 
A significant cyber incident affecting a systemically 
important institution or critical financial market 
infrastructure could disrupt the provision of essential 
financial services, impair payment and settlement 
activities, and potentially undermine confidence in the 
financial system.
In response to the evolving cyber threat 
landscape, including cyberattacks, ransomware, 
phishing, social engineering, and third party 
vulnerabilities, the Central Bank strengthened 
its 
cyber 
resilience 
oversight 
framework 
across the financial sector. Regulatory and 
supervisory initiatives focused on strengthening 
cyber risk governance, enhancing incident reporting, 
modernising critical systems, strengthening oversight 
of third party service providers, and promoting 
regular cyber resilience and business continuity and 
disaster recovery arrangements. These measures 
aim to improve the preparedness and operational 
resilience of the financial system, mitigate emerging 
digitalisation related risks, and support the stability of 
the financial system.
Incidents reported to the regulator indicate 
that digital scams and phishing accounted for 
the majority. While most incidents did not result 
in a direct business impact, potential reputational 
consequences, particularly the erosion of customer 
trust 
and 
confidence, 
remain 
key 
concerns. 
Meanwhile, reported system outages and interruptions 
also underscore the importance of maintaining the 
availability and operational resilience of critical digital 
financial services.
Amid the rising prevalence of online banking fraud, 
phishing attacks, social engineering schemes, 
and fraudulent investment activities, authorities 
and industry stakeholders strengthened fraud 
prevention and consumer protection measures.
