The continued pursuit of structural reforms, 
underpinned by sustained policy discipline, 
remains vital to further strengthening 
Sri Lanka’s economic resilience and 
securing sustainable economic growth 
in an era of heightened uncertainty. 
The global and regional landscape is 
increasingly characterised by severe and 
frequent economic shocks, underscoring 
the imperative of building and preserving 
adequate buffers across fiscal, external, 
and monetary fronts to safeguard 
macroeconomic stability. The value of such 
buffers has been clearly demonstrated 
through their role in absorbing the impact 
of Cyclone Ditwah and mitigating potential 
spillovers from the Middle East war. 
Preserving and reinforcing these hard-
earned gains in macroeconomic stabilisation 
requires unwavering commitment to fiscal 
consolidation to enhance debt sustainability 
and maintain policy credibility. In this 
context, the successful completion of the 
current IMF-supported programme in 
2027 will be pivotal in reinforcing investor 
confidence, while any need for subsequent 
arrangements remains contingent on 
future developments. Looking ahead, 
sustaining the growth momentum will 
depend critically on strengthening economic 
diversification, enhancing competitiveness, 
and raising productivity. In an increasingly 
volatile and shock-prone environment, the 
country’s capacity to respond with timely, 
well-calibrated, and credible policy actions 
will be central to preserving macroeconomic 
stability and ensuring a resilient, inclusive, and 
sustainable growth trajectory for Sri Lanka.

2025, external debt restructuring has been largely completed, except for a small remaining portion.

(b)	 With effect from 27 November 2024, the OPR is defined as the policy interest rate of the Central Bank under the single policy rate mechanism. SDFR and SLFR are linked to the OPR with a pre-determined margin as decided by the Central Bank, and continue 
to serve as interest rates applicable under the standing facilities of the Central Bank.    
(c)	 The rate at which the Central Bank grants advances to banking institutions as the lender of last resort (LOLR). Up to April 2020, the Bank Rate was a fixed rate determined by the Monetary Board. Since 16 April 2020, the Bank Rate was allowed to be 
determined automatically with a margin of 300 bps above the SLFR. Since 03 November 2022, Bank Rate was allowed to commensurately be adjusted in line with the monthly Average Weighted New Deposit Rate (AWNDR) published by the Central Bank 
with a margin of +700 bps. This margin was subsequently reduced to +300 bps with effect from 02 January 2023, with the resulting rate rounded to the nearest half percentage point. Since 01 March 2023, Bank Rate was delisted from monetary policy 
instruments and it is to be considered as a policy instrument that the Central Bank uses as the LOLR to support the stability of the banking and financial system.
(d)	 The Average Weighted Deposit Rate (AWDR) is calculated by the Central Bank monthly, based on interest rates pertaining to all outstanding interest bearing rupee deposits held with licensed commercial banks (LCBs).
(e)	 The Average Weighted Fixed Deposit Rate (AWFDR) is calculated by the Central Bank monthly, based on interest rates pertaining to all outstanding interest bearing rupee time deposits held with LCBs.
(f)	 The Average Weighted New Deposit Rate (AWNDR) is calculated by the Central Bank monthly, based on interest rates pertaining to all new interest bearing rupee deposits mobilised by LCBs during a particular month.
(g)	 The Average Weighted New Fixed Deposit Rate (AWNFDR) is calculated by the Central Bank monthly, based on interest rates pertaining to all new interest bearing rupee time deposits mobilised by LCBs during a particular month.

Note: With the establishment of the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) under the Ministry of Finance (MOF), the responsibility for recording and publishing Sri Lanka’s public debt now falls under the PDMO, as mandated 
by the provisions of the Public Debt Management Act, No. 33 of 2024. Accordingly, the Quarterly Statistical Debt Bulletin, published by the PDMO, serves as the official source for debt statistics. The Central Bank compiles and 
present this table based on data received from the MOF, to ensure the data continuity.	
	
(a) 	 As per the guidelines of compiling government debt statistics based on the Public Sector Debt Statistics Framework published by the IMF, non resident holdings of outstanding SLDBs have been classified under foreign debt and resident holdings of 
outstanding ISBs of the  Sri Lankan Government have been classified under domestic debt. Further, debt statistics are presented on net basis (net of deposits).	
(b) 	From 1950 to 1973, the outstanding balance is reported as at end September and thereafter as at end December.
(c)	 From 2023 onwards, domestic debt compilation method was changed and is based on the data confirmed by the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development.
(d) 	Rupee denominated Treasury bills issued to foreign investors from 2008 onwards are excluded from domestic debt and included in foreign debt	
(e) 	 Rupee denominated Treasury bonds issued to foreign investors from 2007 onwards are excluded from domestic debt and included in foreign debt.
(f) 	 Data are based on GDP estimates compiled by DCS. From 2010 onwards, data are based on the GDP estimates (base year 2015) of DCS. GDP estimates for 2023 and 2024 are revised based on the GDP estimates released on 17 March 2026.
(g) 	The central government debt statistics at end 2019 could increase should the adjustment for payment arrears in government expenditure as per the Ministry of Finance be incorporated into the net financing of the budget deficit in 2019. However, 
such an adjustment would have no impact on the outstanding central government debt at end 2020.
(h) 	 Foreign loan debt statistics and classification of foreign debt for 2024 and 2025 are prepared based on the data sourced from the Commonwealth Secretariat Debt Recording and Management System (CS-DRMS) maintained by MOF, and extracted 
on 27 February 2025 and 31 January 2026, respectively.	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
(i)  	 Provisional
(j) 	 The outstanding central government debt excludes several debt service payments that became overdue after 12 April 2022, the date of which the Interim Policy regarding the servicing of Sri Lanka’s external public debt was announced by the 
Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development. These debt service payments comprise of overdue interest payments of affected debt which deemed to be capitalised as per the Interim Policy. Further, December 2022 balances excluded 
several overdue interest payments in relation to SLDB, from April 2021 till end 2022.
(k) 	 Includes outstanding balance of the government guaranteed foreign currency debt of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation that was absorbed into central government debt.
(l)	 From December 2022 onwards, several outstanding project loans which were previously classified under Ceylon Electricity Board, Airport and Aviation Services Ltd. and Sri Lanka Ports Authority were absorbed into central government debt.
(m)	 The 2024 and 2025 data reflects the impact of external debt restructuring.

1.1   Overview 
Sri Lanka demonstrated resilience in responding 
to the internal and external shocks arising from 
Cyclone Ditwah and the Middle East conflict. 
The conflict poses macroeconomic and fiscal 
risks, most immediately through the sharp 
depreciation of exchange rate, underscoring 
the need for continuous structural reforms over 
the medium term to long term. The fuel prices 
were the first to be affected, with knock-on risks 
to other macroeconomic variables, particularly 
tourist arrivals. To address the urgent needs 
of the people, the Government introduced a 
multifaceted relief programme in April 2026 to 
cushion the cost of living for households and 
vulnerable groups, while providing relief to the 
Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) and other 
fuel suppliers to maintain retail prices below 
the cost-reflective levels, and the National 
System Operator (NSO) for the provision of an 
electricity subsidy for consumers.
The relief programme included:
•	
A fuel subsidy of Rs. 15 billion provided 
to the CPC corresponding to quantities of 
92 Octane Petrol and Lanka Auto Diesel 
sold during April 2026;
•	
An electricity subsidy of Rs. 15 billion to 
the NSO for consumers with monthly 
consumption below 180 units, as well as 
hotels, industries and businesses in the 
relevant consumer categories;
•	
An enhanced fertilizer subsidy for the 
Yala season, increasing the allowance 
per hectare for paddy farmers from Rs. 
25,000 to Rs. 30,000 and for field crop 
cultivators from Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 18,000, 
up to a maximum of two hectares per 
farmer per season;
•	
Targeted cash transfers to Aswesuma 
beneficiaries, raising the Rs. 17,500 
payments to Rs. 25,000 and the Rs. 
10,000 payments to Rs. 15,000; and 
•	
Relief measures to support the fisheries 
sector.
The ongoing Middle East conflict and the 
effective closure of Strait of Hormuz pose risks 
to Sri Lanka’s economic stabilisation across 
several channels and at varying magnitudes. 
The trade deficit is expected to widen, given 
Sri Lanka’s position as a net importer of oil, 
which accounts for approximately 25 percent 
of the total import bill. Remittance inflows face 
downside risk, as the Middle East accounts for 
approximately 50 percent of total remittances, 
notwithstanding the surge in remittances during 
the first four months of 2026. Tourist arrivals 
declined by 2.3 percent to 876,277 persons 
in the first four months of 2026, compared to 
896,884 persons in the same period of 2025, 
with earnings falling by 19.4 percent to USD 
1,111.0 million. Pressure on the exchange rate 
has added to the import burden, while headline 
inflation rose to 5.5 percent in May 2026 from 1.6 
percent in February 2026. Gross official reserves 
of USD 6.8 billion as at end April 2026 provide 
a near-term buffer to manage these pressures. 
However, a prolonged conflict carries significant 
ramifications for macroeconomic stabilization 
and the protection of vulnerable segments of 
society. 
The Government is pursuing a forward-
looking reform agenda  to sustain  the  growth 
momentum, encompassing public financial 
management (PFM) reforms, energy sector 
reforms, 
strengthening 
social 
protection 
through the targeted Aswesuma programme, 
digitalization 
initiatives, 
export 
sector 
diversification, and improvements to the 
investment climate. The Middle East conflict has, 
however, introduced headwinds to the agenda, 
as reflected in key economic indicators. 
2025 marked a significant milestone in Sri Lanka's 
post-crisis economic trajectory.  The gains 
achieved through successive years of difficult 
but necessary reforms were reflected in broad-
based economic expansion, strengthened fiscal 
balances, and improved external resilience. 
Sri Lanka entered 2025 with a renewed policy 
direction, underpinned by a clear mandate, an 
unwavering commitment to structural reform, 
and a firm resolve to sustain macroeconomic 
stabilisation in the long-term interests of the 
country.

Box 1.2 l  Reform, Recovery and Resilience: Sri Lanka's Progress Under the  
IMF Extended Fund Facility 
Sri Lanka introduced a series of structural reforms through a four-year Extended Fund Facility 
arrangement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF-EFF), entered into in March 2023. 
Three years into the programme, it has delivered substantial  gains, moving the country from 
crisis to recovery and now towards stabilisation.  However,  the economy continues to face 
both external and domestic shocks that test its resilience.  In November 2025, Cyclone Ditwah 
struck just as recovery momentum was building, inflicting severe humanitarian and economic 
damage. Subsequently, in late February 2026, the Middle East conflict triggered a renewed 
surge in global energy prices, adding fresh external pressures on an  economy still in recovery. 
Sri Lanka's ability to navigate these sequential and compounding shocks—without abandoning 
fiscal discipline or reversing core reforms—reflects the institutional resilience that sustained 
reform had begun to create. 
From Crisis to Recovery to Stabilization: Gains in 2025
By end-2025, Sri Lanka had achieved substantial and broad-based macroeconomic gains, 
driven by reforms implemented under the IMF-EFF programme.
All end-December 2025 Quantitative Performance Criteria (QPCs) and Indicative Targets (ITs) 
were met, with revenue and primary balance targets significantly exceeded. The central 
government primary balance (floor) target of Rs. 730 billion was surpassed, recording an over 
performance surplus of Rs. 1,756 billion. Central government tax revenue surpassed the QPC 
target of Rs. 4,350 billion by 16.1 percent, reaching Rs. 5,049 billion.

Structural reforms advanced across multiple fronts during 2025: 
•	
The Fiscal Strategy Statement and Fiscal Risk Statement were published in June 2025 
under the Public Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024 (PFMA).
•	
The Integrated Treasury Management Information System (ITMIS) was fully rolled out 
across all spending heads, strengthening expenditure commitment controls.
•	
The Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy 2025–2029 was published by the newly 
operationalized Public Debt Management Office, enhancing transparency in government 
borrowing. 
•	
The Simplified Value Added Tax (SVAT) system was repealed with effect from October 1, 
2025, and replaced with a risk-based refund scheme. 
•	
Cost-recovery pricing for fuel was maintained throughout 2025 under the formula-based 
adjustment framework, while electricity tariffs were restored to cost-recovery levels in 
June 2025 through a 15 percent average tariff increase. 
•	
The Companies Act was amended in August 2025 to introduce beneficial ownership 
requirements in line with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards, and the Beneficial 
Ownership Registry was operationalized. 
•	
Amendments to the Strategic Development Projects Act and Port City Act introduced 
transparent, rules-based eligibility criteria for tax incentives. 
•	
The Aswesuma social protection programme was expanded in 2025, with social spending 
targets met for the first time in the programme's history.
Cyclone Ditwah: Crisis Response and the Rapid Financing Instrument
On November 28, 2025, Cyclone Ditwah struck Sri Lanka, causing over 800 fatalities, affecting 
approximately 2 million people, and displacing more than 100,000 persons while disrupting 
the infrastructure, agricultural lands, and irrigation systems. In response, emergency relief 
measures were financed through expenditure reprioritization within the existing budget, 
rather than through monetary expansion or unplanned borrowing. The PFMA played a critical 
role: by invoking the escape clause under Section 16, the Government has accommodated 
additional relief and reconstruction expenditure through a transparent, rules-based mechanism. 
A supplementary budget was approved by Parliament, accompanied by a commitment to 
publish a fiscal recovery plan outlining the path back to the programme’s established fiscal 
targets. 
The Fifth Review under the IMF-EFF was nearing completion when the cyclone struck; a Staff-
Level Agreement had been reached on October 9, 2025. Given the scale of the disaster 
and the time needed to assess its economic impact, comprehensively, Sri Lanka requested 
emergency financing under the Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI). On December 19, 2025, the 
IMF Executive Board approved SDR 150.5 million (approximately USD 206 million). The RFI 
served as a complementary emergency instrument, not a replacement for the IMF-EFF. 
Combined Fifth and Sixth Review: Maintaining Momentum into 2026
On May 27, 2026, the IMF Executive Board approved the combined Fifth and Sixth Review 
under the EFF, authorizing SDR 508 million (approximately USD 695 million) in disbursements, 
representing the sixth and seventh tranches under the programme.

Key elements of the programme framework for 2026 include:
•	
Temporary fiscal accommodation: Fiscal policy was eased in 2026 to accommodate 
post-cyclone reconstruction permitting primary expenditure to exceed the 13 percent 
of GDP ceiling. The Government is committed to returning to the primary expenditure 
ceiling from 2027 onwards, with a fiscal recovery plan to be published outlining the path 
of adjustment.
•	
Energy sector response: Escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East in early 2026 
drove a sharp rise in global energy prices. Fuel prices were adjusted twice in March 2026 
to partially pass through higher import costs. In response, a targeted and time-bound 
package of fuel, electricity, and fertilizer subsidies was introduced, with a combined cap 
of Rs. 100 billion.  Separately, the Ceylon Electricity Board was formally unbundled in March 
2026, following Electricity Act amendments adopted in 2025— a landmark structural 
reform aimed at improving operational efficiency and transparency in the electricity 
sector.
•	
Structural reform continuity: Most structural benchmarks due by end-June 2026 are 
on track. Key reform priorities for the remainder of 2026 include the adoption of PFMA 
implementing regulations; the development of a Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) 
informed by planned tax diagnostic assessments; the approval by Cabinet of a property 
taxation design and implementation plan; and the finalisation of the debt restructuring 
process by mid-2026.

The Broader Lesson: Reforms Build Resilience and Lay the Foundation for Sustained Growth
The year 2025 illustrates that the value of Sri Lanka's reform programme lies not only in the 
macroeconomic indicators it improved, but in the institutional resilience it built—the capacity 
to absorb severe shocks without abandoning fiscal discipline or reversing core reforms. Fiscal 
consolidation created emergency response capacity. Stronger reserve buffers enhanced 
external resilience. Debt restructuring reduced near-term financing pressures. Governance 
reforms strengthened policy credibility. The PFM framework ensured that even extraordinary 
emergency spending was managed with transparency and accountability. 
Significant challenges remain. Public debt, while declining, remains elevated and will require 
sustained primary surpluses over the medium term. Global trade policy uncertainty and the 
Middle East conflict continue to pose risks to energy costs, trade flows, foreign inflows and 
external financing conditions. Climate-related vulnerabilities remain a major concern, as Cyclone 
Ditwah starkly demonstrated. As the IMF-EFF programme moves towards its conclusion in 
2027, sustaining reform momentum beyond the programme— through domestic ownership of 
reforms, institutional discipline, and a continued commitment to fiscal sustainability—will be 
crucial for durable economic stability and long-term sustainability.

improvements in household incomes and the 
gradual normalisation of domestic economic 
activity.
 
The national savings-to-GDP ratio improved to 
31.2 percent in 2025 from 27.6 percent in 2024, 
reflecting strengthened financial conditions and 
improved income levels across the economy. 
The broad-based nature of this expansion—
encompassing all major sectors and both the 
consumption and investment components 
of demand—suggests that the recovery is 
grounded in improved economic fundamentals 
rather than temporary or sector-specific factors.
Monetary 
policy 
in 
2025 
remained 
accommodative, aimed at supporting the 
ongoing economic recovery while preserving 
the price stability achieved in earlier tightening 
cycles. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) 
reduced the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) by 
25 basis points to 7.75 percent in May 2025, 
maintaining it at that level through the remainder 
of the year, continuing the accommodative cycle 
initiated in June 2023 amid declining inflation and 
improving macroeconomic conditions. However,

Headline inflation, as measured by the year-on-

eleven consecutive months from September

revisions in energy prices and favourable base 
effects. Inflation returned to positive territory 
in August 2025 and increased gradually to 2.1 
percent by end-2025. 
 
Inflation rose to 5.5 percent in May 2026, 
primarily due to elevated global fuel prices 
that necessitated a sharp upward adjustment in 
domestic fuel prices. This uptick is largely supply-
driven, though demand-side pressures have 
strengthened, as reflected in the expansion of 
private sector credit and credit-driven imports,

25, 2026, a maximum loan-to-value (LTV) ratio

Labour market conditions improved, with the

sectors.

Box 1.4 l  Governance Reforms in Sri Lanka: 2025 -2026 and Way Forward contd...
Anti-Corruption Reform 
Anti-corruption has emerged as a key governance pillar of the government, advanced under 
the 'Clean Sri Lanka' initiative across legislative, institutional, and enforcement dimensions. 
The Proceeds of Crime Act, No. 5 of 2025 marks a landmark step in Sri Lanka's anti-corruption 
framework, enabling authorities to seize, freeze, and dispose of illegally acquired assets without 
requiring a prior criminal prosecution. This represents a significant shift in the country's approach 
to combating corruption, strengthening its capacity to recover unlawfully acquired wealth 
and promote greater accountability. Complementing this, the National Anti-Corruption Action 
Plan 2025–2029 (NACAP) was formally launched on 9 April 2025 by the CIABOC with United 
Nations Development Programme (UNDP) support, structured around four strategic pillars 
encompassing prevention, institutional strengthening and enforcement, public education, and 
law and policy reform. The expanded CIABOC mandate under the Anti-Corruption Act, No. 9 
of 2023 further broadened the Commission's jurisdiction to include money laundering, private 
sector bribery, and trading in influence, and resulted in over a dozen major investigations 
involving senior political figures and public officials. At the enforcement level, the Government 
has pursued high profile accountability measures.
Rule of Law and Civil Liberties
Progress in the area of rule of law and civil liberties has been measured, with several legislative 
and accountability commitments at an early stage of implementation. Notably, the Government 
has prioritized strengthening the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of 
Terrorism (AML/CFT) framework, with amendments to the Convention on the Suppression of 
Terrorist Financing Act, No. 25 of 2005, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006, 
and the Financial Reporting Act, No. 6 of 2006 being progressed to strengthen compliance with 
international standards. The Online Safety Act, No. 9 of 2024 is in effect, and amendments are 
under consideration by the Government following public consultation. Sustained institutional 
follow-through across these areas will be essential to fulfilling the Government’s reform 
commitments.
Public Administration and Digital Governance
The Government has demonstrated a sustained commitment to modernizing public 
administration, advancing a comprehensive digital transformation agenda across multiple tiers 
of government. Key initiatives include the establishment of the GovPay system to facilitate 
digital payments for government institutions, the introduction of online platform payments 
in place of cash-based transactions, and the rollout of the Sri Lanka Unique Digital Identity 
Project to support streamlined access to public services.
Further structural developments include the establishment of a Digital Economy Authority, 
the implementation of e-invoicing across relevant institutions, the creation of Virtual Special 
Economic Zones to attract digital investment, and continued investment in broader digital 
infrastructure projects. At the grassroots level, the e-Grama Niladhari Platform has been 
deployed to digitalise village-level administration, while the Digital Economy Advancement 
Programme supports inter-agency communication modernization and capacity-building 
across provincial and local government institutions. 
Collectively, these initiatives are expected to yield measurable gains in government revenue 
through reduced leakages, improved tax compliance, and greater transactional transparency, 
while strengthening the efficiency, accessibility, and accountability of public service delivery. 
These developments reflect a coherent and forward-looking agenda to position Sri Lanka's 
public sector within a modern digital governance framework.

Box 1.5 l  Fiscal Rules and Governance 
Sri Lanka enacted the Public Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024 (PFMA) in 2024, repealing 
the Fiscal Management (Responsibility) Act, No. 03 of 2003 (FMRA), which had established 
a set of numerical fiscal rules. The PFMA introduced a comprehensive legal framework for 
fiscal responsibility, transparency, and accountability, anchored by a set of binding fiscal rules. 
Beyond a mere reporting instrument, the PFMA establishes for transparency, accountability, 
discipline, effectiveness, efficiency in managing public finances, while clarifying institutional 
responsibilities at all levels government.
Key fiscal rules requirements under the PFMA:
	•
Prepare and publish an annual Fiscal Strategy Statement (FSS) on or before 30 June each 
year, providing Parliament and the public with a formal statement of fiscal strategy prior 
to budget preparation;
	•
Maintain a rolling five-year Medium-Term Fiscal Framework (MTFF) that includes a primary 
balance target, a primary expenditure ceiling, and fiscal aggregate projections; and
	•
Publish in-year fiscal position reports, a mid-year fiscal review, and a final budget position 
report to ensure sustained public accountability.
The Four Fiscal Rules outlined in the PFMA
Under the PFMA's fiscal responsibility framework, our interlocking fiscal rules are designed to 
anchor debt sustainability and prevent the recurrence of fiscal crises.

Rule 1: Debt Reduction Objective
The debt reduction objective is particularly significant in Sri Lanka's context. Following the 
2022 debt default and the successful restructuring of external and domestic debt, restoring 
debt sustainability is the cornerstone of the country's macroeconomic recovery programme. 
The PFMA enshrines this debt reduction objective in law, providing it with the statutory force 
necessary to anchor medium-term fiscal framework.

Section 10(a) of the PFMA establishes the overarching fiscal objective to ensure that public 
debt is reduced to and maintained at a sustainable level. This is not a numerical cap but a 
qualitative anchor, all other fiscal targets and policies must be consistent with this objective. 
The proposed timeframe for achieving a sustainable debt level shall be included in the annual 
FSS, ensuring that the debt trajectory is transparently reported and subject to Parliamentary 
scrutiny.
Rule 2: Primary Balance Target
Section 14 of the PFMA requires that the MTFF include an annual primary balance target, defined 
as the difference between government revenue and primary expenditure (i.e., expenditure 
excluding interest payments), expressed as a percentage of forecast nominal GDP and set for 
the upcoming financial year and each of the four succeeding years. This target is required to 
be consistent with the debt reduction objective, linking the fiscal flow target to the stock-of-
debt anchor.
This rule functions as the central medium-term fiscal anchor. Unlike a simple deficit rule, a 
primary balance rule focuses on the part of the fiscal position directly under government 
control (i.e., excluding the inherited cost of existing debt). A sustained primary surplus signals 
the Government's capacity to service debt over time. The IMF-EFF programme has established 
an overall primary balance target of +2.3 percent of GDP, and the PFMA institutionalises the 
practice of setting and publishing such targets in a rolling medium-term framework through 
the annual FSS.
Rule 3: Primary Expenditure Ceiling of 13% of GDP
Section 15 of the PFMA introduces an annual ceiling on primary expenditure—government 
spending excluding interest payments on public debt— which shall not exceed 13 percent 
of estimated nominal GDP in each financial year. This ceiling is operationalised as an absolute 
rupee figure in the annual budget, derived from the GDP percentage limit.
The rule includes an escape clause that allows temporary deviation from the expenditure ceiling 
in the event of a natural disaster, epidemic, national security emergency, or a severe economic 
downturn, subject to Parliamentary notification and the publication of a plan for returning to 
compliance. This provides necessary flexibility while maintaining the rule's credibility as an 
anchor under normal conditions.
Rule 4: Government Guarantee Ceiling of 7.5% of GDP
Section 17 of the PFMA caps the aggregate stock of outstanding government guarantees at 7.5 
percent of the average GDP of the relevant financial year and the two preceding financial years. 
This three-year average base reduces the ceiling's sensitivity to year-to-year GDP volatility, 
providing a more stable benchmark. The limit is subject to review every five years to ensure 
alignment with the prevailing debt reduction objective.
This rule directly addresses one of the key drivers of Sri Lanka's debt crisis: the accumulation 
of large contingent liabilities through guarantees extended to loss-making  SOEs, particularly 
CEB and CPC. By placing a statutory cap on the total guarantee stock, the PFMA limits the 
potential crystallization of off-balance-sheet liabilities into direct government debt.

Governance beyond the numbers
Well designed and credibly enforced fiscal rules are among the most powerful instruments 
of fiscal governance. The empirical literature finds a robust positive relationship between the 
presence of binding fiscal rules and lower public debt, smaller deficits, and stronger fiscal 
discipline, particularly in countries emerging from episodes of fiscal stress. The four rules 
introduced under the PFMA address governance not merely by imposing numerical limits, but 
by fundamentally changing how fiscal decisions are made, disclosed, and held to account. 
Each rule works through distinct governance channels.
Transparency: Making the Fiscal Position Visible and Verifiable
A fundamental weakness of Sri Lanka's pre-crisis fiscal governance was opacity. Public debt 
had been systematically understated, SOE liabilities were kept off-balance sheet, and medium-
term fiscal plans were treated as non-binding. The PFMA's fiscal rules directly reverse this.
The debt reduction objective requires the Government to publicly disclose, in the annual 
FSS, a concrete timeframe and trajectory for reducing public debt to a sustainable level. The 
primary balance target reinforces this by requiring the Government to publish its projected 
fiscal path, expressed in standardized, comparable GDP terms, for five years forward. Citizens, 
market participants, and development partners are thereby enabled to assess not just the 
current fiscal position, but the Government's stated commitment and trajectory.
Most significantly for governance perspective, the government guarantee ceiling brings 
contingent liabilities—historically the least transparent segment of Sri Lanka's public finances— 
within a statutory disclosure and reporting framework. The PFMA requires the outstanding 
stock of guarantees to be calculated, reported, and monitored against a binding limit at the 
end of every financial year. This converts what was previously an off-balance-sheet fiscal risk 
into a visible, auditable, and constrained liability. Fiscal transparency of this kind has been 
shown to be positively correlated with lower sovereign borrowing costs and stronger credit 
ratings, as it reduces the information asymmetry between the government and its creditors.
Accountability: Creating Enforceable Commitments
Fiscal targets that exist only in budget speeches are easily abandoned. The FMRA's targets were 
amended multiple times without consequence, undermining any credibility the framework 
may have had. The PFMA's rules are structurally different; they are embedded in statute, and 
the Act requires a formal assessment of compliance or non-compliance with each target to 
be published in the FSS and in the final budget position report (Annual Report). Any deviation 
from the primary expenditure ceiling must be explained, and a plan for returning to compliance 
presented to Parliament.
The primary balance target creates an explicitly measurable, annually assessed benchmark. 
Because the target is defined as a percentage of GDP and published five years ahead, it is both 
observable and comparable.

The primary expenditure ceiling is particularly strong in its accountability effect. Because it 
applies to every supplementary budget and appropriation bill—not just the original annual 
budget—it prevents the common practice of circumventing fiscal targets through in-year 
supplementary spending. The Minister of Finance seeking to authorize expenditure above the 
statutory ceiling must present a formal escape clause declaration to Parliament, creating a 
clear, visible accountability event. In Sri Lanka's history, unconstrained supplementary budgets 
were a major vehicle for fiscal slippage; the ceiling directly closes this governance gap.
Constraint on Executive Discretion: Limiting the Deficit Bias
The 13 percent primary expenditure ceiling is the most direct constraint on executive discretion. 
By placing a hard statutory limit on aggregate primary spending—regardless of what individual 
ministries demand or what political pressures arise—the rule forces fiscal trade-offs to be 
made explicitly and transparently within the budget process, rather than resolved by deficit 
financing. This shifts the fiscal decision making, from executive convenience toward a rules-
based framework with explicit Parliamentary oversight.
The government guarantee ceiling addresses an indirect but equally important dimension of 
executive discretion. The use of guarantees as a quasi-fiscal instrument to extend politically 
motivated support to SOEs while keeping the expenditure off the budget. The 7.5 percent 
cap transforms what was previously an unconstrained executive privilege into a legislatively 
bounded decision. When the guarantee stock approaches the ceiling, the Government must 
make an explicit, public choice—which guarantee to extend, which to withdraw, and how to 
manage the associated fiscal risk. 
Intergenerational Equity: Distributing Fiscal Burdens Fairly
The PFMA's overarching fiscal responsibility objective, as outlined under Section 9, explicitly 
includes intergenerational equity as a governing principle—the obligation of the current 
generation of decision-makers not to impose unsustainable fiscal burdens on future citizens. 
This principle is operationalised through the fiscal rules.
The debt reduction objective, by requiring a credible and publicly disclosed debt reduction 
trajectory, prevents governments from borrowing today to finance current consumption at the 
expense of future taxpayers who inherit the debt service burden. The primary balance target, 
by requiring a surplus sufficient to reduce the debt to GDP ratio, ensures that each year's 
budget makes a positive contribution to restoring intergenerational fiscal balance. Together, 
these two rules embed a long-horizon discipline. 
Fiscal Credibility: Anchoring Market and Investor Confidence
Fiscal governance operates not only through domestic accountability mechanisms but also 
through its effect on the expectations of creditors, investors, and international partners. In 
Sri Lanka's post-restructuring context, restoring market confidence is both economically 
imperative and essential for re-establishing governance credibility.

Numerical fiscal rules with statutory force provide a stronger credibility signal precisely 
because they are harder to revise silently. Any amendment to the PFMA's fiscal targets requires 
Parliamentary approval, which is observable and politically costly. This is further reinforced by 
publishing a fiscal path five years ahead and providing creditors and investors with a basis for 
assessing the sustainability of the Government's fiscal stance.
Conclusion
The four fiscal rules introduced under the PFMA represent a meaningful advance in Sri Lanka's 
fiscal governance architecture. Rather than merely setting numerical limits, they provide 
Parliament and the public with a structured basis for  scrutinizing how fiscal decisions are made, 
disclosed, and held account. The debt reduction objective and primary balance target impose 
transparency obligations and long-horizon discipline on a political process that previously 
privileged short-term spending. The primary expenditure ceiling constrains executive 
discretion and closes the supplementary budget loophole that historically accommodated 
fiscal slippage. The government guarantee ceiling brings the opaque dimension of public 
liability— SOE contingent risk—within a statutory accountability framework for the first time.

measures. The All-Share Price Index (ASPI) gained 
41.9 percent to 22,624.3 points at end-2025 from 
15,944.6 points at end-2024, while the Standard 
& Poor’s Sri Lanka 20 (S&P SL20) index rose 26.6 
percent to 6,157.4 points from 4,862.1 points over 
the same period. Market capitalisation increased 
by 41.7 percent to Rs. 8,068.6 billion at end-2025, 
from Rs. 5,695.6 billion at end-2024.
2.2 	
Sri Lankan Economy
The Sri Lankan economy grew at a faster pace in 
both 2025 and 2024, compared to a contraction 
of 2.0 percent in 2023. The Agriculture sector 
recorded moderate growth of 1.4 percent in 
2025, up from 0.6 percent in 2024, supported 
by broad-based expansions across sub-sectors. 
The Industry sector expanded by 7.8 percent in 
2025, sustaining the strong momentum observed 
in 2024.  Meanwhile, the Services sector grew by 
3.3 percent in 2025, compared to 2.4 percent in 
the previous year.
GDP at current market prices increased to Rs. 
32,750.8 billion in 2025 from Rs. 30,095.8 billion in 
2024, reflecting a nominal growth of 8.8 percent. 
In USD terms, GDP rose to USD 108.8 billion in 
2025 from USD 99.6 billion in 2024. GDP per capita 
increased to USD 5,003 in 2025 from USD 4,546 in 
2024.
In 2025, investment expenditure grew by 22.4 
percent in current market prices, supported 
by a strong rebound in gross fixed capital 
formation, driven mainly by increased spending 
on 
construction 
and 
transport 
equipment. 
Consumption 
expenditure, 
comprising 
both 
private and government consumption, grew 
moderately by 5.9 percent in 2025, compared 
to 7.0 percent in 2024, reflecting a 6.0 percent 
expansion in private consumption and a 5.6 
percent increase in government consumption, and 
remained the principal contributor to aggregate 
demand.
Meanwhile, 
net 
external 
demand 
declined 
significantly by 61.7 percent in current market 
prices, compared to a decline of 32.6 percent in 
2024, as growth in import expenditure outpaced 
that of exports, exerting downward pressure on 
overall demand.
National savings expanded by 23.2 percent 
in current prices in 2025, compared to 15.9 
percent growth in 2024, driven mainly by an 18.1 
percent increase in domestic savings alongside 
improved net income inflows from the rest of the 
world. Reflecting this improvement, the national

Agriculture Sector
The Agriculture sector expanded  in 2025, driven 
mainly by growth in animal production, oleaginous 
fruits cultivation, and growing of rice. Additionally, 
the forest and logging, agricultural supported 
activities, growing of fruits, tea, sugarcane, 
tobacco and other non-perennial crops, spices, 
aromatic drug and,  pharmaceutical crops, cereals 
(except rice), plant propagation, sub-sectors 
contributed positively to this performance. 
However, a contraction was witnessed in several 
sub-sectors, including freshwater fishing and fresh 
water aquaculture, growing of vegetables, other 
perennial crops, rubber, other beverage crops, 
and marine fishing and marine aquaculture.
At current prices, the Agriculture sector accounted 
for 8.4 percent of GDP in 2025. The sector continues 
to play a critical role in the economy, particularly 
in terms of employment and rural livelihoods. This 
underscores the importance of implementing 
targeted policy measures to enhance productivity, 
and address persistent structural challenges, 
including climate variability, inefficient resource 
utilization, post-harvest losses, limited access to 
quality inputs, and market constraints, to ensure 
sustainable growth in the  sector.

Paddy
In value-added terms, the rice sub-sector recorded 
a moderate growth of 5.3 percent in 2025, up from 
4.0 percent in 2024. Both the gross extent of sown 
and net extent harvested increased in 2025: the 
former rose by 4.2 percent to 1,341,885 hectares 
in 2025 from 1,287,989 hectares in 2024, while 
the latter increased by 4.8 percent to 1,186,455 
hectares in 2025 from 1,131,859 hectares in 2024. 
Total paddy production increased by 7.6 percent 
to 5,053,698 metric tons in 2025, comprising 
2,745,298 metric tons from the 2024/25 Maha 
season and 2,308,400 metric tons from the Yala 
season, compared to 4,698,454 metric tons in 
2024. The yield per hectare increased by 2.6 
percent to 4,259.5 kilograms per hectare in 2025 
compared to 4,151.1 kilograms per hectare in 2024, 
attributable primarily to the high-yielding paddy 
varieties and the adoption of modern farming 
techniques. In line with higher production, rice 
prices declined in 2025 relative to 2024. The 
average retail price of Samba rice at the Pettah 
market fell by 0.9 percent to Rs. 253.81 per kilogram 
in December 2025 from Rs. 256.00 per kilogram 
December 2024. The average retail price of Nadu 
rice declined by 10.2 percent to Rs. 230.00 per 
kilogram in December 2025 from Rs. 256.00 per 
kilogram in December 2024. Similarly, the average 
retail price of Kekulu (Red) rice decreased by 12.7 
percent to Rs. 216.90 per kilogram in December 
2025 from Rs. 248.47 per kilogram in December 
2024. 
The total rice imports increased sharply by 40.7 
percent to 184,750 metric tons in 2025 from 
131,338 metric tons in 2024. The government 
continued the fertilizer subsidy scheme with a 
spending of Rs. 37 billion in 2025. The Government 
Paddy Purchasing Program also continued in 
2025, incurring approximately Rs. 19,633 million 
to purchase 162,257 MT paddy through the Paddy 
Marketing Board (PMB).

Coconut
Coconut subsector expanded by 8.2 percent in 
2025 compared to a contraction of 11.5 percent 
in 2024.  Coconut production increased by 9.0 
percent to 3,042 million nuts from 2,792 million 
nuts in 2024, driven primarily by favorable 
weather conditions that prevailed throughout the 
year. Desiccated coconut production increased 
by 3.6 percent to 308.1 million nuts, from 297.3 
million nuts in 2024. Production of coconut cream, 
coconut milk powder, and coconut milk increased 
significantly, recording a growth of 18.7 percent in 
2025. In contrast, coconut oil production declined 
by 8.1 percent to 49.5 million nuts in 2025 from 
53.9 million nuts in the previous year.
In terms of exports, the total export volume of 
copra increased significantly by 128.5 percent 
to 0.786 million kilograms, while export volume 
of coconut oil increased by 13.0 percent to 26.7 
million kilograms in 2025 compared to 2024. 
The total export volume of desiccated coconut 
decreased by 9.0 percent to 52.1 million kilograms 
in 2025. The average FOB price of coconut 
increased significantly by 57.1 percent to Rs. 125.86 
per nut in 2025 from Rs. 80.13 per nut in 2024.
Minor Export Crops 
The export performance of minor export crops in 
2025 exhibited mixed trends. Cinnamon exports, 
the largest contributor within this category, 
increased marginally by 0.8 percent to 19,965 
metric tons from 19,809 metric tons in 2024. In 
contrast, pepper exports declined significantly 
by 49.2 percent to 13,404 metric tons from 26,388 
metric tons in 2024, weighing on overall export 
performance. Cocoa exports also decreased by 
23.2 percent to 76 metric tons from 99 metric tons 
in 2024.
Meanwhile, several crops recorded notable 
improvements. Cardamom exports increased 
substantially to 23 metric tons from 9 metric tons 
in 2024, while clove exports rose sharply by 161.5 
percent to 2,798 metric tons, reflecting favourable 
market conditions. Exports of nutmeg and mace 
increased moderately by 2.4 percent to 3,042 
metric tons from 2,971 metric tons in the previous 
year.
Overall, the performance of minor export crops 
in 2025 reflects divergent commodity-specific 
trends, with strong growth in certain high-value 
spices.
Tea
In value-added terms, the tea sub-sector recorded 
a marginal growth of 1.4 percent in 2025, compared 
to 1.9 percent in 2024. Total tea production edged 
up by 0.5 percent to 264.1 million kilograms in 
2025 from 262.7 million kilograms in 2024. 
Tea prices at the Colombo Tea Auction (CTA) 
declined by 4.7 percent to Rs. 1,186.50 per 
kilogram in 2025 from Rs. 1,245.10 per kilogram 
in 2024. The average export price (FOB) of tea 
decreased marginally by 0.2 percent to Rs. 
1,760.70 per kilogram in 2025 from Rs. 1,763.61 per 
kilogram in 2024 while, in USD terms, it edged up 
by 0.2 percent to USD 5.85 per kilogram in 2025 
from USD 5.84 per kilogram in 2024.
Rubber
In value-added terms, the rubber sub-sector 
contracted by 6.0 percent in 2025, compared to 
a positive growth of 4.0 percent in 2024, mainly 
due to a reduction in rubber production. Total 
rubber production decreased by 3.9 percent to 
66.5 million kilograms in 2025 from 69.2 million 
kilograms in 2024. 
Prices of RSS1 rubber at the Colombo Rubber 
Auction (CRA) decreased by 0.3 percent to Rs. 
712.14 per kilogram in 2025 from Rs. 714.03 per 
kilogram in 2024. Despite these negative trends, 
the total export value of rubber and rubber 
products increased significantly by 19.8 percent 
to Rs. 9,381 million in 2025, compared to a 
contraction of 15.7 percent to Rs. 7,832 million in 
2024, while the total export volume grew by 4.3 
percent to 9.0 million kilograms, compared to a 
contraction of 31.9 percent to 8.6 million kilograms 
in 2024. The average FOB price of rubber rose by 
14.8 percent to Rs. 1,041.58 per kilogram in 2025 
from Rs. 907.28 per kilogram in 2024, while in 
USD terms it increased by 15.3 percent to USD 
3.47 per kilogram from USD 3.01 per kilogram 
over the same period. The performance of the 
rubber sub-sector in 2025 was constrained by 
weather-related disruptions; therefore, improving 
plantation management practices and enhancing 
productivity remain important for the sustainable 
development of the industry.

Livestock

chicken

feed.

compared to a positive growth of 4.8 percent in 
2024, while the freshwater fishing and freshwater 
aquaculture sub-sector contracted by 45.3 
percent, compared to a contraction of 9.2 percent 
in the previous year. The fishing industry continues 
to face critical challenges, including overfishing, 
unsustainable fishing practices, pollution, and the 
adverse impacts of climate change. Addressing 
these through effective and targeted policy 
measures is essential to ensure the long-term 
sustainability of the sector.

Mining and Quarrying 
Mining and quarrying activities maintained strong 
growth in 2025, expanding by 16.9 percent and 
contributing 1.5 percent to GDP. This performance 
was largely driven by sustained demand for 
construction materials, with the mining of 
construction 
materials 
accounting 
for 
88.6 
percent of total value added and growing by 14.4 
percent. Gem mining recorded a notable increase 
of 34.1 percent, supported mainly by sapphire 
production, while other mineral mining activities 
grew by 16.6 percent.  The value of mineral exports 
declined marginally by 1.7 percent to Rs. 7,284 
million in 2025, compared to a steeper decline 
of 41.5 percent to Rs. 7,412 million in 2024. Export 
earnings from key minerals, including natural 
graphite, natural sands, quartz, and other mineral 
products, all recorded declines compared to the 
previous year. 
Manufacturing
The manufacturing sector, the largest contributor 
to GDP with a share of 17.0 percent, sustained its 
growth momentum in 2025, expanding by 6.2 
percent following a 7.7 percent increase in 2024, 
driven by broad-based improvements across key 
industries. The manufacture of food, beverages, 
and tobacco products, the largest contributor 
within the sector, grew by 5.2 percent in 2025, 
compared to 6.1 percent in 2024. The manufacture 
of textiles, wearing apparel, and leather-related 
products, 
the 
second-largest 
contributor, 
recorded a positive growth for the second 
consecutive year, expanding by 8.0 percent in 
2025 compared to 11.0 percent in 2024. Notably, 
the manufacture of coke and refined petroleum 
products rebounded significantly, growing by 16.9 
percent, following a contraction in the previous 
year. 
The manufacture of other non-metallic mineral 
products recorded a significant growth of 16.2 
percent in 2025, compared 2.5 percent in 2024. 
The manufacture of paper products, printing, 
and reproduction  of media products grew by 
10.5 percent, while manufacture of wood and 
products of wood and cork products expanded by 
5.0 percent in 2025. Rubber and plastic product 
manufacturing recorded an increase of 2.6 
percent in 2025 compared to the previous year. 
The manufacture of machinery and equipment 
expanded marginally by 1.4 percent, and furniture 
manufacturing recorded a modest growth of 
2.9 percent. The sub-sector comprising other 
manufacturing activities, including the repair and 
installation of machines was the only sub-sector 
within the industry sector to record a contraction 
of 5.8 percent in 2025 compared to the growth of 
8.5 percent in 2024.
Construction
In value-added terms, the construction sector 
sustained its growth momentum in 2025, 
expanding by 9.2 percent, albeit at a more 
moderate pace than the 20.1 percent recorded 
in 2024. This strong performance was primarily 
driven by improved availability of construction 
materials and easing cost pressures. Large-scale 
infrastructure developments, particularly those 
financed through foreign funding, were key 
contributors to this growth, supported further 
by increased foreign investment in tourism-
related construction, including hotel and resort 
developments. Notably, local cement production 
increased significantly by 22.0 percent, while 
imported cement declined by 18.6 percent, 
resulting in an overall expansion of 13.3 percent in 
total cement supply. Reductions in prices of key 
construction inputs—cement, iron and steel, and 
timber further facilitated sectoral growth. Overall, 
the continued expansion reflects sustained 
construction activity, underpinned by both 
supply-side improvements and favourable cost 
conditions.

External Sector
Sri Lanka’s external sector strengthened in 2025, 
recording a current account surplus, despite 
a higher trade deficit stemming from import 
expenditure 
significantly 
outpacing 
export 
earnings. Continued recovery in export earnings, 
strong inflows from workers’ remittances and 
steady growth in tourism and service receipts 
supported this outcome. However, the near-term 
outlook for the external sector remains volatile, 
particularly due to heightened geopolitical 
tensions in the Middle East.
Earnings from exports increased by 6.3 percent 
to USD 13,581.4 million in 2025 compared to USD 
12,772.0 million in 2024, driven mainly by higher 
earnings from industrial and agricultural exports. 
Meanwhile, import expenditure increased by 14.0 
percent to USD 21,479.9 million in 2025 from USD 
18,841.4 million in 2024, driven mainly by higher 
expenditure on consumer goods. As a result, the 
trade deficit widened to USD 7,898.6 million in 
2025 from USD 6,069.4 million in 2024. 
The current account recorded a surplus of USD 
1.7 billion in 2025, compared to a USD 1.2 billion 
surplus in 2024, with the current account surplus 
as a percentage of GDP rising to 1.6 percent in 
2025 from a surplus of 1.2 percent of GDP in 2024. 
The service account surplus increased to USD 
3.7 billion in 2025 from USD 3.4 billion in 2024, 
supported by increased inflows from tourism and 
sea transport. The capital account recorded a 
deficit of USD 7.0 million in 2025, compared to a 
surplus of USD 12.0 million in 2024, due to limited 
capital transfers to both the Government and 
private sector. The financial account recorded a 
net balance of   USD 904 million in 2025, compared 
to USD 965 million in 2024, reflecting inflows 
from the IMF-EFF programme and disbursements 
from the Asian Development Bank. Foreign 
Direct Investment inflows including foreign loans 
amounted to USD 1,154 million in 2025, compared 
to USD 845 million in 2024.

Exports 
Earnings from exports increased significantly by

and

2.5 	
Inflation
Headline inflation, measured by the year-on-year 
(Y-o-Y) change in the Colombo Consumer Price 
Index (CCPI, 2021=100), turned to positive territory 
in August 2025 following a prolonged deflationary 
period of 11 consecutive months from September 
2024 to July 2025.  Inflation gradually increased 
to 2.1 percent by end December 2025, remaining 
below the Central Bank’s  medium-term inflation 
target of approximately 5 percent.
The temporary deflation was driven by base effects 
from previously high prices, tight monetary policy, 
supply-side factors-especially several rounds of 
downward revisions to electricity tariffs, fuel, and 
LP gas prices-as well as domestic supply-side 
improvements and the recovery of global supply 
chains. As economic activity recovered, inflation 
showed a moderate upward trend, reflecting 
improving demand conditions.
The CCPI index increased from 192.6 in January 
to 195.8 in December 2025, indicating a gradual 
rise in the general price level and cost of living. 
However, price movements were uneven: early 
2025 saw slight declines, while mid-to-late 2025 
recorded gradual increases. A notable spike 
occurred in December, mainly due to adverse 
weather-related supply disruptions, though year-
on-year inflation remained subdued due to base 
effects.
Core inflation, which reflects the underlying 
inflation in the economy, showed a gradual 
and consistent upward trend throughout 2025, 
indicating 
strengthening 
underlying 
price 
pressures despite low headline inflation. At the 
beginning of the year, year-on-year core inflation, 
as measured by the CCPI, stood at 1.2 percent, 
reflecting weak demand conditions and the 
lagged effects of tight monetary policy. However, 
from mid-2025 onwards, it began to steadily 
increase alongside the economic recovery, rising 
to 2.0 percent by August–September and further 
accelerating in the final quarter. By December 
2025, year-on-year core inflation, as measured 
by the CCPI, reached 2.7 percent, up from 2.4 
percent in November, highlighting a continued 
build-up of demand-driven inflationary pressures. 
This upward movement suggests that, although 
headline inflation remained low due to base 
effects and temporary factors, underlying inflation 
was normalising, indicating a gradual transition 
toward the Central Bank’s medium-term inflation 
target.
Headline inflation, as measured by the year-on-
year (Y-o-Y) change in the National Consumer 
Price Index (NCPI, 2021=100), which also entered 
negative territory in September 2024, recorded 
its lowest point of -4.0 percent in January 2025. 
It returned to positive territory in May 2025, 
recording 0.6 percent, and gradually increased 
to 2.9 percent by December 2025. Similarly, 
core inflation, as measured by the NCPI, entered 
negative territory in January 2025, recording -0.2 
percent, returned to positive territory in May 2025, 
recording 0.3 percent, and gradually increased to 
2.6 percent by end 2025.

2.6 	
Employment and Unemployment
The unemployment rate decreased to 3.9 percent 
in 2025 from 4.4 percent in 2024, driven by an 
increase in the employed population, reflecting 
the gradual absorption of workers into economic 
activities. The unemployment rate for males 
decreased to 2.8 percent in 2025 from 3.0 percent 
in 2024, while the unemployment rate for females 
decreased to 6.1 percent in 2025 from 7.1 percent 
in 2024.
The labour market in 2025 reflected a gradual 
recovery following the severe economic crisis 
of 2022-2023. Improvements in macroeconomic 
stability, 
declining 
inflation, 
and 
renewed 
economic activity contributed to moderate gains 
in employment. However, structural challenges 
such as youth unemployment, skills mismatch, and 
low female labour force participation continued 
to pose challenges.
The total labour force at end-2025 was recorded 
at 8.554 million, marking a 2.9 percent increase 
from 8.316 million at end-2024. This growth was 
supported by increased economic activity in the 
construction, services, tourism, and trade sectors, 
which contributed significantly to the expansion 
of the labour force.
The distribution of the workforce across major 
sectors indicates that 23.9 percent were engaged 
in agriculture, 26.2 percent in industry, and 
49.9 percent in services at end-2025. This trend 
reinforces the dominant role of the services 
sector as the principal provider of employment. 
Meanwhile, the share of the agriculture sector 
recorded a slight decline, while the industry sector 
experienced a marginal increase compared to the 
previous year.
The labour force participation rate increased 
to 49.4 percent in 2025 from 47.4 percent 
in 2024, indicating a gradual recovery from 
previous declines. Male and female labour force 
participation rates increased to 69.1 percent 
and 32.5 percent, respectively. This reflected 
increasing engagement in economic activities, 
particularly as economic conditions improved and 
more individuals entered the workforce.
2.7 	
Equity Market Development
The equity market in Sri Lanka recorded a strong 
performance 
in 
2025, 
reflecting 
improved 
macroeconomic stability and renewed investor 
confidence following the economic crisis period. 
Market activity remained robust throughout the 
year, with notable improvements in turnover 
and trading volumes. Investor participation, 
particularly by domestic investors, played a key 
role in driving the market activity. Lower interest 
rates encouraged a shift from traditional savings 
instruments, such as fixed deposits, towards 
equities, thereby enhancing market liquidity. 
The All-Share Price Index (ASPI, 1985 = 100), which 
measures the movement of share prices of all 
listed companies, increased significantly by 41.9 
percent to 22,624.3 points at end-December 2025 
from 15,944.6 points at end-December 2024. The 
Standard and Poor’s Sri Lanka 20 (S&P SL20, 2004 
= 1,000) index, which reflects the performance 
of 20 leading publicly traded companies listed 
on the Colombo Stock Exchange, also increased 
significantly by 26.6 percent to 6,157.4 points at 
end-December 2025, up from 4,862.1 points at 
end-December 2024. 
This upward trend was mainly driven by increased 
participation from domestic investors, supported 
by government reforms aimed at improving the 
business environment and boosting investor

3.3 	
Global Inflation
Global headline inflation declined to 4.1 
percent in 2025 after peaking during 2022-
2023, reflecting the combined effects of 
tight monetary policies, easing supply chain 
pressures, and softer global demand. In 
advanced economies, inflation declined more 
sharply to 2.5 percent, moving closer to 
central bank targets, supported by moderating 
energy prices and improved supply conditions. 
However, in EMDEs, inflation remained relatively 
elevated at around 5.2 percent, driven by 
exchange rate pressures, food price volatility, 
and structural supply constraints.
Despite 
the 
overall 
disinflation 
trend, 
inflationary pressures persisted in certain 
sectors, 
particularly 
services, 
due 
to 
still-tight labour markets and wage adjustments 
in many advanced economies. Furthermore, 
the escalation of geopolitical tensions in 
the Middle East, particularly the Iran–Israel 
conflict 
and 
associated 
US 
involvement, 
introduced renewed volatility in global energy 
markets, placing upward pressure on fuel and 
transportation costs. Food prices also remained 
susceptible to climate-related disruptions, 
increased transportation costs, and trade 
restrictions, particularly in vulnerable regions.
However, global headline inflation is projected 
to rise to 4.4 percent in 2026 before declining 
to 3.7 percent in 2027, reflecting expected 
increases in energy and food prices. In 
advanced economies, inflation is expected 
to broadly align with target levels by 2026, 
while EMDEs are likely to experience a slower 
convergence due to structural constraints and

3.5.1 	
Fiscal Deficits
Fiscal deficits in 2025 remained elevated across 
most economies, reflecting persistent structural 
spending pressures and rising interest costs. 
The global fiscal deficit stood at 5.0 percent of 
GDP in 2025, highlighting limited progress in 
fiscal consolidation despite the recovery from 
pandemic-related shocks. 
In 
advanced 
economies, 
fiscal 
deficits 
recorded 4.4 percent of GDP, while EMDEs 
averaged 5.9 percent of GDP, showing only 
modest improvement, with deficits remaining 
elevated due to sustained public spending, 
rising defence expenditures, and increasing 
interest payments. In the United States, the 
fiscal deficit narrowed to 6.8 percent of GDP 
in 2025 from 7.9 percent in 2024, supported in 
part by higher revenues, including tariff-related 
income, although underlying fiscal pressures 
remain significant. 
In contrast, fiscal deficits in EMDEs' generally 
widened in 2025, reflecting both higher interest 
expenditures and weaker primary balances.

deficits widened to around 4.7 percent of 
GDP in 2025 from 4.3 percent of GDP in 2024,

3.5.2	
Government Debt
Global government debt continued to rise in 
2025, reflecting sustained fiscal deficits and 
higher borrowing costs. Global public debt 
increased to 93.9 percent of GDP in 2025, around 
2 percentage points higher than in 2024, and is 
projected to continue rising over the medium 
term, potentially reaching 100 percent of GDP 
by 2029.
Advanced economies continued to account 
for the largest share of global debt, with debt 
levels remaining above 108 percent of GDP 
in 2025, reflecting long-standing structural 
pressures, including ageing populations, high 
public spending, and rising interest burdens. In 
contrast, while debt levels in emerging markets 
were relatively lower, vulnerabilities remained 
elevated due to exchange rate pressures, higher 
financing costs, and limited fiscal buffers.
Governments and companies expected to 
borrow USD 29 trillion globally from markets in 
2026, which is nearly USD 4 trillion expansion 
compared to 2024 according to the Global Debt 
Report 2026 (OECD). The global debt stock is 
expected to increase further to 95.3 percent 
in 2026 and 97.2 percent in 2027, respectively, 
from 93.9 percent in 2025. The public debt-to-
GDP ratio in advanced economies increased 
marginally to 108.0 percent in 2025 from 107.6 
percent in 2024 and is expected to rise further 
to 108.2 percent in 2026. The government debt-
to-GDP ratio in EMDEs increased to 73.9 percent 
in 2025 from 69.9 percent in 2024 and the ratio 
is expected to widen to 77.2 percent in 2026 
and 80.2 percent in 2027. 
The government debt-to-GDP ratio in Latin 
American countries increased to 74.2 percent in 
2025 from 70.5 percent in 2024 and is expected

3.7 	
World Trade
Global trade grew by 5.1 percent in 2025, up 
from 3.7 percent growth in 2024, reflecting 
front-loading of trade activity in anticipation 
of rising trade restrictions and tariffs. However, 
this strong performance is expected to be 
temporary; 
global 
trade 
volume 
growth 
projected to decline sharply to 2.8 percent 
in 2026 before recovering to 3.8 percent in 
2027.  Global trade continues to be shaped 
by structural shifts, including increasing trade 
fragmentation, reconfiguration of global supply 
chains, and rising protectionist measures. 
In 2025, the volume of exports by advanced 
economies grew by 3.7 percent compared to 2.1 
percent growth in 2024. The volume of exports 
by EMDEs grew by 7.4 percent compared to 6.6 
percent in 2024.  In 2025, the volume of imports 
by advanced economies grew by 4.7 percent 
compared to 2.2 percent growth in 2024, while 
the volume of imports by EMDEs grew by 5.7 
percent compared to 6.0 percent in 2024. 
The export volume growth in advanced 
economies is anticipated to decline to 2.5 
percent in 2026 and 2.7 percent in 2027. 
Similarly, the export volume growth in EMDEs 
is anticipated to decline to 3.5 percent in 2026 
before increasing to 5.4 percent in 2027.  
Further, the   import volume growth in advanced 
economies is anticipated to decline to 2.6 
percent in 2026 and 3.1 percent in 2027. In the 
same vein, the   import volume growth in EMDEs 
is expected to decline to 2.7 percent in 2026 
before increasing to 4.9 percent in 2027. 
Over the near-term forecast, exports of both 
goods and services are projected to decline as a 
share of global GDP, with the decline in services 
trade being considerably less pronounced. In 
addition, the reorganization of supply chains 
toward more geopolitically aligned partners. A 
practice known as ‘friend-shoring’, is expected 
to alter trade patterns without necessarily 
reducing overall trade volumes in the long term.
Over the medium term, global imbalances are 
expected to decline modestly. Expansionary 
fiscal policies in some surplus economies 
may contribute to this adjustment, although 
this effect could be partially offset by 
increased investment linked to technological 
transformation and supply chain restructuring. 
Overall, the global trade outlook remains subject 
to significant downside risks, particularly from 
further escalation of trade tensions, geopolitical 
fragmentation, and disruptions to key shipping 
routes.

3.8.2 	 Agricultural Prices
Agricultural 
commodity 
prices 
remained 
broadly stable in 2025, following the easing 
of supply-side pressures in 2024. Improved 
harvest conditions, declining fertilizer costs, 
and normalizing freight rates contributed to 
moderate price movements. However, prices 
remained vulnerable to climate risks, including 
heatwaves and El Niño-related disruptions, 
which continued to pose localized threats to 
agricultural production. 
The 
agricultural 
price 
index 
increased 
marginally to 115.7 in 2025 from 115.0 in 2024, 
and is projected to decline to 109.3  in 2026. 
Agriculture raw materials price index increased 
by 2.0 percent in the first quarter of 2026, 
mainly attributable to gains in natural rubber 
prices. The index is expected to remain stable 
throughout 2026 before declining by almost 
3 percent in 2027, reflecting improved supply 
conditions.  
Wheat and maize productions are projected 
to edge down in 2026-2027 after improving 
supply conditions and a rise in stocks-to-use 
ratio in 2025-2026. Accordingly, both wheat 
and maize prices are projected to increase by 4 
percent in 2026. 
While agricultural prices are projected to 
moderate in 2026 under the baseline scenario, 
the increasing frequency and severity of 
extreme weather events continue to pose 
risks to agricultural supply conditions and may 
exert upward pressure on food prices over the 
medium term. In addition, geopolitical tensions 
and trade-related disruptions pose uncertainty 
for global agricultural markets.
3.8.3 	 Metal and Mineral Prices
Prices of metals and minerals increased in 2025, 
following the moderate increase observed in 
2024, reflecting robust demand for industrial 
metals amid supply constraints in key producing 
economies. The metal and mineral price index 
increased by 5.5 percentage points to 112.2 
points in 2025, from 106.7 points in 2024 and is 
projected to increase further to 130.8 points in 
2026 before moderating in 2027. 
The rise in metals and minerals prices was 
mainly attributable to increased demand for 
copper, aluminum, tin and zinc, driven by 
the global energy transition, expansion of 
renewable energy capacity, electric vehicle 
production, and increased investment in data 
centers and related infrastructure. Despite the 
overall increase, prices of some critical minerals, 
including iron ore, lead and nickel, recorded 
declines, reflecting slower growth in China’s 
construction sector.
In contrast, precious metals experienced 
strong price increases in 2025, driven by 
elevated geopolitical uncertainty and increased 
safe-haven demand. Gold prices increased 
significantly by 44.1 percent to USD 3,442 per 
troy ounce (toz) in 2025, from USD 2,388 toz 
in 2024, and are projected to increase to USD 
4,700 per toz in 2026 before easing in 2027. 
The increase was further supported by financial 
market uncertainty and continued central bank 
purchases, with prices remaining well above 
historical averages. 
Similarly, silver prices increased due to both 
investment demand and expanding industrial 
use in renewable energy and electronics 
sectors. Platinum prices were underpinned by 
supply constraints in key producing economies 
and steady industrial demand. Looking ahead, 
the metals and minerals price index is projected 
to decline by 7 percent in 2027 relative to 2026 
levels, reflecting easing the supply conditions, 
according to the World Bank CMO.

Global 
economic 
developments 
in 
2025 
presented a mixed outlook for Sri Lanka, with

East

While 
earlier 
expectations 
anticipated easing global inflation and improving 
financial conditions, the intensification of the 
conflict has adversely affected Sri Lanka’s 
external sector through several key channels. 
In particular, the decline in tourist arrivals 
and inward remittances from the Middle East, 
together with higher energy import costs, has 
placed renewed pressure on the balance of 
payments and domestic price stability.
Notwithstanding these pressures, evolving 
global demand conditions and trade disruptions 
have created an increasingly challenging 
environment for Sri Lanka’s export sector. Key 
export industries, particularly apparel and tea, 
have experienced some moderation in growth, 
reflecting softer external demand and increased 
uncertainty in major markets. However, Sri 
Lanka’s established position in global value 
chains, together with ongoing efforts to 
diversify export markets and enhance product 
competitiveness, is expected to provide a 
measure of resilience. In addition, continued 
demand for necessity goods and specialized 
products, along with gradual improvements 
in global trade conditions over the medium 
term, is likely to support a recovery in export 
performance.
A further external challenge arises from the tariff 
imposed by the US United States on selected 
Sri Lankan exports in 2025. Importantly, through 
diplomatic engagement by the Government 
of Sri Lanka, the initially proposed tariff of 44 
percent was successfully reduced to around 20 
percent, thereby substantially mitigating the 
adverse impact on the external sector. While the 
revised tariff level may still exert some pressure 
on price competitiveness, particularly in the 
apparel sector, it represents a considerable 
easing of external constraints relative to the 
originally proposed tariff rate. 
Sri Lanka’s export sector is expected to 
navigate these pressures through continued 
market diversification, enhanced productivity, 
and increased value addition. In addition, well-
established trade relationships, adherence to 
international standards, and ongoing policy 
support are likely to mitigate the overall impact 
and underpin export sector recovery over the 
medium term.
In 
response 
to 
these 
challenges, 
the 
Government of Sri Lanka has intensified efforts 
to mitigate external vulnerabilities, including 
diplomatic engagement with key trading 
partners, diversification of export markets, 
and strengthening trade and investment 
linkages with emerging regions, particularly 
Asia. In addition, policy measures aimed at 
enhancing export competitiveness, promoting 
tourism recovery, and facilitating remittance 
inflows remain essential to sustaining external 
sector stability. However, given the scale and 
persistence of external shocks, these measures 
may yield results gradually, necessitating 
sustained and coordinated macroeconomic 
policy support.
Overall, the evolving global environment 
underscores 
the 
heightened 
vulnerability 
of  small open economies such as Sri Lanka 
to external shocks. Heavy reliance on a 
concentrated set of export products, tourism 
markets, and remittance sources increases 
exposure to geopolitical disruptions and 
global demand fluctuations. These structural 
vulnerabilities highlight the urgent need for 
Sri Lanka to diversify its export base, expand 
into new markets, strengthen domestic value 
addition, and build external buffers. Enhancing 
economic 
resilience 
through 
prudent 
macroeconomic 
management, 
structural 
reforms, and improved competitiveness will be 
essential for sustaining stability and supporting 
long-term growth in an increasingly complex 
and interconnected global economy.

4.1.  Overview
In 2025, the Government continued its fiscal 
consolidation process while advancing critical 
fiscal structural reforms. The government 
revenue and fiscal balances exceeded the 
budgeted targets driven by higher revenue 
collections from motor vehicles, VAT on 
domestic activities, taxes on external trade 
and a slower pace of capital expenditure 
implementation.
The 
hard-earned 
gains 
from 
the 
fiscal 
reforms have further strengthened the fiscal 
consolidation process, as reflected in the 
following key outcomes:
(i)	
The tax revenue-to-GDP ratio rose to 15.4 
percent in 2025, up from 7.3 percent in 
2022—the highest level recorded since 
1997;
(ii)	
A primary surplus of 5.4 percent was 
achieved in 2025, compared to the 
primary deficit of 3.7 percent in 2022;
(iii)	
 A current account surplus of 0.7 percent 
of GDP was recorded in 2025, marking the 
first time in the country’s history; and
(iv)	
 The fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.3 percent 
of GDP in 2025, down from 10.2 percent in 
2022.
In nominal terms, government revenue including 
grants increased significantly by 34.1 percent 
to Rs. 5,485.6 billion in 2025 from Rs. 4,090.8 
billion in 2024. This significant expansion in total 
government revenue was primarily driven by 
growth in Value Added Tax (VAT) collections. 
The revenue from VAT rose by 33.4 percent to 
Rs. 1,746.9 billion in 2025, from Rs. 1,309.7 billion 
in 2024. This increase is mainly attributed to 
improved domestic consumption, enhanced 
taxpayer compliance, higher revenue from VAT 
on financial services, and the inclusion of motor 
vehicles in the VAT net. 
Excise Duty was also a major contributor to 
overall revenue performance in 2025.  With 
the exception of excise duty on cigarettes, 
revenue collection from Excise Duty, recorded a 
positive growth across all subcategories during 
the year. Notably, revenue from Excise Duty on 
motor vehicles more than doubled its annual 
target for 2025, reflecting the relaxation of the 
temporary import suspension that had been in 
place since 2020. Following the resumption of 
vehicle imports in February 2025,  revenue from 
Excise Duty on motor vehicles rose significantly 
by Rs. 413.2 billion, from Rs. 58.6 billion in 2024 
to Rs. 471.8 billion in 2025. Revenue from Excise 
Duty on petroleum increased by 20.2 percent 
to Rs. 240.6 billion in 2025 from Rs. 200.2 billion 
in 2024 while the revenue from Excise Duty on 
liquor grew by 8.5 percent to Rs. 231.5 billion in 
2025, from Rs. 213.4 billion in 2024. In contrast, 
the revenue from Excise Duty on cigarettes 
declined by 13.2 percent to Rs. 102.7 billion in 
2025 from Rs. 118.3 billion in 2024.
Revenue from income tax surpassed Rs.1 trillion 
for the second consecutive year in 2025, 
reaching Rs. 1,139.4 billion, up from Rs. 1,026.2 
billion in 2024. This represents a year-on-year 
growth of 11.0 percent and a realization of 97.6 
percent of the revenue estimate for 2025. This 
fiscal performance was attributable to targeted 
rate increases from 40 percent to 45 percent in 
liquor, tobacco and betting and gaming sectors, 
a broadening of the taxable base driven by rising 
nominal salaries in both the public and private 
sectors, and the introduction of a 15 percent 
income tax on service exports to capture 
revenue from the growing digital economy. 
The achievement of 97.6 percent of the revenue 
target reflects a significant improvement in tax 
administration and an overall strengthening of 
taxpayer compliance.
Similarly, revenue from the Social Security 
Contribution Levy (SSCL) increased by 17.4 
percent to Rs. 294.5 billion in 2025, from Rs. 
250.9 billion in 2024, achieving 111.6 percent 
of the estimate for the year. This growth was 
mainly driven by the full-year impact of the 
reduction in the registration threshold from 
Rs. 120 million per annum to Rs. 60 million per 
annum, effective from January 01, 2024.
Revenue from taxes on external trade increased 
by 49.1 percent to Rs. 711.7 billion in 2025 from 
Rs. 477.5 billion in 2024, driven by the growth in 
revenue from Ports and Airports Development 
Levy (PAL), Special Commodity Levy (SCL), 
Customs Import Duty (CID) and CESS. Revenue 
from CID significantly increased by 148.2 percent 
to Rs. 275.9 billion in 2025, from Rs.  111.1 billion 
in 2024, mainly due to the imposition of CID on 
motor vehicles during the year. The revenue 
from SCL exceeded its estimate for 2025 by
