4.2   Tax Policy Reforms
In 2025, Sri Lanka maintained its fiscal 
consolidation path under the Extended Fund 
Facility of the International Monetary Fund 
(IMF-EFF), focusing on correcting structural 
imbalances 
while 
navigating 
unforeseen 
external shocks. The year was characterized by 
a delicate balancing act of providing targeted 
relief to the public while broadening the tax 
base through modernized tax administration.
Key tax policy measures undertaken in 2025 
included the revision of personal income tax 
thresholds and rates with a view to providing 
relief to individual taxpayers. The annual tax-free 
threshold was increased from Rs. 1,200,000 per 
annum to Rs. 1,800,000 per annum, effective 
from April 01, 2025. In parallel, the Corporate 
Income Tax (CIT) rate applicable on the gains 
and profits from the manufacture and sale of 
liquor, tobacco, and betting and gaming was 
revised upwards from 40 percent to 45 percent. 
Additionally, a new CIT rate of 15 percent 
was introduced for income earned in foreign 
currency and repatriated to Sri Lanka through 
a licensed bank, covering both professional 
services rendered to overseas clients and other 
foreign income.
In addition to the income tax measures 
introduced, 2025 brought reforms to VAT, SSCL 
and Excise Duties. The Simplified Value Added 
Tax System (SVAT), was also repealed with 
effect from October 1, 2025. This reform, which 
is a key structural benchmark under the IMF-EFF 
programme, aims to minimise revenue leakage 
and administrative complexity. The SVAT system 
has been replaced by a modern, Risk-Based 
Refund Scheme (RBRS).

Box 4.1 | Phasing out CESS: Transforming Sri Lanka’s Trade Landscape 
Sri Lanka is undertaking a major reform of its tariff structure through the phased removal of the 
CESS levy under the Export Development Act, No. 40 of 1979. This reform marks a decisive shift 
from a complex, protection-oriented regime toward a simpler, more transparent, and globally 
competitive trade framework.
For years, CESS functioned as both a revenue source and a protective tool for domestic industries. 
However, its expansion—alongside other para-tariffs—has led to a fragmented tariff structure, 
increasing the cost of imported inputs and weakening export competitiveness. It has also reduced 
transparency and predictability in trade policy.
Recognizing these challenges, the Government has initiated a phased reform to rationalize tariffs, 
reduce production costs, and promote export-led growth.
Policy Framework and Implementation
The reform was introduced under Budget Proposal No. 34.6 of 2023 and implemented through 
Gazette No. 2325/06. It was further strengthened under Budget Proposal No. 35.3 of 2026, which 
removed CESS on fabrics while introducing VAT to maintain competitive neutrality.
With Cabinet approval on 03 March 2026, Gazette No. 2479/38 formalized the phased removal 
of CESS on 2,634 HS codes over four years, aligned with commitments under the World Bank’s 
Development Policy Operation (DPO).
The classification follows the UN Broad Economic Categories (BEC), ensuring consistency across 
capital, intermediate, and consumption goods.

Economic Impact of the Reform
1.    Local Manufacturers
Removal of CESS on inputs and machinery reduces production costs, enabling improved 
efficiency, technology adoption, and product quality. However, increased competition from 
imports may pressure less competitive firms.
2.    Importers
Lower duties reduce import costs and expand business opportunities. However, increased 
market entry may intensify competition and compress margins.
3.    Exporters
Exporters benefit significantly from reduced input costs, improving price competitiveness in 
global markets and supporting export growth and diversification.
4.   Consumers
Consumers gain from lower prices, improved quality, and a wider variety of goods due to 
increased competition

Safeguarding Domestic Industries
As Sri Lanka liberalizes trade, it has strengthened WTO-consistent safeguards to protect domestic 
industries from unfair practices.
1.    Trade Remedies
Under the Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Duties Act, No. 2 of 2018: and regulations have 
already been published by Gazette Extraordinary Notification No.2429/32 dated 27.03.2025.
	
• Anti-dumping measures address imports sold below fair value 
	
• Countervailing duties offset foreign subsidies 
These measures ensure fair competition without restricting legitimate trade.
2.   Standards and Technical Regulations
Strengthened product standards and certification—implemented by the Sri Lanka 
Standards Institution—ensure quality and safety of imports.
	
• Mandatory certification for key products 
	
• Testing and inspection at borders 
	
• Rejection of substandard goods 
These measures protect consumers while maintaining fair competition.
3.  Institutional Coordination
Key institutions—including the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, 
Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development, Department of Trade and Investment 
Policy, and Department of Import and Export Control, Sri Lanka Standard Institution and Sri 
Lanka Customs are working together to strengthen enforcement and align regulations with 
international standards.
A Strategic Policy Shift
The phased removal of CESS reflects a transition from broad tariff protection to targeted, 
rules-based trade policy instruments. It enhances:
	
• Transparency and predictability 
	
• Ease of doing business 
	
• Export competitiveness 
	
• Integration into global value chains 
At the same time, strengthened safeguards ensure domestic industries remain protected 
from unfair trade practices.
 Conclusion
The CESS phase-out is a critical step in modernizing Sri Lanka’s trade regime. By lowering 
costs, improving efficiency, and aligning with global best practices, the reform supports 
sustainable, export-led growth. Its success will depend on effective implementation, 
institutional coordination, and the ability of domestic industries to adapt to a more competitive 
environment and the government is committed to safeguard local industries and consumers.

Box 4.2 | The 4 - Band Customs Import Duty Reform 
1. Overview
The introduction of the 4-Band Customs Import Duty (CID) framework, published on 03 March 
2026 under Gazette Notification No. 2478/03, with effect from 1 April 2026, marks a significant 
structural reform under Sri Lanka’s National Tariff Policy (NTP). The reform rationalizes the 
existing tariff regime, enhances transparency, and aligns with international best practices.
The reform supports the national development agenda of “Thriving Nation, A Beautiful Country” 
and contributes towards achieving the medium-term export target.
2. Key Features of the Reform
The reform introduces a streamlined and standardized tariff structure with the following 
features:
•	 Adoption of a four-band tariff system
•	 Alignment with United Nations Broad Economic Categories (BEC) Rev.5
•	 Reduction of tariffs on inputs to support domestic production
•	 Rationalization of tariffs on consumption goods
•	 Maintenance of stability across the majority of tariff lines
3. Tariff Structure

Key Tariff Adjustments under the 4-Band Structure
The following key adjustments have been introduced under the 4-Band CID Reform:
(a) Reduction of tariffs on intermediate goods 
Intermediate goods previously subject to 15 percent tariffs are reduced to 10 percent to 
lower input costs and enhance industrial competitiveness.
(b) Rationalization of tariffs on consumption goods 
Consumption goods are restructured at 20 percent or 30 percent based on essentiality 
and domestic production considerations.
(c) Retention of selected goods at 20 percent 
Certain intermediate goods are temporarily retained at 20 percent, taking into account 
revenue implications and sector-specific considerations.
(d) Streamlining of mixed-rate structures 
Mixed-rate tariffs are rationalized and adjusted in line with the revised tariff bands.
(e) Maintenance of stability across tariff lines 
A majority of tariff lines remain unchanged to ensure continuity and investor confidence.
(f) Sector-specific adjustments 
Targeted adjustments are made in selected sectors to balance production support, 
revenue mobilization, and consumer considerations.
(g) Exclusions from the 4-band structure 
Goods subject to Specific rates, as well as tobacco and liquor products, remain outside 
the framework to maintain revenue certainty and policy objectives.
 6.  Fiscal Impact 
The estimated impact on Government revenue is less than 0.1 percent of Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP), based on calculations derived from import statistics for the years 2024 and 
2025 based on data from Sri Lanka Customs and GDP data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka.
7.  Expected Outcomes
The reform is expected to:
•	Improve industrial competitiveness by lowering the cost of production 
•	Enhance investment attractiveness
•	Increase transparency in tariff administration
•	Support export growth
•	Strengthen the production base of the economy 
8.  Conclusion	
The 4-Band Tariff Reform establishes a streamlined, transparent, and rules-based tariff 
framework aligned with international best practices in goods classification and national 
economic objectives. Lower tariffs on intermediate and capital goods, together with the 
application of 20 percent or 30 percent bands on consumption goods, support industrial 
competitiveness, export growth, and efficient resource allocation. Stability across most tariff 
lines, supported by targeted safeguards, ensures a smooth transition with minimal disruption, 
thereby strengthening the foundation for a competitive and resilient economy.

5.1 	
Overview
Sri Lanka’s 2025 public expenditure focused 
strongly on navigating post-crisis economic 
recovery and adhering to the fiscal rules set 
by the Public Financial Management Act, while 
structurally continuing the ongoing stabilization 
policies of 2024.
The total government expenditure in 2025 in level 
figures and as a percentage of GDP increased 
compared to 2024. Primary expenditure and 
its components i.e., recurrent expenditure and 
capital expenditure and net lending increased 
in year 2025 compared to year 2024, while 
expenditure on interest payments recorded a 
decrease during the compared time period. 
The fiscal deficit, in terms of overall balance and 
primary balance improved significantly in year 
2025, compared to the previous year. 
Meantime, budgetary support was promptly 
extended for the provision of immediate relief 
to the people affected by the Cyclone “Ditwah”, 
in the month of December 2025, through re-
allocation of savings of provisions under 2025 
Budget, with the approval of Parliament.
5.2. 	
Government Expenditure in 2025
In 2025, Government expenditure in total 
increased by 1.6 percent to Rs. 6,230.4 billion 
from Rs. 6,130.7 billion in 2024. This was due 
to the increase in expenditure on personal 
emoluments, 
transfers 
including 
welfare 
programmes, retirements benefits and grants 
to provincial councils as well as overall increase 
in Capital Expenditure. However, the total 
recurrent expenditure decreased by 2.0 percent 
to Rs. 5,232.4 billion in 2025 from Rs. 5,339.9 
billion in 2024, whereas capital expenditure 
and net lending increased by 26.2 percent to 
Rs. 998.0 billion in 2025 from Rs. 790.8 billion 
in 2024. 
Interest payments decreased by 7.0 percent 
to Rs. 2,500.7 billion in 2025, from Rs. 2,689.5 
billion in 2024. This was due to a net impact of 
the decrease of foreign interest payments by 
14.5 percent and decrease of domestic interest 
payments by 5.7 percent. Non-interest recurrent 
expenditure increased by 3.1 percent to Rs. 
2,731.7 billion in 2025 from Rs. 2,650.4 billion in 
2024. This was mainly driven by an increase in 
spending on salaries and wages by 9.2 percent 
to Rs. 1,163.9 billion, largely stemming from the 
increase in salaries. 
Expenditure on subsidies and transfers was Rs. 
1,233.1 billion in 2025, remained almost same 
as previous year. This was mainly driven by 
spending on Social Security Programs including 
Aswasuma Household Cash Transfers and 
Pension and Retirement Benefits, Social Welfare 
programmes including Medical Supplies for 
Government Hospitals, Welfare Programmes 
on Health and Nutrition including School 
Nutritional Food Program and Development 
Subsidies including Fertilizer Subsidy. 
Public investment increased by 24.3 percent to 
Rs. 1,015.8 billion in 2025 from Rs. 817.1 billion in 
2024.
As 
a 
percentage 
of 
GDP, 
government 
expenditure 
slightly 
decreased 
by 
1.3 
percentage points to 19.0 percent in 2025 
from 20.4 percent in 2024. This reduction was 
primarily driven by a decrease in recurrent 
expenditure by 1.8 percentage points to 16.0 
percent of GDP in 2025 from 17.7 percent in 
2024. As a percent of GDP, interest payments 
decreased by 1.3 percentage points to 7.6 
percent in 2025 from 8.9 percent in 2024. Public 
investment as a percent of GDP increased to 3.1 
percent in 2025 from 2.7 percent in 2024.

Box 5.1 l  Cyclone Ditwah 2025: Post-Disaster Needs Assessment and Recovery Outlook
Cyclone Ditwah, which made landfall in Sri Lanka on 28 November 2025, caused extensive 
damage across 22 districts, severely affecting lives, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure. 
The disaster led to widespread displacement, disruption of essential services, and significant 
impacts on economic activity. Notwithstanding these challenges, the resilience demonstrated 
by affected communities, local authorities, and emergency responders has been commendable.
In response, the Government of Sri Lanka, under the mandate of the “Rebuilding Sri Lanka” 
Presidential Task Force, initiated a comprehensive Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA). 
The assessment was led by the Disaster Management Centre and the Ministry of Defense, 
in collaboration with the Department of National Planning of the Ministry of Finance, with 
the support of all relevant government agencies and key development partners. The PDNA 
provides a rigorous, evidence-based evaluation of damages, economic losses, and recovery 
needs, forming the basis for coordinated recovery planning and resource mobilization.
The findings highlight the urgent need to restore housing, re-establish essential services 
including health, education, water, energy, and transport and revitalize livelihoods and local 
economies. Particular attention is given to vulnerable groups, including female-headed 
households, older persons, persons with disabilities, and low-income communities. The 
assessment further emphasizes the importance of adopting “Build Back Better” principles to 
ensure that recovery efforts strengthen resilience to future climate and disaster risks.
Key Highlights of the PDNA
Cyclone Ditwah triggered severe flooding, landslides, and storm surges, inundating over 1.1 
million hectares at its peak and displacing more than 232,000 people. As of January 2026, 
the disaster resulted in 646 fatalities, with 173 persons reported missing, while over 169,000 
individuals remained displaced.
The disaster caused extensive infrastructure damage, including over 1,200 km of roads, 
numerous bridges, irrigation systems, and utility networks. More than 113,000 houses were 
damaged, with a significant number of households requiring relocation. 
Economic disruptions affected over 45,000 enterprises and approximately 149,000 workers, 
with disproportionate impacts on informal sector workers and women. Agricultural losses 
were also substantial, with serious implications for rural livelihoods and food security.
The PDNA, initiated in January 2026, covers 
22 districts and serves as the analytical 
foundation for the Government’s recovery 
strategy under the “Rebuilding Sri Lanka” 
initiative. The total estimated impact 
amounts to LKR 618.1 billion in damages 
approximately 
and 
LKR 
416 
billion 
approximately in economic losses. Overall 
recovery and reconstruction needs are 
estimated at approximately LKR 1.0225 
trillion approximately over a three-year 
period.

Recovery needs are geographically concentrated, with the highest requirements identified 
in Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Badulla, Puttalam, and Kegalle districts, alongside notable impacts in 
Colombo. The Sectoral priorities are primarily concentrated in transport, housing, commerce 
and industry, and agriculture.
The event further exposed structural gaps in disaster risk management systems, including 
deficiencies in early warning mechanisms, land-use planning, and climate resilience. 
Environmental degradation has compounded these challenges by weakening natural protective 
systems.
Going forward, recovery efforts will priorities risk-informed and climate-resilient reconstruction, 
strengthened governance and disaster risk reduction systems, and inclusive approaches 
to ensure equitable outcomes. The PDNA findings will be operationalized through the 
development of a Disaster Recovery Plan (PDRP), to guide the prioritization, sequencing, and 
financing of recovery interventions.

Curative Healthcare Services
With the increasing prevalence of non-
communicable diseases such as cardiovascular 
diseases, cancers, diabetes and kidney diseases, 
the government committed to strengthening 
curative healthcare services. Rs. 154.1 billion was 
spent in 2025 for the procurement of essential 
medicines and biomedical equipment. Of that 
Rs.147.3 billion was spent on medical supplies 
while Rs. 6.8 billion was spent on bio medical 
equipment.
The year 2025 witnessed the successful 
completion of several key hospital infrastructure 
projects. These included the completion of the 
Specialized Maternity Care Unit at De Soysa 
Maternity Hospital for Women, the construction 
of a building for the office of Medical Officer 
of Health (MoH) at Wadugoda, Payagala, the 
development of the proposed Nephrology, 
Dialysis, and Transplant Unit at Teaching Hospital 
Karapitiya, the construction of a Specialized 
Pediatric Wards Complex at General Hospital, 
Ampara, and the establishment of an MRI Scan 
Unit at Provincial General Hospital, Badulla.
Accordingly, a sum of Rs. 67.6 billion was 
transferred to Provincial Councils for capital 
expenditure in 2025. The transfer for recurrent 
expenditure increased by 14.9 percent in 2025 
from Rs. 409 billion in 2024. This increase in 
recurrent expenditure was due to increased 
salaries and wages in terms of the Public 
Administration Circular No. 10/2025 dated 
25.03.2025. The transfer for capital expenditure 
has also been increased by 76.9 percent in 2025 
from Rs. 38.2 billion in 2024.

Preventive Health care  
In the area of preventive healthcare, government 
efforts continued to focus on communicable 
diseases 
such 
as 
dengue, 
rabies, 
and 
tuberculosis and non-communicable diseases 
including hypertension, diabetes, and kidney-
related ailments. The total public investment for 
preventive healthcare in 2025 rose to Rs. 4,505.6 
million. The National Thriposha Programme 
continued to be a cornerstone initiative, with an 
expenditure of Rs. 2,188 million, serving 614,955 
registered beneficiaries including pregnant and 
lactating mothers and children aged three to 
five years. The programme remains pivotal in 
enhancing nutritional outcomes for vulnerable 
segments of population.
Promotion of Indigenous Medicine
The recognition and integration of traditional 
healing practices into the national health system 
remained a priority. The total investment in the 
promotion of indigenous medicine was Rs. 
3,010.4 million in 2025. Efforts were made to 
strengthen research on medicinal plants, along 
with conservation and awareness programmes 
aimed at enhancing the global standing of Sri 
Lanka’s indigenous medical system.
In addition, several projects for enhance 
administrative and support facilities including 
the construction of intern doctors’ quarters at 
General Hospital Kalutara, as well as a three-
story ambulance garage and minor staff rest 
facility at the same hospital were completed.
2025 marked the near completion of several 
projects, including a six-story accommodation 
building at the National Training School 
of Nursing in Sri Jayawardenapura and the 
construction of a linear accelerator room and 
radiotherapy department at Teaching Hospital 
Rathnapura.
The year 2025 witnessed the successful 
installation of essential machinery across 
several hospitals. Notably, a CT scan facility 
was installed at Teaching Hospital, Kalutara. In 
addition, a CT scanner was supplied to Teaching 
Hospital, Kurunegala, and a cath lab machine 
was provided to Teaching Hospital, Karapitiya.

Box 5.2 l  Sri Lanka in the Digital Age: Opportunity, Readiness, and the Road Ahead
The global economy is undergoing an unprecedented structural transformation. The digital 
economy now accounts for approximately 15 percent of global GDP—roughly $16 trillion—
and is fundamentally reshaping how nations produce, trade, and grow. Forecasts indicate it 
will expand at a compound annual growth rate of 7 percent, reaching $16.5 trillion by 2028 
and representing 17 percent of global GDP 1. For a small island nation like Sri Lanka—still in 
the process of rebuilding from its most severe post-independence crisis—this is not merely a 
global trend to observe, but a critical opportunity to seize.
The digital economy extends far beyond smartphones and social media. It encompasses 
e-commerce, digital finance, cloud computing, IT-enabled services, artificial intelligence, and 
the data infrastructure that underpins modern governance and industry. Research shows that 
every dollar invested in digital transformation generates $8.30 in returns within a country’s 
broader digital economy—a multiplier effect few other investment categories can match2. 
Countries that lead in digital infrastructure advance decisively, while those that fall behind risk 
permanent exclusion from the fastest-growing segment of global trade.
Sri Lanka’s economic recovery, which rebounded with approximately 5 percent growth in 
2024 following a sharp contraction, has demonstrated resilience. However, the country must 
now shift from stabilization to transformation. The digital economy offers a clear pathway to 
achieve this.

4Sri Lanka’s Digital Readiness: High Connectivity, Uneven Capability
Sri Lanka’s digital readiness is characterized by strong connectivity infrastructure paired with 
uneven capability across sectors and regions.
Connectivity
Mobile internet penetration now exceeds 60 percent, while 4G coverage spans over 85 percent 
of the island. The ongoing rollout of 5G in urban hubs such as Colombo and Kandy is further 
narrowing the technological gap.
Payments
The LankaPay network has proven transformative. In 2025, digital payment volumes through 
the platform surpassed LKR 2 trillion, reflecting a significant shift in consumer trust toward 
digital transactions5 .
The Divide
Despite 80 percent smartphone ownership, a digital divide persists. While 52 percent of 
internet users make monthly online purchases—led by clothing (43 percent) and electronics 
(22 percent)—this activity remains heavily concentrated in the Western Province.

Box 5.3 l  Social Safety Nets
Sri Lanka has a long history of social protection systems, which began with traditional 
community support mechanisms and gradually evolved into formal, government-sponsored 
welfare programs. During the British colonial period, limited forms of government assistance 
such as poor relief and pensions were introduced; however, these were not implemented on a 
large scale. Following independence in 1948, Sri Lanka developed into a strong welfare state, 
introducing policies such as free education, free healthcare, and food subsidies etc. However, 
with the introduction of the open economic policy in 1977, there was a gradual shift from 
universal welfare benefits toward targeted assistance programs. Accordingly, programs such 
as Janasaviya and Samurdhi, which included financial assistance and community development 
initiatives aimed at poverty alleviation, were introduced.
In particular, during the period from 2020 to 2022, in response to the COVID-19 global pandemic 
and the most severe economic crisis faced by Sri Lanka, efforts were made to strengthen and 
improve the efficiency of the social protection system to ensure better support for vulnerable 
populations without exclusion. By 2023, the Government restructured its welfare system and 
introduced the Aswesuma program to expand coverage, improve efficiency, and enhance 
targeting accuracy. Beneficiaries are selected based on a multidimensional poverty index. 
To address shortcomings in previous programs and improve beneficiary coverage while 
minimizing inclusion and exclusion errors, a Social Registry Information System (SRIS) containing 
information on social protection beneficiaries has been established. Through the Aswesuma 
program, monthly financial assistance is provided to low-income households categorized as 
extremely poor, poor, and vulnerable.
In addition, the annual budget allocation for this program has been increased, along with 
the number of beneficiaries. Accordingly, effective from January 2025, the allowance for the 
extremely poor category has been increased from Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 17,500, while the allowance 
for the poor category has been increased from Rs. 8,500 to Rs. 10,000. The allowance of Rs. 
5,000 for the vulnerable category continues to be provided without interruption.
Furthermore, the program has been expanded to include support for elderly individuals, 
persons with disabilities, and individuals suffering from chronic kidney disease within low-
income families. From April 2025, the monthly allowance for kidney patients and persons with 
disabilities has been increased from Rs. 7,500 to Rs. 10,000, while the allowance for elderly 
individuals has been increased from Rs. 3,000 to Rs. 5,000.

In 2025, Sri Lanka’s social protection system has played a crucial role in protecting vulnerable 
groups and supporting economic recovery. With the introduction of the Aswesuma program, 
the social protection process has become more efficient through improved targeting and 
digitalization. However, further improvements are ongoing to ensure that the system remains

Section 20 of the Public Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024 introduces an important reform 
aimed at strengthening fiscal transparency and public accountability. It requires the preparation 
and publication of a public-friendly version of the annual budget, designed to communicate the 
key elements of government fiscal policy in a clear, concise, and easily understandable manner. 
This initiative recognizes that traditional budget documents—often structured around Ministries, 
Departments, and expenditure Heads—can be highly technical and difficult for the general public 
to interpret. As a result, many citizens and taxpayers may not fully understand how public funds are 
raised and utilized.
The public-friendly budget seeks to bridge this 
gap by presenting information in a simplified and 
accessible format. It highlights the government’s 
main revenue sources, expenditure priorities, 
and policy objectives, enabling citizens to better 
understand 
how 
their 
tax 
contributions 
are 
allocated. By focusing on key sectors, programmes, 
and development projects, the document provides 
a more meaningful picture of how public resources 
are directed towards areas such as education, 
health, infrastructure, and social protection.

6.1    Overview
The 
government’s 
continuous 
revenue-
enhancing strategies have shifted the financial 
operations of 2025 from crisis management to 
a period of robust revenue mobilization and 
fiscal stabilization. Driven by the successful 
implementation 
of 
revenue-based 
fiscal 
consolidation measures and the structural 
reforms guided by the IMF-EFF program, total 
cash inflows through revenue reached an 
unprecedented level of Rs. 5,247.7 billion in 
2025, surpassing the original estimate of Rs. 
4,981.1 billion. This surge was primarily fueled 
by a historic performance in Tax Revenue 
collection, which totaled Rs. 4,999.4 billion, 
reflecting the impact of the upward revisions 
of tax rates, broadened tax base, and improved 
collection efficiency. 
By significantly outperforming initial projections 
during the year, the Treasury strengthened its 
cash flow performances notably and moved 
toward more sustainable budget execution. Sri 
Lanka’s government financial position reflected 
a notably improved liquidity status, supported 
by 
stronger 
revenue 
collection, 
prudent 
expenditure 
management, 
and 
enhanced 
access to both domestic and external financing, 
which helped maintain steady cash inflows. 
In addition, successful debt restructuring 
efforts and support from international financial 
institutions contributed to easing short-term 
repayment pressures, allowing the government 
to meet its obligations more comfortably. This 
positive liquidity position strengthened investor 
confidence, stabilized domestic money and 
capital markets, and provided a more resilient 
foundation for managing market interest rates 
at the desired level. 
During 
2025, 
government 
expenditure 
behavior reflected a continued shift toward 
fiscal consolidation and disciplined spending 
following earlier economic challenges. The 
Government prioritized essential and high-
impact areas such as social welfare, public 
sector salaries, and debt service payments, 
while exercising tighter control over non-
essential expenditures. The composition of 
spending showed a significant share allocated 
to debt servicing, highlighting the ongoing 
burden of public debt, even as restructuring 
efforts helped ease immediate pressures. At the 
same time, targeted subsidy reforms and better 
expenditure tracking improved efficiency and 
increased capital expenditure during latter 
part of the year reflected in the improved 
public investments. Overall, the government’s 
spending approach in 2025 demonstrated a 
careful balancing act between maintaining fiscal 
discipline and supporting vulnerable groups 
and economic recovery alongside efforts to 
provide relief to populations affected by natural 
disasters, including Ditwah. 
6.2    Treasury Cash Flow Management 
Total cash inflows from revenue and other 
receipts excluding borrowing reached Rs. 
5,247.7 billion in 2025, from which the majority 
or 95.3 percent contributed from tax revenue 
of Rs. 4,999.4 billion. Accordingly, tax revenue 
reflects a year-on-year increase of 37 percent 
over 2024 of Rs. 3,645.2 billion. This performance 
was primarily anchored by improved tax 
revenue collection which reached, significantly 
outperforming the initial estimate of Rs. 4,590.0 
billion. In addition, non-tax revenue collection 
during the year was recorded as Rs. 247.9 billion 
which accounted for 4.7 percent of the total 
with an increase of Rs 43.8 billion or 21.5 percent 
over the previous year. These outcomes reflect 
the successful implementation of revenue-
based fiscal consolidation measures, which have 
effectively transformed the government cash 
flow status through enhanced mobilization and 
disciplined fiscal policy.
Aligning with strict fiscal discipline, the Treasury 
maintained a rigorous expenditure management 
strategy throughout 2025 to ensure that outflows 
remained confined to approved budget to 
facilitate operational requirements and public 
investments. Accordingly, total funds released for 
recurrent payments for the period were recorded 
at Rs. 5,039.3 billion, against the estimate of 
Rs. 5,693.0 billion including interest cost of 
the government. The actual interest expenses 
incurred during the year 2025 was amounted 
to Rs. 2,431.6 billion reflecting 48 percent of the 
total recurrent expenditure complying with the 
government expenditure commitments. The 
second majority of the recurrent expenditure 
category of Rs. 1,324.6 billion was represented 
by Personal Emoluments, which was remained 
below the respective estimated thresholds.

6.5.2.1   External Debt Restructuring Process
In line with the interim policy adopted by 
the Government, debt servicing payments 
to affected bilateral and commercial external 
creditors have been temporarily suspended 
for an interim period commencing from 12 
April 2022.  Sri Lanka had almost completed 
its external debt restructuring process by 
concluding debt treatment agreements with 
the Official Creditor Committee (OCC), signing 
the debt restructuring agreement with the 
Export-Import Bank of China in June 2024, 
and reaching an agreement in principle with 
International Sovereign Bond (ISB) holders 
in September 2024. Thereafter, Sri Lanka 
successfully 
completed 
the 
restructuring 
of 
ISBs 
in 
December 
2024, 
exchanging 
approximately 98% of the outstanding ISBs into 
new instruments. Moreover, by end-2025, Sri 
Lanka had concluded approximately 95% of its 
bilateral debt restructuring agreements with 
lenders.
Accordingly, by end-2025, unpaid debt service 
obligations had recorded to a principal amount 
of USD 897.4 million and interest amounting to 
USD 285.7 million. This amount includes the 
2022 ISB holdout obligations amounting to 
approximately USD 268 million, as well as the 
remaining 5% of bilateral debt restructuring 
agreements yet to be finalised. 
6.5.2.2.   Maturity Structure of ISBs (Pre and 
               Post Restructuring)
Prior to restructuring, Sri Lanka faced a highly 
concentrated repayment profile, with large 
ISB maturities falling due between 2023 and 
2029, creating significant refinancing and 
liquidity pressures. Following the restructuring, 
the maturity profile has been considerably 
smoothed and extended over a longer period 
from 2022 to 2038. The new maturity structure 
reduces the bunching of repayments in the 
short to medium term and distributes debt 
service obligations more evenly across future 
years.

Box 6.1 l  Strengthening Sri Lanka’s Public Debt Management Framework: Paving the Way for a 
New Era in Debt Management
Following the economic crisis in 2022, Sri Lanka embarked on a comprehensive reform agenda to 
strengthen the country’s public debt management framework with the objective of restoring debt 
sustainability, improving fiscal resilience, and enhancing macroeconomic stability. A major milestone 
in this reform journey was the enactment of the Public Debt Management Act, No. 33 of 2024 (PDMA), 
which established a unified legal and institutional framework for public debt management through 
the establishment of the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO). By consolidating debt management 
functions that were previously dispersed across multiple institutions, the new framework significantly 
strengthened coordination, governance, accountability, and operational efficiency in public debt 
management.
During 2025, several important measures were introduced to further strengthen the legal and 
institutional framework governing public debt management. The issuance of Public Debt Management 
Regulations No. 01/2025 and No. 02/2025, together with operational guidelines and institutional 
procedures, significantly enhanced governance arrangements, risk management practices, and internal 
controls within the debt management process. These reforms paved the way for a more rules-based, 
transparent, and disciplined approach to debt management. In order to further strengthen institutional 
coordination and governance, the Public Debt Coordination Committee (PDCC) was appointed in 
January 2025 to facilitate effective coordination between debt management, fiscal policy, and monetary 
policy operations.
A key reform achievement was the introduction and publication of Sri Lanka’s first Medium-Term Debt 
Management Strategy (MTDS) for the period 2025-2029 and Annual Borrowing Plan (ABP) for the year 
2025 under the PDMA. This marked a paradigm shift from ad-hoc borrowing practices towards a more 
strategic and cost-risk based approach to government financing, ensuring greater consistency with the 
Government’s medium-term fiscal and macroeconomic objectives.

Box 6.1 l  Strengthening Sri Lanka’s Public Debt Management Framework: Paving the Way for a 
New Era in Debt Management
Another landmark reform was the transfer of responsibility for conducting domestic government 
securities auctions from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka to the PDMO in December 2025. This transition 
strengthened the institutional separation between debt management and monetary policy functions 
in line with international best practices, while enhancing the operational independence and 
governance of government borrowing activities.
To support this transition, the Debt and Cash Management Committee (DCMC) and the Auction Steering 
Committee (ASC) were established within the Ministry of Finance to oversee strategic borrowing 
decisions and government securities auction operations. These institutional arrangements further 
strengthened governance, transparency, and decision-making within the domestic borrowing process.
The reform framework also introduced stronger mechanisms for managing fiscal risks associated with 
government guarantees and on-lending operations through the adoption of risk-based measures such as 
guarantee fees and on-lending premiums, thereby improving the management of contingent liabilities 
and safeguarding public finances.
Enhancing transparency and investor engagement has been another important pillar of Sri Lanka’s 
public debt management reforms. Measures have been introduced to improve the availability, quality, 
and timeliness of debt-related information, while strengthening communication and engagement with 
investors and other stakeholders. These initiatives have contributed to improving investor confidence 
and reinforcing Sri Lanka’s commitment to transparent and accountable public financial management 
practices.
Overall, Sri Lanka’s public debt management reforms signify a major transformation in the country’s 
debt management architecture, laying a strong foundation for prudent borrowing, improved fiscal risk 
management, and long-term debt sustainability.

Box 7.1 | Digital Transformation for Inclusive Economic Growth: 
Strengthening MSME Development through Innovation
As an Implementing Agency the Department of Development Finance (DFD) continued its 
transformative journey in 2025 by deepening digitalization across its core operations, reinforcing 
its role as a catalyst for inclusive economic growth. Anchored in the Government’s broader 
digitalization agenda, these initiatives have significantly enhanced the efficiency, transparency, and 
accessibility of financial support mechanisms particularly for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises 
(MSMEs), a critical pillar of Sri Lanka’s economic development.
A key milestone in this journey has been the full operationalization of the Loan Management 
System (LMS), which was introduced in 4th Quarter of 2024 to replace the previously manual and 
paper-based processes associated with administering subsidized loan schemes. The LMS has 
revolutionized the way Participating Financial Institutions (PFIs) interact with the DFD by enabling 
end-to-end electronic submission, processing, and approval of loan applications. This transition has 
substantially reduced processing times, minimized administrative burdens, lowered operational 
costs, and enhanced transparency and accountability in public financial management.
The LMS has been successfully deployed across several flagship MSME financing programmes, 
including the Re-Energizing MSME Sector Loan Scheme, SMELoC, SMELoC–Revolving Loan Scheme, 
and the Pledge Loan Scheme. Furthermore, in response to Cyclone Ditwah, this Department 
demonstrated agility and responsiveness by digitally administering the Disaster Relief Loan Scheme 
with 3 percent interest, ensuring timely financial assistance to affected enterprises and supporting 
business continuity during a period of crisis.
Expanding the scope of digital service delivery, also implemented as a nationwide digital 
mechanism under Budget 2025 to operationalize the additional 3 percent interest incentive for 
senior citizens’ over 300,000 nos. of fixed deposits. This system has connected around 3000 
branches of participating banks through a centralized web portal, enabling real-time data sharing, 
automated calculations, and the prevention of duplicate claims. As a result, the efficiency, accuracy, 
and integrity of the subsidy programme have been significantly improved.
The integration of financial institutions into the LMS marks another significant achievement. To date, 
the head offices of nineteen (19) government and private banks have been successfully linked to the 
system, allowing seamless submission of loan applications and digital processing by departmental 
officials. This connectivity has strengthened coordination between the public and financial sectors, 
creating a more responsive and streamlined financing ecosystem for MSMEs.
Building on this progress, the DFD is actively working to expand its digital infrastructure. Systems for 
additional programmes, including the NCRCS Loan Scheme and the Farming System Sustainability 
Programme (FSSP), are currently under development, with the latter nearing completion. Moreover, 
with the support of the Asian Development Bank, two new loan schemes are being introduced 
alongside the development of an advanced loan management platform. This presents a strategic 
opportunity to integrate all existing loan systems into a unified, interoperable framework capable 
of interfacing directly with the internal systems of participating banks.
Looking ahead, we have planned to introduce a dynamic dashboard interface that will provide real-
time insights into programme performance and fund utilization. This dashboard will be accessible 
to key stakeholders, including the decision making authorities in the Ministry of Finance, banks, 
and other relevant authorities, thereby facilitating informed decision-making and strengthening 
oversight. Additionally, it will enhance the ability to effectively monitor and supervise the 
implementation of development finance initiatives.
The digital transformation of the Department of Development Finance represents a significant step 
forward in modernizing public service delivery. By leveraging technology to improve efficiency, 
transparency, and accessibility, the Department is not only enhancing its operational effectiveness 
but also empowering MSMEs—the backbone of the national economy—to thrive in an increasingly 
competitive and dynamic environment.

Institutional Support for SMEs
7.2.4.1	 National Credit Guarantee Institution 
Limited (NCGIL)
With the approval of the Cabinet of Ministers, 
the National Credit Guarantee Institution 
Limited (NCGIL) was established as a public–
private partnership between the Government 
of Sri Lanka and thirteen (13) shareholder 
financial institutions (SFIs) and incorporated as 
a public limited company (No. P B 00271461). 
The objective of NCGIL is to support the 
development of the Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprise 
(MSME) 
sector 
by 
providing 
credit guarantees for term loans granted by 
participating financial institutions.
Under the approved capital structure, the 
Government has invested USD 50 million with 
financial support from the Asian Development 
Bank, 
while 
the 
SFIs 
have 
contributed 
proportionately, maintaining an approximate 
90:10 ratio between the Government and SFIs.
NCGIL commenced their operations on January 
20, 2025. As at 31 December 2025, a total of 
1,234 loans amounting to Rs. 7,435 million have 
been covered by issuing guarantees valued 
at Rs. 5,099 million. Of this, Rs. 939 million 
(approximately 20%) has been extended to 244 
women-owned MSMEs, while Rs. 1,296 million 
(25%) has been directed towards priority 
sectors including agriculture, IT, exports, and 
tourism. The trading sector accounts for the 
largest share, with guarantees amounting to Rs. 
1,914 million (approximately 40%).
Within its first year of operations, NCGIL has 
demonstrated significant progress in facilitating 
access to finance for MSMEs, particularly those 
lacking collateral, by promoting cash flow-
based lending.
For 2026, NCGIL aims to further expand 
operations by supporting at least 2,500 MSMEs 
with guarantees exceeding Rs. 10,000 million, 
with a focus on women-led enterprises, exports, 
IT, tourism, agriculture, and environmentally 
sustainable businesses.

farmers. Under this approach, funds are credited 
directly to farmers’ bank accounts, enhancing

farmer livelihoods, promote the efficient use 
of agricultural inputs, enhance agricultural 
productivity, and contribute to the stability and 
resilience of the country’s agricultural sector.

In order to increase the production of the main 
export crops by empowering the smallholder 
planters, the Government offered subsidies for 
new planting, re-planting, preparation for land,

to tea, rubber and coconut smallholders. 
Accordingly, Rs. 1,958 million was distributed 
among 110,156 such planters of which, Rs. 745 
million was provided for 21,159 tea planters,

7.2.5.4	 Compulsory Crop Insurance
The compulsory Crop Insurance Scheme was 
introduced with the objective of providing 
extensive insurance coverage for crop damage 
of paddy and other commercial crops i.e. 
maize, soya, big onions, potatoes and chilies. 
The scheme covers the losses caused due to 
droughts, floods and wild elephant attacks up 
to the maximum land extent of 5 acres for paddy 
and 2.5 acres for other commercial crops and 
the insurance coverage per acre is Rs. 40,000. 
This scheme is free for farmers and operated 
with a premium contribution which is made 
by the Government. Additional coverage can 
be obtained for damages caused by pests and 
diseases, other animal attacks and fire paying 
a premium by the farmers. Insurance coverage 
can also be obtained for additional cultivation 
extents and a higher sum insured up to the cost 
of cultivation by paying an additional premium. 
During the 2024/25 Maha season around Rs. 
1,559 million was paid to 75,197 farmers as 
compensation for crop damages in cultivated 
land areas of 88,882 acres. 
In addition, for the 2025 Yala season, around Rs. 
57 million was paid for 3,007 number of farmers 
for crop damages in cultivated land areas of 
2,430 acres.  The General Treasury has provided 
Rs. 5,323.87 million to Agriculture and Agrarian 
Insurance Board (AAIB) for these endeavors

budgetary allocation approved under the 2026 
fiscal framework.

7.3.3	
Government Storage Facilities for 
Agricultural Products
The Government, with financial support from 
the World Bank, has established five modern 
Farmers’ Grain Preservation Centers (FGPCs) 
in key agricultural districts: Anuradhapura, 
Monaragala, 
Mannar, 
Kilinochchi, 
and 
Polonnaruwa. 
Equipped 
with 
advanced 
preservation technology and managed under 
an incentive-based model, these centers 
provide high-quality storage services for grains 
i.e. paddy, maize, soybean, and black gram. 
With a combined storage capacity of 17,200 
mt, the centers help farmers reduce exposure 
to seasonal price volatility by securely storing 
produce until market conditions are favorable.
In addition to storage, the centers offer value-
added services such as professional drying, 
cleaning, and grain quality certification. A key 
feature is the Warehouse Receipt Financing 
(WRF) mechanism, which allows farmers to 
use stored produce as collateral to access 
concessional credit, thereby integrating rural 
producers into the formal financial system.
Performance Highlights (2024–2025):
•	 Total Grain Inflow: Increased by 28.5%, 
from 4,537 mt in 2024 to 5,828 mt in 2025, 
reflecting growing farmer confidence.
•	 Registered Farmer Participation: Rose by 
7.4%, from 3,897 to 4,187 farmers, with 
particularly strong growth in Mannar district.
•	 Warehouse Receipt Financing: Total credit 
disbursement increased by 36.1%, from Rs. 
257.92 million to Rs. 351.00 million, improving 
access to formal agricultural credit.
Despite 
progress 
in 
service 
expansion, 
operational income declined slightly from Rs. 
20.60 million in 2024 to Rs. 19.57 million in 2025, 
while operational costs increased from Rs. 
23.41 million to Rs. 24.93 million, widening the 
operational deficit. Nevertheless, the growth 
in storage volumes and financial integration 
indicates stronger value-chain linkages and 
enhanced rural economic participation.
Moving forward, strategic priorities include 
optimizing capacity utilization, improving cost 
recovery mechanisms, and leveraging growing 
storage demand to ensure long-term financial 
sustainability and increased resilience in the 
agricultural sector.

8.1  	 Overview
The State Owned Enterprises (SOEs), particularly 
the main 51 SOEs, play a significant role in the 
socio-economic development of the country 
through their engagement in 15 key sectors, 
including banking and finance, insurance, energy, 
water, ports, plantations, and health. Their 
contribution extends beyond revenue and profit 
generation to encompass employment creation, 
price stabilization, the provision of public 
services and utilities, infrastructure development, 
financial inclusion, poverty alleviation, and the 
maintenance of fiscal stability.
During the year 2025, excluding the Ceylon 
Electricity Board, the remaining 50 SOEs 
reported a total profit of Rs. 483.2 billion, 
reflecting an increase of 21.5 percent compared 
to the total profit of Rs. 397.5 billion recorded in 
2024. However, owing to the net loss of Rs. 38.7 
billion incurred by the Ceylon Electricity Board 
in 2025, compared to the net profit of Rs. 141.6 
billion recorded in 2024, the overall profitability 
of the main 51 SOEs declined by 17.6 percent to 
Rs. 444.4 billion.
The improved performance of the SOE sector 
was reflected in its increased contribution 
to the Consolidated Fund through levies and 
dividends. Accordingly, collections from SOEs 
by way of levies and dividends increased to 
Rs.56.5 billion in 2025, compared to Rs. 41.1 
billion in 2024.
In line with the Government’s policy on 
reforming the SOE sector, several initiatives 
were undertaken during the year 2025. These 
included the approval of the Cabinet of Ministers 
for the closure, restructuring, or merger of 
several non-commercial SOEs based on the 
recommendations of the Cabinet-appointed 
Committee; approval for the liquidation of 33 
non-functional SOEs; and approval to draft the 
Public Commercial Enterprises Management 
Bill with the objective of ensuring that all 
public commercial enterprises are managed 
professionally, 
independently, 
productively, 
and in accordance with commercial principles, 
while adhering to the highest standards of 
governance, accountability, and transparency. 
Meanwhile, in line with the Cabinet-approved 
State-Owned Banks (SOB) Reform Policy, key 
reforms were implemented in State-Owned 
Banks. These reforms included the appointment 
of independent directors, with the assistance 
of a committee of professionals, resulting in 
independent directors constituting the majority 
of the Boards of the SOBs.
The enactment of the Sri Lanka Electricity 
(Amendment) Act, No. 14 of 2025 in August 
2025 was followed by several key reforms in 
the power sector, including the introduction 
of the National Energy Policy and the National 
Tariff Policy, as well as the establishment of six 
Government-owned companies to unbundle 
the functions of the Ceylon Electricity Board. 
These reforms are expected to enhance 
efficiency, transparency, and accountability 
within the power sector.
The Government continued to support the 
reform initiatives of SriLankan Airlines (SLA) 
by assisting its debt restructuring process, 
including the restructuring of the USD 175 
million international bond, with the objective 
of easing liquidity pressures and improving 
the airline’s financial stability. Accordingly, the 
General Treasury infused Rs. 25.28 billion as 
equity capital into SLA during 2025.
During the year 2025, with a view to enhancing 
the governance of SOEs through improved 
reporting practices, the General Treasury, 
with the approval of the Cabinet of Ministers, 
introduced a comprehensive guideline for the 
preparation of annual reports. Further, in order 
to enhance financial discipline, transparency, 
equitable treatment of all stakeholders, and 
enhancing efficiency in decision-making through 
the empowerment of Boards of Directors, a 
circular was issued providing guidelines on 
sponsorships, donations, indirect business-
related promotional expenses, and corporate 
social responsibility activities of SOEs.

8.2.2 	 Ceylon Petroleum Corporation
In 2025, the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation 
(CPC) recorded an improved financial and 
operational performance compared to 2024 
with the continued implementation of the 
cost-recovery pricing formula, which enabled 
CPC to better align domestic retail prices with 
global petroleum prices and exchange rate 
movements. The CPC experienced favorable 
movements in international oil prices during 
the year, with Average Brent crude oil prices 
declined from around USD 80.5 per barrel 
in 2024 to around USD 69.1 per barrel in 
2025, thereby easing the CPC’s import cost 
compared to year 2024. The combined effect of 
lower international oil prices and the continued 
implementation of the cost-recovery pricing 
formula helped preserve operating margins and 
improve profitability in 2025.
During 2025, United Petroleum of Australia 
exited the domestic fuel retail market, citing 
unfavorable operational conditions and the 
limited scale of the local market. Nevertheless, 
given its relatively limited market presence, 
the exit is unlikely to have materially affected 
CPC’s sales performance compared to 2024, 
while competition remained from Lanka IOC, 
Sinopec, and RM Parks.
Reflecting the improved market environment 
and continued demand recovery, CPC’s total 
sales volume increased by 6.3 percent to 4,144.8 
million litres in 2025 from 3,898.3 million litres 
in 2024. This increase was mainly driven by 
higher demand for fuel used for transport and 
power generation sectors. Sales of Petrol 92 
Octane increased by 3.4 percent from 1,056.8 
million litres in 2024 to 1,092.6 million litres in 
2025, while Auto Diesel sales rose marginally 
from 1,205.7 million litres to 1,209.5 million 
litres. In addition, Jet A-1 fuel sales increased by 
9 percent to 644.8 million litres compared to 
2024, reflecting improved aviation and tourism-
related activity.
Despite an 8.7 percent decline in total revenue 
to Rs. 848.4 billion in 2025 from Rs. 929.6 billion 
in 2024, CPC recorded a profit before tax of 
Rs. 36.5 billion in 2025, reflecting an increase 
of 6.6 percent from Rs. 34.2 billion in 2024. This 
improvement was mainly attributable to the 9.6 
percent reduction in cost of sales to Rs. 766 
billion, together with decreases in sales and 
distribution, administrative, and finance costs 
by 11 percent, 29 percent, and 98 percent, 
respectively.
As evidence of its continued fiscal responsibility, 
CPC remitted Rs. 6 billion to the Consolidated 
Fund, reaffirming its role as a contributor to 
the national economy and a responsible public 
sector enterprise.

8.3 	
State Banks
The banking sector continued its recovery and 
strengthening momentum in 2025, operating 
within a gradually stabilizing macroeconomic 
environment. Most banks maintained sound 
stability, supported by strong capital adequacy 
ratios and improved liquidity ratios above the 
regulatory requirements. Sector profitability 
remained robust, although growth moderated 
compared to the exceptional performance 
recorded in 2024. This performance underscores 
the sector’s resilience and its pivotal role 
in supporting national economy. Despite 
external challenges, including the impact of 
Cyclone Ditwah during the latter part of the 
year, banks effectively implemented proactive 
business continuity measures and prudent risk 
management practices to mitigate financial 
disruptions and sustain strong performance.
Credit 
risk 
indicators 
showed 
further 
improvement, with the decline in stage III loan 
ratio  to 9.7 percent at the end of 2025 from 12.3 
percent at the end of 2024. This improvement 
was mainly supported by expansion of credit, 
together with the strengthened recovery 
mechanisms.
In 2025, state-owned banks in Sri Lanka, 
particularly the Bank of Ceylon (BoC), People’s 
Bank (PB), and the National Savings Bank (NSB), 
continued to play a significant role in the banking 
sector. These institutions remained aligned with 
the Government’s economic priorities, while 
delivering a wide range of financial services 
to the customers. Their contribution was 
instrumental in supporting economic recovery, 
facilitating credit flows, and promoting financial 
inclusion across the country. Concurrently, 
these banks continued to focus on addressing 
legacy non-performing loans and accelerating 
digital transformation initiatives to enhance 
service delivery and operational efficiency.
During 2025, the performance of major state-
owned banks reflected a combination of 
improved asset quality, stable funding bases, 
and prudent cost management, although 
variations were observed across institutions 
depending 
on 
their 
respective 
business 
models, sectorial exposures, and pace of 
recovery in key lending segments. Overall, the 
sector demonstrated a gradual normalization of 
earnings following the high growth recorded in 
the previous year, while maintaining adequate 
buffers to withstand potential risks.
In 2025, the total profit before tax of the state 
banks increased by 41 percent to Rs. 236.3 
billion, compared to Rs. 178.2 billion in 2024. 
This growth was mainly driven by a strong 
recovery in credit growth, lower impairment 
charges, and increased digital adoption. The 
total assets of the state banks increased by 10 
percent to Rs. 11,490 billion at the end of 2025, 
supported by a resumption of credit growth 
driven by an accommodative monetary policy 
and stabilizing domestic economic conditions. 
In view of the challenges relating to minimum 
capital requirements and operational constraints 
faced by both the Housing Development 
Finance Corporation (HDFC) Bank and the 
State Mortgage and Investment Bank (SMIB), 
the Cabinet of Ministers granted approval for 
strategic restructuring measures. Accordingly, 
approval was granted for BoC to acquire the 
Government’s shareholding in HDFC Bank and 
for PB to acquire the entire shareholding of 
SMIB, thereby enabling HDFC Bank and SMIB to 
function as subsidiaries under the management 
and oversight of BoC and PB, respectively. 
These initiatives are currently in progress.
A key milestone achieved during 2025 was the 
progress in the appointment of independent 
directors to the Boards of state-owned banks. 
As part of the ongoing governance reforms, a 
structured and transparent selection process 
was 
implemented, 
ensuring 
that 
board 
appointments were based on merit, professional 
competence, and independence.

growth rate of 10.9 percent.

Corporation Bank 
The HDFC Bank, primarily engaged in providing 
credit facilities for housing purposes, is the only 
state-owned bank listed on the Colombo Stock 
Exchange. HDFC Bank operates with a branch 
network of 39 branches. 
HDFC Bank’s profit before tax recorded a 
significant decline of 85 percent to Rs. 10 
million in 2025. This substantial decrease in net 
profit primarily stemmed from the decline of 
other income by 10.7 percent to Rs. 301 million 
in 2025, compared to Rs. 337 million in 2024. 
This resulted in a return on equity of negative 
1.22 percent in 2025, compared to negative 
2.43 percent in 2024. Though the net assets per 
share of the bank decreased to Rs. 116.71, the 
share price at the end of December 2025 stood 
at Rs. 57.90.
The lending portfolio of the HDFC Bank dropped 
by 14 percent to Rs. 34.5 billion at the end of 
2025, compared to the 21.4 percent growth in 
the industry. However, the stage III loan ratio of 
the Bank increased from 45.92 percent at the 
end of 2024 to 47.04 percent at the end of 2025. 
The deposit base of the bank also decreased 
by 2.8 percent to Rs. 50.6 billion at the end of 
2025, compared to Rs. 52 billion at the end of 
2024, whilst the average growth in the banking 
sector stood at 10.9 percent.

The Employees’ Trust Fund Board (ETFB) is 
the second largest superannuation fund in Sri 
Lanka. All private sector employees and semi-
government sector employees are members of 
this fund, while their employers are required to 
remit 3 percent of the total monthly earnings 
of their employees to the fund. In addition, 
migrant workers and self-employed individuals 
may join the fund on voluntarily basis by making 
a specified minimum contribution. The number 
of migrant workers registered with the ETFB 
increased marginally by 36 in 2025, bringing 
the cumulative number to 327. In contrast, total 
departures for foreign employment during the 
year 2025 stood at 311,223, as reported by 
the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment. 
This disparity indicates a notably low level 
of participation to the Fund among migrant 
workers, which underscores the necessity 
of strengthening awareness and outreach 
initiatives targeting migrant workers and self-
employed individuals to promote voluntary 
enrolment. 
Beyond its primary role of fund management, 
ETFB provides a range of social and welfare 
benefits to its members covering health care 
support, housing assistance and financial aid 
for the education of members’ children during 
their period of employment.

assets increasing to Rs. 673 billion at the end of 
2025, compared to Rs. 591 billion at the end of 
2024. The ETFB maintained a strong focus on 
ensuring both safety of the fund and a reasonable 
rate of return for its members. During the year,

The National Water Supply and Drainage Board 
(NWS&DB) continues to uphold its commitment 
to achieving Sustainable Development Goal 
6, ensuring the availability and sustainable 
management of water and sanitation for all, 
in alignment with national policy priorities. 
Accordingly, NWS&DB improved its service 
coverage through piped water to 51.2 percent 
of the population in 2025, compared to 49.2 
percent in 2024. Meantime, the total piped 
water coverage, including the piped water 
supply by the community-based organizations 
and the local authorities, at the end of 2025 
stood at 62.5 percent.  However, safe drinking 
water coverage declined to 93.9 percent in the 
year under review, compared to 98.8 percent 
in 2024, mainly due to the revision of data on 
dug wells, hand pumps and other point sources 
published by the Department of Census and 
Statistics in 2025. The total number of water 
supply connections provided by the Board 
increased to 3.2 million at the end of 2025, 
compared to 3.1 million at the end of 2024, 
along with the completion of 03 water projects. 
Meanwhile, piped sewerage coverage showed 
a slight improvement from 2.08 percent to 2.11 
percent at the end of 2025 and the Non-Revenue 
Water (NRW) percentage declined to 24.35 
percent, compared to 24.8 percent at the end 
of 2024.
Following the water tariff revisions implemented 
during 2022–2024, NWS&DB continued to 
record an improvement in financial performance, 
in terms of total revenue and net profit for the 
third consecutive year. However, water sales

the reduction in electricity tariffs during the

Sri Lanka Ports Authority 
Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) continued to play 
a pivotal role in advancing Sri Lanka’s maritime 
and trade connectivity in 2025, operating as a 
key driver of economic recovery and external 
sector resilience. Amid evolving global shipping 
dynamics, 
SLPA 
maintained 
operational 
continuity, strengthened port efficiency, and 
supported national logistics competitiveness. 
Through prudent management and ongoing 
modernization 
initiatives, 
the 
Authority 
reinforced its strategic position as a regional 
maritime hub while contributing to government 
revenue and broader macroeconomic stability.
Economic growth across Asia, particularly in 
India presents significant opportunities for the 
future. As the premier hub port in South Asia, 
the Port of Colombo (PoC), Sri Lanka’s main 
port, is strategically positioned to capitalize on 
this growth by complementing the expansion 
of the subcontinent’s port sector. Alongside 
the development of the PoC, SLPA is actively 
advancing and positioning with other regional 
ports to meet the future demands.
The SLPA reported a 4.2 percent increase in 
ship arrivals in 2025, reaching 5,127 vessels 
compared to 4,920 ship arrivals in 2024. 
However, its performance declined in container 
and cargo handling, with container volumes 
falling by 1.2 percent to 2.38 million TEUs in 
2025 from 2.41 million TEUs in 2024, and cargo 
volume dropping by 7.4 percent to 43.1 million 
metric tons in 2025, compared to 46.5 million 
metric tons in 2024.

8.6 	
Insurance
The insurance sector remains a key component 
of Sri Lanka’s financial system, particularly in 
an environment marked by past economic 
uncertainty and the increasing frequency of 
natural disasters. The industry comprises fifteen 
(15) licensed insurers in the long-term insurance 
sector and fourteen (14) licensed insurers in 
the general insurance sector. Government 
participation is evident through Sri Lanka 
Insurance Corporation General Ltd (SLICGL), Sri 
Lanka Insurance Corporation Life Ltd (SLICLL), 
and the National Insurance Trust Fund (NITF). 
In addition, other state-owned enterprises, 
namely, the Agricultural and Agrarian Insurance 
Board (AAIB) and the Sri Lanka Export Credit 
Insurance 
Corporation 
(SLECIC) 
provide 
specialized insurance services, including crop 
insurance and export credit insurance.
As at end 2025, total assets base of the insurance 
sector increased by 17 percent to Rs. 1,432.2 
billion, compared to Rs. 1,223 billion at the end 
of 2024. Gross written premium increased by 19 
percent in 2025, when compared to year 2024. 
This growth appeared in both life and general 
insurance subsectors.  However, profit before 
tax of the general and long-term insurance 
subsectors decreased by 9.9 percent and 0.6 
percent, respectively in 2025, compared to the 
previous year.
In 2025, general insurance sector experienced 
substantial claims due to the impact of Cyclone 
Ditwah, which is around Rs. 58.5 billion, 
as reported by the Insurance Regulatory 
Commission of Sri Lanka.

from a direct insurer to a holding company. 
As at end 2025, SLICLL and SLICGL reported

During 2025, SLICLL recorded revenue of

in 2024. Gross Written Premium (GWP) also

the non-life insurance segment.
In terms of profitability, SLICLL’s profit after tax 
decreased by 11.5 percent to Rs. 2.3 billion

At the holding company level, SLIC reported 
a profit before tax of Rs. 6 billion in 2025, 
compared to Rs. 3.1 billion in 2024, reflecting an 
overall improvement in financial performance. 
Dividend distributions of the company recorded 
as Rs. 1.5 billion in 2025, compared to Rs. 1.3 
billion in the previous year.

8.7 	
Commuter Transportation
8.7.1	
Sri Lanka Transport Board
The Sri Lanka Transport Board (SLTB), as the 
largest public passenger transport services 
provider in the country, continues to play a vital 
role in ensuring safe, affordable, and accessible 
mobility across the island. SLTB fulfills 40 to 
50 percent of the daily passenger transport 
service demand of the country. In 2025, SLTB 
deployed nearly 4,424 buses daily, operating 
through an extensive network comprising 
over 100 depots, 09 sub-depots, 12 regional 
offices, 12 provincial workshops, and 21 driving 
training schools. With a workforce exceeding 
24,000 employees, SLTB continues to uphold a 
strong operational capacity, particularly in rural 
and underserved areas where private sector 
participation is limited. This extensive reach 
highlights SLTB’s strategic importance not 
only as a transport provider, but also as a key 
facilitator of economic and social connectivity.
SLTB is responsible for meeting around 40 
percent of the total timetable requirement 
allocated by the National Transport Commission 
(NTC). However, existing fleet capacity remains 
a constraint in fully meeting the service 
demand, indicating a persistent gap between 
required service levels and available resources. 
In line with ongoing modernization efforts, 
SLTB continued to expand and upgrade its 
fleet during the year, including the introduction 
of new buses under government-supported 
initiatives and arrangements through newly 
established subsidiary, Metro Transit Lanka 
(Private) Limited (LMTL). The LMTL aims to 
streamline and modernize public mobility 
across key city corridors through an integrated 
transport solution. These interventions reflect 
a gradual shift from reactive fleet replacement 
toward a more structured modernization 
strategy, although the pace of renewal may 
still be insufficient to offset long-term asset 
deterioration.
In fulfilling its public service mandate, SLTB 
continued to operate essential transport 
services, namely Nisi Seriya and Sisu Seriya with 
the support of the government through subsidy 
programs. During 2025, SLTB deployed 471 
buses for Nisi Seriya and 819 buses for Sisu Seriya 
program. These initiatives ensure night-time 
transport services and facilitate affordable and 
safe travel for school children. 
The average number of buses operated per 
day by SLTB in 2025 decreased to 4,424 buses, 
compared to 4,556 buses in 2024. However, 
SLTB’s operational performance recorded only 
a marginal decline in 2025, with total operated 
kilometers decreased to 362 million kilometers, 
compared to 372 million kilometers in 2024. 
In terms of financial performance, SLTB’s total 
revenue declined marginally to Rs. 73,783 
million in 2025, compared to Rs. 75,710 million 
in 2024, mainly due to the cumulative impact 
of continuous bus fare reductions implemented 
during 2024 followed by the slight reduction in 
2025. 
Total expenses of SLTB also decreased to 
Rs. 70,521 million, compared to Rs. 75,614 million 
in 2024 primarily driven by an average fuel 
price reduction of around 10 percent. Despite 
the marginal decline in the revenue, due to 
decrease in total expenses and the increase in 
financial assistance from government, SLTB’s 
net profit increased significantly in 2025 to 
Rs. 4,312 million, compared to Rs. 547 million 
in 2024, representing an increase of more than 
sevenfold. In 2025, SLTB paid Rs. 65 million as 
levy to the consolidated fund, compared to 
Rs. 330 million in 2024.
In line with SLTB’s public service obligations, 
Government support continued in the form of 
subsidies to maintain concessionary travel and 
operate uneconomical routes. Accordingly, the 
General Treasury released Rs. 13,150 million and 
Rs. 2,000 million for season ticket subsidies and 
uneconomic routes, respectively, compared to 
Rs. 10,500 million and Rs. 2,000 million in 2024. 
Despite ongoing improvements, SLTB continues 
to face structural challenges, particularly due to 
its aging fleet, with around 46 percent of buses 
exceeding 15 years of service by end 2025. This 
has led to higher maintenance requirements, 
increased downtime, and reduced service 
reliability. To address these issues, SLTB 
implemented several modernization initiatives 
during 2025, including the refurbishment of 120 
buses with new engine installations at a total 
cost of Rs. 724 million. However, these measures 
have only partially mitigated the challenges, 
highlighting the need for a more accelerated

8.8.2  SriLankan Airlines Ltd.
SriLankan Airlines Limited (SLA) recorded an 
improvement in passenger revenue and earnings 
from core business operations during 2025/26, 
supported by higher operational performance. 
Passenger revenue increased from Rs. 234.5 
billion in 2024/25 to Rs. 265.9 billion in 2025/26, 
reflecting improved passenger demand and 
network performance. Cargo revenue remained 
relatively stable at Rs. 31.4 billion compared to 
Rs. 32.4 billion in the previous year. Accordingly, 
total net traffic revenue increased from Rs. 298.9 
billion to Rs. 333.5 billion during the year.
Operational expenditure increased from Rs. 275.7 
billion in 2024/25 to Rs. 307.1 billion in 2025/26, 
mainly due to higher fuel cost, airport, aeronaut 
and passenger expenses and maintenance 
costs. Aircraft fuel expenditure rose from 
Rs. 91.7 billion to Rs. 96.1 billion, while airport, 
aeronaut and passenger expenses and aircraft 
maintenance expenses increased significantly 
by 17 percent and 22 percent, respectively to 
Rs. 53.1 billion and Rs. 53.6 billion, respectively, 
reflecting increased operational activity and 
maintenance requirements. However, rentals on 
leased aircrafts declined from Rs. 3.6 billion to 
Rs. 1.9 billion, partially easing the cost burden. 
Earnings before interest and tax increased by 
13.8 percent from Rs. 23.2 billion in 2024/25 to 
Rs. 26.4 billion during the year concerned. 
Nevertheless, SLA continued to face significant 
financial pressures arising from debt servicing 
obligations and exchange rate fluctuations. In this 
context, the Government continued to support 
the airline through ongoing debt restructuring 
initiatives, including the restructuring of the 
USD 175 million international bond, which 
generated a positive one-off financial impact 
during the year. Further, the Government 
continued servicing loan obligations to Bank 
of Ceylon and People’s Bank on behalf of SLA 
in order to support liquidity and uninterrupted 
operations. Accordingly, interest cost which 
was Rs. 36.2 billion in 2024/25 has reduced to 
Rs. 24.7 billion in 2025/26. However, adverse 
exchange differences mainly from transactions 
and liabilities amounting to Rs. 6.4 billion and 
Rs. 18.6 billion, respectively  have significantly 
affected overall financial performance. With this 
effect, net loss before tax increased from Rs. 7.6 
billion in 2024/25 to Rs. 23.2 billion in 2025/26.
The financial position of the Company reflects 
gradual 
improvement 
despite 
continuing 
balance 
sheet 
challenges. 
Total 
assets 
increased from Rs. 182 billion by end March 
2025 to Rs. 204.6 billion by end March 2026. 
Total liabilities declined from Rs. 585.1 billion 
to Rs. 544.4 billion, reflecting progress in debt 
restructuring and liability management efforts. 
Negative equity also improved from Rs. 403.2 
billion to Rs. 339.7 billion during the year.
Overall, SLA demonstrated improved operational 
performance and stronger earnings generation 
during 2025/26. However, the airline continues 
to face structural financial challenges due to 
high debt servicing costs and exposure to 
exchange rate volatility. Continued Government 
support and the successful implementation of 
debt restructuring initiatives remain critical 
for the long-term financial sustainability of the 
airline.

8.10 	
Lotteries
The lottery industry in Sri Lanka is a well-
regulated segment and constitutes a significant 
component of the country’s broader gaming 
sector. The industry operates as a duopoly 
market structure with two State Owned 
Enterprises, namely National Lotteries Board 
(NLB) and the Development Lotteries Board 
(DLB). These institutions are responsible for 
the design, distribution and management of a 
diverse range of lottery products targeted at 
the general public.
In terms of market structure, the NLB held 
a market share of 53 percent, while DLB 
accounted for the remaining 47 percent in 
2025. The NLB’s product portfolio comprised 11 
lottery brands, including 9 passive and 2 instant 
lotteries. Similarly, the DLB offered 9 passive 
lottery brands.
A distinctive feature of the lottery industry 
in Sri Lanka is its contribution to national 
development. Proceeds from lottery operations 
are channeled towards a range of public welfare 
initiatives including education, healthcare and 
infrastructure development. The NLB contributes 
directly to the consolidated fund, while the DLB 
is a major contributor to the President’s Fund, 
with a portion of such funds further allocated 
to the Mahapola Higher Education Trust Fund. 
During 2025, the NLB and DLB were able to 
channel Rs. 5,699 million to the Consolidated 
Fund and Rs. 7,361 million to the President’s 
Fund, respectively. In 2025, the total lottery 
sales income amounted to Rs. 91,107 million, 
reflecting a growth of 33 percent compared to 
the previous year. Meanwhile, approximately an 
aggregate of Rs. 46,735 million prizes declared 
by both institutions, representing a 32 percent 
year- on –year growth. 
Despite ongoing efforts towards digitization, 
the customer base of the lottery industry 
remains 
concentrated 
among 
the 
older 
generation, 
who 
demonstrates 
a 
strong 
preference for traditional paper– based lottery 
tickets. In contrast, participation among the 
younger demographics remains relatively low, 
indicating limited engagement with lottery 
products. Accordingly, beyond the expansion 
of digital sales platforms, a comprehensive, 
digitally enabled strategy, including product 
innovation, enhanced user experience and 
target marketing will be critical to attracting 
younger demographics and broadening the 
industry’s customer base.  
8.10.1	 National Lotteries Board
NLB recorded its highest-ever sales income of 
Rs. 48,313 million in 2025, reflecting a 27 percent 
increase compared to Rs. 37,983 million in 2024. 
The total value of prizes declared also increased 
significantly to Rs. 24,879 million, representing 
a 26.8 percent growth over the previous year. 
During the year under review, NLB awarded its 
highest-ever super prize amounting to Rs. 470 
million. NLB’s contribution from lottery sales 
and levy to the Consolidated Fund recorded 
a notable increase of 25 percent, rising from 
Rs. 5,570 million in 2024 to Rs. 6,949 million in 
2025.

diverse 
geographical market segments across the 
island. In addition to traditional dealer channels, 
passive lotteries are also distributed through 
SMS dealers, further enhancing accessibility.

portfolio and expanding its market share. As 
part of this strategy, the “Lucky 7” lottery was 
discontinued with effect from end January, 2025 
and replaced it with “NLB Jaya” which generated 
sales income of Rs. 3,527 million. Furthermore, 
a new lottery product “Suba Dawasak” was

income of Rs. 1,722 million during the year.
The Board sustained its strong financial

of Rs. 7,487 million in 2025, a year-on-year

employees, LSL remains deeply committed to 
its core mandate of safeguarding consumer 
welfare and contributing to national food 
security. Despite maintaining an approximate 
5 percent market share in a highly competitive 
business environment, LSL’s growth and market 
position are increasingly challenged by the

sector supermarket chains.

Rs. 51,534 million, reflecting a slight decrease
