in the previous year. At the same time, LSL’s 
gross profit ratio recorded a marginal decrease 
to 12.34 percent in 2025, compared to 12.43 
percent in 2024.  However, due to the decrease 
in other expenditure by 20 percent to Rs. 7,445 
million compared to Rs. 9,412 million in 2024, 
despite the decrease in other income by 3.9 
percent, the LSL’s operating loss decreased 
to Rs. 56 million in 2025, compared to the 
operating loss of Rs. 1,775 million in 2024.

expenses by 26 percent from Rs. 649 million

8.13 	
Plantation
Sri Lanka State Plantations Corporation (SLSPC) 
and Janatha 
Estates 
Development 
Board 
(JEDB) were established with the objective 
of strengthening the contribution of the state 
plantation sector towards the national economy. 
The majority of estates under their ownership 
have been leased out to 23 Regional Plantation 
Companies while allotting the Golden Share of 
each RPC to the government. The government 
has retained the ownership of Kurunegala 
Plantations Limited (KPL), Chilaw Plantations 
Limited (CPL), Elkaduwa Plantations Limited 
(EPL) and Kalubovitiyana Tea Factory Limited 
(KTFL) from the above RPCs, in order to ensure 
the sustainability of the state plantation sector 
contribution towards the national economy.
Total revenue of KPL increased by 29 percent 
to Rs. 1,868 million in 2025, compared to 
Rs. 1,448 million in 2024, mainly due to high 
net sales average prevailed during the year 
amidst the drop in coconut production as a 
result of the impact of the weather pattern of 
the area. Meantime, the company’s cost of sales 
increased by 12.7 percent to Rs. 896 million in 
2025. However, KPL recorded a net profit of 
Rs. 635 million in 2025, an increase of 53 percent 
compared to Rs. 415 million in 2024, mainly 
due to the improvement in gross profit ratio 
from 38 percent in 2024 to 47 percent in 2025 
and increase in other operating income by 33 
percent to Rs. 83.6 million in 2025, compared 
to Rs. 62.7 million in 2024. 
Total revenue of CPL increased by 54 percent to 
Rs. 1,845 million in 2025, compared to Rs. 1,200 
million in 2024 due to the increased net sales 
average in 2025 and increase in coconut 
production by 10 percent to 11 million nuts in 
2025 from 10 million nuts in 2024. Accordingly, 
net profit before tax of the CPL increased by 
almost 197 percent to Rs. 650 million in 2025, 
compared to Rs. 219 million in 2024.
EPL’s total revenue increased by 18 percent 
to Rs. 649 million in 2025 from Rs. 550 million 
in 2024, mainly driven by higher tea sales, 
which were supported by increased green leaf 
production and improved yield per hectare due 
to the proper application of chemical fertilizer. 
As a result, the company recorded a net profit 
of Rs. 271 million in 2025, compared to Rs. 12 
million in 2024. 
KTFL’s total revenue increased by 18 percent to 
Rs. 2,052 million in 2025, compared to Rs. 1,737 
million in 2024, primarily due to the increase 
in made tea production by 15 percent to 1,489 
metric tons in 2025, compared to 1,294 metric 
tons in 2024. Accordingly, KTFL recorded a net 
profit of Rs. 87 million in 2025, compared to the 
net loss of Rs. 7 million in 2024.
SLSPC manages 4,200 hectares across 15 tea 
estates and 01 rubber estate while the JEDB 
manages 3,572 hectares across 15 tea estates 
and 02 rubber estates. As the main crop, tea 
production of JEDB increased by 15 percent to 
1,256 metric tons in 2025 due to increase in tea 
yield per hectare to 466 kg, compared to 403 
kg in 2024. In the meantime, tea production 
of SLSPC also increased by 8.1 percent to 1,116 
metric tons due to increase in tea yield per 
hectare to 501 kg in 2025, compared to 439 kg 
in previous year. 
Total revenue of JEDB decreased by 8 percent to 
Rs. 1,602 million in 2025, compared to Rs. 1,732 
million in 2024 and the total revenue of SLSPC 
increased by 13 percent to Rs. 1,340 million in 
2025, compared to Rs. 1,183 million in 2024. 
Accordingly, the JEDB and SLSPC recorded 
net losses of Rs. 222 million and Rs. 35 million, 
respectively.
As approved by the Cabinet of Ministers, the 
unutilized lands/properties of JEDB, SLSPC 
and Regional Plantation Companies have 
been identified to be leased out to potential 
investors on a long-term basis for optimal use 
to strengthen agricultural exports. Moreover, 
the government increased the daily minimum 
wage for estate workers from Rs. 1,350/- to 
Rs. 1,750/- as a crucial step towards improving 
the livelihoods of plantation workers and 
addressing the challenge of dwindling the 
estate workforce.

8.14. 	 Health
8.14.1 	 State Pharmaceuticals Corporation
The State Pharmaceuticals Corporation (SPC) 
is engaged in the importation and trading 
of pharmaceuticals and health care items, 
as well as the supply of such products to 
the Department of Health Services (DHS). In 
addition, SPC undertakes limited manufacturing 
activities, producing selected pharmaceuticals 
and health care products such as Jeevanee, 
Glucose and Benzyl Bensovate Cream. SPC 
continues to ensure its geographical presence 
through open market operations supported 
by 61 Osusala outlets, 121 franchised Osusala 
outlets and 53 distributors.
In 2025, sales to DHS increased by 26 percent, 
rising from Rs. 51,018 million in 2024 to Rs. 64,197 
million. Meanwhile, sales of SPC open market 
operations recorded a marginal decline from 
Rs. 11,069 million in 2024 to Rs. 11,043 million 
in 2025. Overall, SPC’s total revenue increased 
by 21 percent to Rs. 75,240 million in 2025, 
compared to Rs. 62,087 million in 2024. 
SPC’s total cost of sales increased by 23 
percent to Rs. 68,008 million in 2025, compared 
to Rs. 55,138 million in 2024. As a result, the 
gross profit margin declined to 9.6 percent 
in 2025, compared to 11.2 percent in 2024. 
Meanwhile, financing costs decreased by 28 
percent to Rs. 1,263 million in 2025, compared 
to Rs. 1,758 million in 2024, reflecting the easing 
of domestic interest rates during the period. 
Benefiting from the favorable impact from the 
decreasing finance cost, SPC recorded a 52 
percent increase in profit before tax to Rs. 3,772 
million in 2025, compared to the profit before 
tax of Rs. 2,474 million in 2024. 
In compliance with the Government’s levy 
policy, SPC paid Rs. 487 million to the 
Consolidated Fund in 2025, representing 30 
percent of the profit after tax of Rs. 1,623 million 
in 2024. This contribution reflects the SPC’s 
commitment to supporting fiscal stability, while 
continuing to ensure uninterrupted supply of 
essential pharmaceuticals to the health system 
of the country. 
The persistence of long outstanding receivable 
balances continued to exert significant fiscal 
pressure on SPC’s operating cash flow and 
liquidity position. At the end of 2025, total 
receivables from the Medical Supplies Division 
(MSD) amounted to Rs. 39,233 million, of which 
Rs. 23,867 million were outstanding payments 
for medical supplies procured from the SPC 
during the period 2018-2023 by the MSD of the 
Ministry of Health and Mass Media. Accordingly, 
in January 2026, Cabinet of Ministers approved to 
settle the due amount of Rs. 23,867 million to the 
SPC for the period of 2018-2023 in installments 
by managing the relevant provisions allocated 
to the Ministry of Health and Mass Media for the 
year 2026. 
By end April 2026, Ministry of Health and Mass 
Media was able to settle Rs. 23.8 billion to the 
SPC. Furthermore, actions are being taken to 
reconcile the remaining balance due from 2008 
to 2012. The implementation of these measures 
is expected to enhance SPC’s liquidity position 
and strengthen its short-term financial stability.
A key strategic development in 2025 was the 
continued strengthening of SPC’s laboratory 
function, marked by the initiation of the ISO 
17025 accreditation process. This milestone 
reflects SPC’s commitment to aligning with 
internationally recognized standards in testing, 
ensuring 
accuracy, 
reliability 
and 
quality 
management. Through these efforts, SPC aims 
to enhance public confidence and institutional 
credibility, while further reinforcing the scientific 
and regulatory framework that underpins the 
national pharmaceutical supply.
Moreover, under the patronage of the Asian 
Development Bank (ADB), an Enterprise Resource 
Planning (ERP) system is set to be introduced 
to strengthen Sri Lanka’s pharmaceutical supply 
chain. The implementation of this system is 
expected to significantly improve operational 
efficiency, reduce costs and enhance overall 
supply chain effectiveness. This initiative is 
to be further supported at the policy level 
through the development of pharmaceutical 
procurement guidelines and manual by the 
National Procurement Commission.

9.1	
Overview
The submission of Regulations under the Public 
Financial Management Act No. 44 of 2024 to 
Parliament and the implementation of the e-GP 
system have been recognized as Structural 
Benchmarks under the International Monetary 
Fund 
(IMF) 
Extended 
Financing 
Facility 
programme. 
Accordingly, with the assistance of Development 
Partners including the International Monetary 
Fund, Asian Development Bank, and the 
United 
Nations 
Development 
Programme, 
new Regulations are currently being drafted 
while the Financial Regulations issued in 1992 
are being reviewed and revised to ensure 
consistency with the Act. 
Public procurement has also been identified as 
a key area for reform, with the deployment of a 
revamped Electronic Government Procurement 
(e-GP) system aimed at enhancing transparency, 
efficiency, and accountability in government 
procurement 
processes. 
A 
significant 
proportion of public funds is expended on 
procurement activities, including the acquisition 
of goods and services by various ministries, 
departments, and other public sector agencies. 
Consequently, improvements in the efficiency 
and effectiveness of procurement processes 
can 
contribute 
substantially 
to 
reducing 
government expenditure. In this context, the 
adoption of an e-GP system is considered 
an essential mechanism for promoting best 
practices in government procurement and 
strengthening transparency and accountability 
in the use of public resources.
9.2	
Public Financial Management Act
With a view to implementing the provisions 
stipulated in the Public Financial Management 
(PFM) Act, the Minister of Finance is required 
to formulate and issue Regulations under 
the Section 67(1) of the Act. Accordingly, 
new Regulations under the PFM Act are 
being formulated, and the existing Financial 
Regulations (FRs) are being updated to ensure 
consistency with the provisions of the PFM Act. 
This process also necessitates the removal of 
redundant provisions contained in the existing 
Financial Regulations issued in 1992, as well as 
the introduction of new sets of Regulations to 
operationalize newly introduced areas under 
the PFM Act, including Public Investment 
Management 
and 
Fiscal 
Responsibility. 
Meantime, directives by way of circular and 
guidelines will be issued to cover existing and 
new provisions that are not included in the 
Regulations.
In order to achieve this objective, several 
rounds of consultations were conducted with 
external stakeholders, with particular emphasis 
on identifying special Regulations that had 
been incorporated into the existing Financial 
Regulations and on determining areas of 
redundancy. In this context, the Department 
of Public Finance is in the process of finalizing 
the Regulations with the assistance of the 
respective Treasury Departments.
Although the issuance of Directives is not an 
IMF structural benchmark, it is imperative that 
such Directives be issued simultaneously with 
the Regulations in order to ensure the effective 
implementation of the provisions of the Public 
Financial Management Act. Accordingly, the 
Department of Public Finance is also in the 
process of finalizing the required Directives, 
with the assistance of the respective Treasury 
Departments. The process was supported 
by Development Partners through technical, 
advisory, and institutional support.
Review of Statutory and Non-Statutory Funds
Ministries, 
Departments 
and 
State-Owned 
Enterprises maintain various Funds outside 
the Consolidated Fund under their respective 
purview. These include both statutory funds 
established through statutes and non-statutory 
funds created for specific operational purposes. 
The governance framework for such funds 
is set out in Part VIII, Section 39 of the Public 
Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024. 
Under the Article 149 of the constitution, it is 
articulated that funds outside the Consolidated 
Fund can be maintained only under specific 
circumstances. As such, through the PFM Act, 
all public entities have been requested to either 
wind up non-statutory funds or to convert 
them to statutory funds through statutes, if 
retention of such funds are critical and those 
functions cannot be carried out through regular 
budgetary allocations.

Under Section 39(4) of the PFM Act, the Secretary

institutions. The Review Committee’s Report 
was submitted to the Cabinet of Ministers, 
and approval was obtained to implement its 
recommendations.
The  Department of  Public Finance issued

Circular

dated 
28.02.2025, 
providing detailed guidance to Chief Accounting 
Officers (CAOs) on fund management, reporting 
requirements, and governance standards. In 
addition, approximately 70 clarifications and 
specific instructions were issued to CAOs 
to reinforce compliance and ensure sound 
financial oversight. Initial steps were also 
taken to formulate Regulations and Directives 
relating to statutory funds in alignment with the 
PFM Act. Further in accordance with Section 
39(2) of the Act, a Consolidated Report on 
the performance of statutory funds for the 
year 2024 was prepared and submitted to the 
Cabinet of Ministers during the year 2025. The 
Cabinet of Ministers has subsequently granted 
approval to implement the recommendations 
contained in the Report. Overall, these 
measures strengthened regulatory oversight, 
improved transparency, and ensured greater 
compliance with the provisions of the PFM Act, 
thereby enhancing the governance and financial 
discipline of statutory and non-statutory funds.
9.3	
Procurement Management 
Adherence to sound procurement practices 
has been emphasized at every level to ensure 
a transparent, efficient, and timely public 
procurement process that guarantees value for 
money and fair dealing, thereby safeguarding 
the public interest. In this context, the 
government procurement system represents 
a fundamental element of Public Financial 
Management (PFM), supporting transparency, 
efficiency, and the responsible management of 
public resources.
The Electronic Government Procurement (e-
GP) system, capable of facilitating goods 
procurement under the Shopping Method, has 
been deployed and is currently in operation. 
To date, the e-GP platform has enabled the 
registration of approximately 875 Procuring 
Entities and 5,900 vendors. By the end of 2025, 
more than 400 Government Procuring Entities 
had undertaken their procurements through the 
e-GP platform, and over 61,500 procurements 
had been conducted through the system. 
With the notable progress achieved in the 
implementation of the e-GP platform, Procuring 
Entities have been instructed to upload 
information relating to major procurements 
to enhance transparency and ensure public 
accessibility to procurement information.
During the year, the Department of Public 
Finance assumed full operational control of the 
e-GP platform following the termination of the 
contract with the former System Implementation 
Partner (SIP). Meanwhile, preliminary work 
relating to the design and development of 
the e-GP platform to cover procurement 
methods beyond the Shopping Method, by 
way of obtaining the services of new System 
Implementation Partner (SIP) with the technical 
and financial support of the World Bank, has 
been initiated and is currently in progress.
Furthermore, the Department of Public Finance 
has taken steps to integrate SLT Rainbow’s 
registered vendor database with the e-GP 
platform. The necessary system developments 
for both platforms have been completed, and 
the registration of such vendors on the e-GP 
platform is currently underway.
Moreover, the public is able to access 
procurement notices covering all procurement 
categories, including those with Total Cost 
Estimates exceeding Rs. 200 million, while 
details of contract awards exceeding Rs. 200 
million have been made publicly available 
through the e-GP portal with effect from 01 July 
2022. Circular No. e-GP/ICT/Awards (sp)/2025 
dated 2025/08/05 has been issued in this 
regard by the Secretary to the Treasury.
In addition, recommendations and feedback 
have been provided to the National Procurement 
Commission (NPC) for the development of new 
Procurement Guidelines and revision whenever 
requested during the year. The process of 
appointing High-Level and Cabinet-Appointed 
Procurement 
Committees 
has 
also 
been 
continued to ensure the effective oversight of 
major government procurements.

Box 9.1 | Non-Financial Assets Management of the Government
As the productive use of the Non- Financial Assets of the Government have been deteriorated due to the 
lack of a focused agency to adhere to an effective system to oversee the efficient utilization of assets, secure 
assets adequately and for the maintenance and improvement of assets, the Comptroller General’s Office is 
mainly entrusted with overseeing the management of these assets of the Government. Hence, it is required to 
maintain an updated comprehensive central data base for the Non-Financial Assets of the Public Institutions 
(Government Agencies (Ministries, Departments, District Secretariats, Special Spending Units, Foreign 
Missions), Public Enterprises and Provincial Councils & Local Governments) and to formulate and implement 
Non - Financial Assets management policies, identifying idle resources and ensuring effective use of these 
assets, to strengthen the development framework of the Government. 
In order to ensure the proper management of Non- Financial Assets of the Government, it is required to enact 
the Public Assets Management Law.  
The online Non-Financial Assets Management System (NFAMS) has been introduced by issuing the Assets 
Management Circular No 06/2023, for the Non-Financial Assets management of the Government. This system 
has been implemented with effect from 01st September 2023 and module on vehicles has been implemented 
as the first module of this system. Through this system, a web-based centralized comprehensive real time data 
recording system is established, which consists of essential information including assets valuation required 
for the Non-Financial Assets management. The design, software development, implementation, improvement 
and maintenance of NFAMS is done by the Comptroller General’s office and the Department of Information 
Technology Management, without incurring an additional cost to the Government. The other modules in 
NFAMS will be implemented gradually, in due course.
As recorded in NFAMS as at 18th May 2026, the vehicle fleet of the Public Institutions amounts to 96,027 ( 92,116 
in running condition and 3,911 not in running condition). Under the module on vehicles in NFAMS, there are 
registered 2,159 data reporting entities as at 18th May 2026, to record the vehicle details. The age analysis of

10.1    Overview
In 
2025, 
Sri 
Lanka 
recorded 
a 
broad-
based recovery across multiple sectors of 
the economy. In support of this positive 
trajectory, previously stringent human resource 
management policies were moderately relaxed. 
This policy adjustment was undertaken despite 
ongoing fiscal constraints and persistent 
challenges related to expenditure control and 
cost containment. 
The legal framework governing public sector 
human resource management was further 
strengthened in 2025 with the enactment of the 
Public Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024, 
which vests authority in the Minister of Finance 
over the cadre management of public entities. 
Within this framework, the Minister of Finance is 
vested with the authority to determine salaries, 
wages, and other forms of remuneration of 
officers and employees of public institutions, 
in compliance with national remuneration 
policies. This legal framework is intended to 
enhance accountability, transparency, and 
fiscal discipline in the management of the 
public workforce and its associated financial 
obligations.
Acknowledging 
the 
necessity 
of 
robust 
public service delivery, a comprehensive 
assessment was conducted to identify cadre 
requirements and critical vacancies. Priority 
was accorded to filling essential technical 
positions and establishing new positions 
necessary to accelerate public service delivery 
and strengthen the implementation capacity 
of 
national 
development 
projects. 
This 
targeted approach extended to state-owned 
commercial enterprises, self-financing entities, 
and vital sectors such as health, education, 
and defence. A significant milestone achieved 
in 2025 was the effective management of 
substantial recruitment demands across various 
government institutions. Accordingly, approval 
was granted to fill 76,988 vacancies as at 31 
December 2025.
In 2025, initiatives were implemented to 
increase public sector remuneration with 
the aim of ensuring a satisfactory standard 
of 
living 
for 
government 
employees 
while strengthening their motivation and 
commitment towards effective public service 
delivery. This initiative was also intended 
to strengthen the government’s capacity 
to attract and retain skilled and competent 
personnel, while maintaining fiscal discipline 
and avoiding undue pressure on the national 
budget. The salary revision was designed to be 
implemented in a phased manner across three 
stages, commencing in April 2025, followed by 
subsequent adjustments in January 2026 and 
January 2027. The increase in the minimum basic 
salary of public service employees has been 
correspondingly extended to judicial service 
personnel, employees of public corporations 
and statutory boards, university staff, and officers 
of the tri-forces, ensuring uniform applicability 
on an equivalent basis across these sectors. 
Circulars were issued to revise the salary 
structures of the respective service categories. 
Notwithstanding the existence of distinct salary 
frameworks for Sri Jayewardenepura Hospital 
and Wijaya Kumaratunga Hospital, the absence 
of an applicable circular for these institutions 
was effectively addressed in 2025.
The measures taken in 2025 to formalize 
semi government sector are noteworthy. In 
particular, the issuance of circulars establishing 
a standardized framework for the payment of 
allowances to resource persons engaged in 
training programmes, seminars, and capacity 
development initiatives conducted by public 
corporations, 
fully 
government-owned 
companies, and statutory bodies contributed 
to enhancing the quality of such programmes. 
Furthermore, the introduction of provisions 
facilitating the attachment of trainees to these 
institutions for practical training represented 
a 
significant 
step 
toward 
strengthening 
institutional capacity and promoting skills 
development.
The initiation of a cadre review process in 
2025, aimed at fostering a more qualitative and 
optimally structured workforce within identified 
priority 
sectors, 
represents 
a 
significant 
measure in strengthening public sector human 
resource management. Accordingly, the first 
phase of these cadre reviews was successfully 
commenced in the Health, Agriculture, and 
Provincial Council sectors. Furthermore, a 
notable milestone was achieved with the 
submission of a comprehensive report to the 
Cabinet of Ministers by 31 March 2025, which 
provided detailed information on the approved 
and actual cadre strengths of the public sector 
as at 31 December 2024. This submission

MINISTRY OF FINANCE, PLANNING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT, SRI LANKA | FINAL BUDGET POSITION REPORT 2025
represents a significant development, as it 
marks the first instance since the COVID-19 
pandemic that such comprehensive personnel 
data has been systematically presented to the 
Cabinet.
Expenditure on salaries, wages, and pensions 
accounted for more than 30 per cent of the total 
government recurrent expenditure in 2025. 
Spending on salaries and wages increased by 
approximately 10 percent, rising to Rs. 1, 293 
billion in 2025 from Rs. 1,178 billion in 2024. 
Similarly, pension payments grew by nearly 
12 percent, reaching Rs. 445 billion in 2025 
compared to Rs. 396 billion in the previous year. 
This situation further underscores the necessity 
of rationalizing human resource management 
practice in the public sector.
As of the end of 2025, the total approved cadre 
in the public sector stood at 1,677,039, reflecting 
a marginal decline of 0.2 percent compared to 
2024. This slight reduction is largely due to the 
suppression of certain vacant positions, which 
were retained on a personal-to-holder basis.
In parallel, the total number of deployed 
employees in the public sector experienced

Box 10.1 | Cadre Review in Public Sector 
A cadre review is a systematic and comprehensive assessment of the staffing structure of an 
organization with the objective of ensuring that the number, composition, and distribution of 
employees are aligned with institutional mandates, service delivery requirements, and policy 
priorities. In the public sector, cadre review serves as a strategic human resource management tool 
that evaluates existing posts, identifies gaps or redundancies, and recommends optimal staffing 
arrangements to enhance efficiency and effectiveness.
Cadre reviews typically examine several key dimensions, including the number of approved and 
actual staff, the relevance of job roles, workload distribution, skills and competencies of employees, 
and the alignment between organizational objectives and human resource capacity. This process is 
often supported by data analysis, stakeholder consultations, and benchmarking against comparable 
institutions.
In this context, cadre reviews should be conducted on a periodic basis to achieve optimal outcomes. 
Accordingly, the Department of Management Services initiated a comprehensive cadre review for 
the period 2025–2026. The first phase of cadre reviews was successfully commenced in key priority 
sectors, including Health, Agriculture, and Provincial Councils. Furthermore, the postal service 
sector has also been identified as an additional area for review in line with prevailing operational 
and service delivery considerations. The primary focus of the cadre review was to,
•	 Promote efficiency by ensuring cost-effective utilization of human resources, thereby 
minimizing both over-staffing and under-staffing. 
•	 Enhance service delivery by aligning staff capacity with operational requirements, enabling 
institutions to respond more effectively to public demands. 
•	 Support fiscal discipline through evidence-based decision-making on recruitment, 
promotions, and remuneration. 
•	 Facilitate organizational restructuring and modernization by identifying outdated roles and 
recommending new positions in line with emerging priorities, such as digital governance and 
performance management. 
Building upon the aforementioned objectives, it is noteworthy that approximately 30 percent of the 
total approved cadre in the public sector is concentrated within the Provincial Councils. Despite 
this significant share, a comprehensive cadre review of Provincial Council institutions had not been 
undertaken for nearly a decade. In this context, the initiation of a comprehensive cadre review 
encompassing all Provincial Councils in 2025 represents a significant milestone towards achieving 
optimal cadre management and improved resource allocation.
Furthermore, the Agriculture sector was identified as a priority area for cadre review, given its 
devolved nature and the shared responsibilities between Provincial Councils and the Central 
Government.  Accordingly, field inspections were conducted across the relevant institutions, 
and preliminary evidence was  systematically collected during 2025 to support informed 
decision-making.
The Health sector, given its critical role in sustaining a free public healthcare system, was also 
prioritized. Rationalizing the costs associated with healthcare delivery is essential for strengthening 
public financial management. In this regard, field inspections for the cadre review of the Health 
sector were initiated in 2025, covering the first phase of selected institutions, including Teaching 
Hospital Anuradhapura, District Hospital Polonnaruwa, District Hospital Matale, National Hospital 
Kandy, Teaching Hospital Peradeniya, Sirimavo Bandaranaike Children’s Hospital – Peradeniya, 
Teaching Hospital Kalutara, and the National Institute of Mental Health.
In addition, the preliminary activities pertaining to the cadre review of the Department of Posts 
was successfully completed in 2025. This process enabled the identification of operational 
requirements of the postal service and facilitated the reorganization of the cadre in alignment with 
service delivery needs. Furthermore, the review recognized the Department of Posts as a business-
oriented entity and assessed its market competitiveness, thereby providing a basis for enhancing 
its operational efficiency and strategic positioning.

Box 10.2 | Salary Revision for the Public Sector Employees - 2025
Aimed at sustainably improving the living standards of the public sector employee, while 
strengthening their motivation and commitment towards effective public service delivery; steps 
were taken as per budget proposals 2025 to increase the minimum monthly basic salary in the public 
sector to Rs. 40,000/- and to increase the value of the annual salary increment by 80%. Accordingly, 
this salary increase was effected with a ratio of 1:4.375 between the minimum and maximum salaries 
in the public service.
In proceeding as above, monthly allowance of Rs. 5,000/- granted for the Public Service in terms 
of Public Administration Circular No. 03/2022 dated 13.01.2022, monthly allowance of Rs. 5,000/- 
granted for the Public Corporations, Statutory Boards  and Government Owned Companies in terms 
of Public Enterprises Circular No. 01/2022 dated 10.01.2022 and the monthly interim allowance of 
Rs. 2,500/- granted for the Public Service in terms of Public Administration Circular No. 09/2019 
dated 22.04.2019 were integrated in to the basic salary and with the implementation of these salary 
revisions, the said circulars were rescinded.
Percentage of allowances paid as a percentage of the basic salary was revised so as not to exceed 
the financial value of that allowance to ensure that the take home salary is increased only by the 
amount of the basic salary increase.
In view of prevailing fiscal constraints, the comprehensive salary revision was structured within the 
Treasury’s fiscal capacity and is being executed across three distinct phases. The total projected 
expenditure for this initiative is estimated at approximately Rs. 325 billion. Under the phased 
implementation framework, all public sector employees received an initial increment effective April 
1, 2025, comprising Rs. 5,000 plus 30% of the balance exceeding that amount. The remaining 70% of 
the net increase was scheduled for disbursement on a proportionate basis on January 1, 2026, and 
January 1, 2027, respectively.

10.6    Way Forward
Managing human resources in the public 
sector has become increasingly complex in 
recent years, largely due to constrained fiscal 
space and the growing burden of salary and 
wage expenditures. The relatively large size 
of the public workforce, when compared 
with 
international 
benchmarks, 
together 
with long-term liabilities arising from a non-
contributory pension system, continues to 
exert significant pressure on public finances. 
In addition, persistent skill mismatches across 
employee categories, resistance from trade 
unions and staff groups, and deeply rooted 
social and cultural factors have constrained 
efforts to optimize workforce structures. These 
challenges have remained prevalent for nearly a 
decade and are likely to persist in the absence 
of a comprehensive and systematic assessment 
of actual cadre requirements.
In this context, cadre review emerges as a 
critical strategic instrument for strengthening 
public sector human resource management. 
Moving forward, it is essential that cadre reviews 
are institutionalized as a regular and continuous 
process, rather than being undertaken on an 
ad hoc basis. Periodic reviews would enable 
the timely identification of staffing gaps, 
redundancies, and emerging skill requirements, 
thereby facilitating a more responsive and 
adaptive workforce. Furthermore, it is imperative 
to undertake a comprehensive cadre review 
across the entire public sector to assess current 
staffing requirements and identify opportunities 
for technological integration to enhance service 
delivery.
A key priority in this regard is the systematic 
updating and rationalization of Schemes of 
Recruitment across the public sector and 
State-Owned Enterprises. Aligning recruitment 
frameworks with evolving service delivery 
needs, 
technological 
advancements, 
and 
performance standards would ensure that the 
right competencies are attracted and retained 
within the system. This should be complemented 
by the introduction of competency-based 
recruitment and promotion mechanisms, which 
would help address existing skill mismatches 
and improve overall productivity.
Furthermore, 
rationalizing 
salaries 
and 
remuneration structures remains essential to 
ensure fiscal sustainability while maintaining 
employee motivation and retention. This 
requires a balanced approach that links 
compensation with roles, responsibilities, and 
performance, while also ensuring equity and 
transparency across institutions. Such reforms 
would contribute to improved expenditure 
management without undermining the quality 
of public service delivery.
In addition, greater emphasis should be placed 
on workforce planning and data-driven decision-
making. The establishment of integrated human 
resource information systems would facilitate 
real-time monitoring of cadre positions, staff 
deployment, 
and 
performance 
indicators, 
thereby enhancing the effectiveness of cadre 
management. 
Strengthening 
institutional 
capacity for conducting evidence-based cadre 
reviews is also crucial in this regard.
Equally important is the need to manage 
change in a consultative and inclusive manner. 
Constructive engagement with trade unions 
and 
employee 
representatives 
can 
help 
mitigate resistance and build consensus around 
necessary reforms. Awareness and capacity 
building initiatives should also be undertaken to 
address social and cultural barriers that hinder 
organizational transformation.
In conclusion, the way forward for cadre 
management in the public sector lies in adopting 
a holistic, evidence-based, and forward-looking 
approach. By institutionalizing periodic cadre 
reviews, modernizing recruitment frameworks, 
rationalizing remuneration, and strengthening 
data systems, the government can move 
towards achieving an optimal, efficient, and 
sustainable workforce that is better aligned 
with national development priorities.

Significant Accounting Policies
01.	
Reporting Entity
These Financial Statements of the Government 
encompass the Reporting Entity of the 
Government 
comprising 
of 
Government 
Ministries, Departments, Special Spending Units 
and District Secretariats. However, Commercial 
Public Corporations, State Owned Enterprises 
and Government Owned Companies or other 
Companies and Statutory Boards, are not 
covered in these Financial Statements. Cash 
outflows from Government to those entities 
taken place during the reporting period and the 
Government’s total interest in the Commercial 
Public Corporations, State Owned Enterprises 
and Government owned Companies or other 
Companies held in the form of equity and loans 
are taken into consideration. The Revenue 
and Expenditure of Provincial Councils are 
not considered as a part of these Financial 
Statements, since there is no significant control 
by the Government over the financial and 
operating activities of Provincial Councils.
The Financial Statements of the Government 
for the year ended 31 December 2025 were 
authorized for issue by the Department of State 
Accounts.
02.	
Basis of Preparation
These Financial Statements have been prepared 
on the historical cost convention in conformity 
with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. 
Historical cost basis has been adopted for 
measurement while adopting modified cash 
based accounting for reporting.
The Cash Flow Statement is prepared using the 
direct method.
All financial information presented in Sri Lankan 
Rupees has been rounded to the nearest rupee, 
except where indicated otherwise.
03.	
Reporting Period
The reporting period of these Financial 
Statements is from 1st of January 2025 to 31st 
December 2025.
04.	
Change in Presentation Formats 	
	
	
of Financial Statements
Presentation formats of Government Financial 
Statements from the year 2023 has been 
changed in order to improve fair presentation. 
New 
presentation 
formats 
are 
prepared 
to serve financial reporting requirements, 
Constitutional requirements and reporting 
budget performance. Reconciliations have 
provided where necessary and comparative 
figures have restated as applicable.  
Presentation formats for Ministries, Departments, 
Special Spending Units and District Secretariats 
remain unchanged for the year 2025.
05.	
Basis of Consolidation
Expenditure incurred and revenue collected 
under revenue codes specified in the budget 
classification by respective Ministries and 
Departments in the form of financial assets, 
liabilities, revenue and expenditure are reported 
using same classification codes for preparation 
of consolidated accounts.
06.	
Revenue
The 
Government 
provides 
non-income 
generating goods, services and benefits to the 
general public. The revenue is raised by way of 
taxes, levies, fees and charges imposed under 
various statutes approved by Parliament to 
finance the expenditure incurred on provision of 
such goods, services and benefits. All revenue, 
so collected through relevant Ministries and 
Departments are identified and accounted at 
the time of collection. Investment income is 
accounted for the period during which such 
income is actually collected.
07.	
Premiums and Discounts
Premiums and discounts on issue of debt 
instruments are adjusted against the cost of 
borrowings.
08.	
Expenses
All expenses are accounted in the period in 
which payments have been made.

241

09.	
Foreign Currency Transactions
Foreign Currency Transactions are converted 
into Sri Lanka Rupees using the exchange 
rate prevailed on the date of the transaction. 
Exchange 
differences 
arising 
from 
the 
settlement of these transactions are duly 
accounted through corresponding main ledger 
accounts. 
Net foreign exchange gain / loss generated in 
conversion of foreign loan balances, local loan 
balances in foreign currency and balances of 
on-lending to local currency has adjusted to the 
Statement of Financial performance.
10.	
 Investments
Value of the Government’s equity investments 
in State Owned Enterprises is recorded at 
cost and shown separately in the Financial 
Statements. However, investments in Statutory 
Boards are not separately identified and 
disclosed since such entities are relying on 
the Government for their recurrent and capital 
expenditure requirements similar to those of 
the other Government Departments.
11.	
Borrowings
In the Statement of Financial Position, all local 
borrowings are recorded at cost. Since foreign 
borrowings are subject to change in exchange 
rates, foreign monetary liabilities are converted 
to Sri Lanka Rupees using exchange rates 
prevailed at the end of the reporting period. 
Statement of individual loan details are shown 
in the Note - 26(I), 26(II), 26(III), 26(iv) and 26(v).
Details on project loans restructured during the 
year 2025 are stated in Note – 26(ii).
12.	
Employee Entitlements
Employee entitlements to salaries and wages, 
pre-retirement leave and other similar benefits 
have been recorded when they actually accrue 
to or utilized by the employees. Retired 
Government employee entitlements for pension 
payments are also recorded on the same basis.
13.	
Contingent Liabilities & 	
	
	
	
Commitments
Contingent 
Liabilities 
and 
Commitments 
are recorded at the point of contingency or 
commitment is evident. Rs. 1,080,182,693,483 
was recorded in 2025 and Rs. 1,454,254,752,096 
was recorded in 2024. (Schedule I) 
14.	
Comparatives
To ensure consistency with the current period 
and classification method adopted in making 
a fair presentation of financial information, 
comparative figures have been restated where 
appropriate.
15.	
Cash & Cash Equivalents / Bank 	
	
	
Overdrafts
The Cash & Cash Equivalents comprises of 
all favorable balances and bank overdrafts 
comprises all unfavorable balances which 
include cash book balances for the bank 
accounts operated in the name of the Deputy 
Secretary to the Treasury, sum of unsettled 
imprest balances of Ministries and Departments 
which are treated as cash in transit and rupee 
equivalent amount of all foreign currency 
bank accounts balances as at end of the 
reporting period. When there is an Over Draft, 
it is considered for the Borrowing Limit of the 
respective year.
16.	
Non-Financial Assets
All non-financial assets i.e. Property, Plant and 
Equipment is recognized at cost or grant value. 
The cost includes expenditure that is directly 
attributable to the acquisition of the items.
In a situation, where an assets is acquired in 
a non-exchange transaction on free of charge 
or nominal consideration, the asset is initially 
measured at its grant value or cost. The 
corresponding credit is recognized as income 
in the statements of Financial Performance 
unless there are conditions on the assets’ use.
Capital work in progress includes cost of 
buildings under development as at the Balance 
Sheet date.
The 
Government 
derecognizes 
items 
of

Property, Plant and Equipment upon disposal.
The sales proceeds received upon disposal of 
non-financial assets is recognized as revenue. 
17.	
Leases
The Government as a lessee, finance lease are 
leases that transfer substantially all the risk 
and benefits incidental to ownership of the 
leased asset to the Government. Assets held 
under a finance lease are capitalized at the 
commencement of the lease at the value of the 
leased asset. The Government also recognizes 
the associated lease liability at the inception of 
the lease. 
Operating leases are leases that do not transfer 
substantially all the risks and benefits incidental 
to ownership of the leased item to the 
Government. Operating lease made during the 
year are recognized as an operating expense in 
the Financial Performance Statement on cash 
basis over the lease term.
18.	
Intangible Assets
Intangible assets which are acquired separately 
are initially recognized at cost. The cost of 
intangible assets acquired in a non-exchange 
transaction is considered at their cost or grant 
value at the date of exchange and subsequently 
such intangible assets are carried at cost.
19.	
Advances
Advances consist of advances to Public Officers 
of the Government and provincial councils 
and to Government Departments through the 
treasury authorized advance account which is 
recognized on cash basis.
20.	
Sundry Accounts
Sundry Accounts consist of main ledger 
accounts operated for special purposes.
21.	
Prior Year Adjustment
During the current financial year, an exchange 
loss amounting to Rs. 3,862,677,744 relating 
to the financial year ended 31 December 
2024 in respect of Foreign Loan Adjustment 
Accounts, was identified as having not been 
recognized in the financial statements of that 
year. Accordingly, the error has been corrected 
retrospectively. 
As a result, the comparative figures for the year 
ended 31 December 2024 have been restated, 
and the opening balance of retained earnings 
as at 1 January 2025 has been reduced by Rs. 
3,862,677,744.

Treasury Bond Face Value

method on reporting Treasury Bonds 
was revised from the year 2016.

value, and required adjustments 
have 
been

accordingly.

discount value of the Treasury 
bonds issued prior to 2016.

Infrastructure Development

amount

out of the expenditure incurred

identified as the Government’s 
investment 
in 
infrastructure 
development. Such amount is 
reported in the Financial Position 
under

on 
Public

5.1.1 	
Investment in shares of the Canwill 
Holdings (Pvt) Ltd
In terms of Cabinet Decision No. 
23/1899/604/187 dated 09 October 
2023, issued pursuant to the Cabinet 
Memorandum titled “Mechanism to 
Transfer the Investment in Subsidiaries 
of Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation 
to the Secretary to the Treasury,” the 
ownership of Canwill Holdings (Pvt) Ltd 
held by Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation 
(SLIC) was transferred to the Secretary 
to the Treasury in 2024. Accordingly, 
1,085,294,117 
shares, 
representing 
52.05% of the Company’s issued share 
capital, were issued to the Secretary to 
the Treasury at a designated value of Rs. 
10,399,358,000. This amount remains 
receivable from the General Treasury in 
the books of SLIC.
Further, in terms of Cabinet Decision 
No. 
25/1273/804/097-I 
dated 
13 
July 2025, based on the Cabinet 
Memorandum titled “Transfer of Shares 
Held by Litro Gas Lanka Ltd in Canwill 
Holdings (Pvt) Ltd to the Secretary to 
the Treasury,” approval was granted to 
transfer the shareholding of Litro Gas 
Lanka Ltd in Canwill Holdings (Pvt) Ltd 
to the Secretary to the Treasury at a 
carrying value of Rs. 5,000,000,000. 
The corresponding amount remains 
receivable from the General Treasury 
as at 31 December 2025 in the books of 
Litro Gas Lanka Ltd.
Moreover, 
in 
terms 
of 
Cabinet 
Memorandum No. 25/2327/804/097-IV 
dated 21 November 2025, submitted by 
the Hon. Minister of Finance, Planning 
and 
Economic 
Development, 
and 
the corresponding Cabinet Decision 
dated 15 December 2025 regarding 
the acquisition of shares held by the 
Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) in 
Canwill Holdings (Pvt) Ltd, the Secretary 
to the Treasury acquired the entire EPF 
shareholding of 500,000,000 shares for 
a consideration of Rs. 5,000,000,000. 
This consideration was settled during 
2025.
Accordingly, upon completion of the 
above transactions, the Secretary to the 
Treasury became the sole shareholder 
of Canwill Holdings (Pvt) Ltd, holding 
100% of the issued share capital of the 
Company.

Treasury to pay an appropriate amount 
of interest subsidy to the NSB from the 
total interest subsidy calculated on the 
low yield held to maturity portfolio as of 
31st March 2023, to ensure the solvency 
of the Bank.

06.	
Nature and Purpose of Reserves	
	
The Government creates and maintains 
reserves in terms of specific local 
requirements.
07. 	
Consolidated Fund 
	
The funds of the Republic not allocated 
by law to specific purposes form the 
Consolidated Fund into which shall be 
paid the produce of all taxes, levies, rates 
and duties and all other revenues and 
receipts of the Republic not allocated to 
specific purposes.
08. 	 Contingency Fund
	
A Fund Created by Parliament by law for 
the purpose of providing for urgent and 
unforeseen expenditure.
09. 	 General Fund 
	
The 
balance 
of 
the 
General 
Fund 
represents 
the 
cumulative 
financial 
performance of the Government after 
accounting for all receipts and payments 
through the Consolidated Fund and 
the adjustments recorded in Nominal 
Accounts. Surpluses or deficits arising 
during the reporting period are reflected 
directly in the General Fund balance.
10. 	
Foreign Loan Adjustment Accounts
	
Accounts created for recording loan 
receipts 
and 
reimbursements 
for 
expenditure incurred.
11. 	
Public Service Provident Fund Account
	
A Fund established to afford Provident 
Fund benefits to those public servants 
who are not pensionable.
12. 	
Teachers Widows Orphans Pension Fund
	
A fund established for the payment of 
pension to widowers and orphans of 
teachers who are entitled to the payment 
of pension under the Minutes of pension.
